News.title: Spies catch Russian hitman who ‘planned to kill popular rapper helping launch drone strikes on Moscow’
News.content:
SHADOW WAR Spies catch Russian hitman who ‘planned to kill popular rapper helping launch drone strikes on Moscow’

SPIES have caught a Russian hitman who allegedly planned to kill a popular rapper helping launch drone strikes on Moscow.

The suspected assassin was allegedly dispatched by Russian intelligence to “execute” Ukrainian-American rapper Slevin Dadyan, 34, in a chilling bid to silence the Kremlin’s alleged enemy.



Polish security services swooped on the 29-year-old Russian national in Warsaw after allegedly foiling the sinister plot.

He was detained last Friday in Mokotow, a residential district just south of central Warsaw, by the capital’s counterterrorism and homicide police.



Polish authorities said the suspect was allegedly acting on orders from a Russian intelligence agency and was plotting to kill the US and Ukrainian citizen.

It comes after at least 13 people died when Ukrainian drones blasted around 20 Wildberries houses last month.



Ukraine has intensified its attacks on Wildberries facilities this month, launching strikes on 11 hubs that inflicted major damage on seven.

The strikes on the regime’s biggest online marketplace are part of Volodymyr Zelensky‘s cunning plan to cripple the logistics operation that supplies Russia‘s military with drone parts and other equipment.

Dadyan, formerly known as Albert Vasilyev, performs under the alias Kyivstoner and has been accused by Russia’s Federal Security Service of masterminding the “logistics of delivering drones to the Moscow region”.

The FSB claims the deadly drones were destined for attacks on “strategic facilities” in Moscow and its sprawling surroundings.



Polish media reported the alleged weapons pipeline ran from Slovakia through Poland and Belarus before reaching the Moscow region.

Moscow has since branded Dadyan an extremist and terrorist, adding the rapper to its notorious blacklist.

The Kremlin also accuses him of working with Ukrainian security services – claims the musician flatly denies.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the country’s ABW domestic intelligence service had smashed the alleged hit plot at the last minute.

“We must assume that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient [to it] for various reasons, in various places around the world,” he said.



Tusk refused to expose further details, saying the explosive investigation remains live.

Polish authorities are also believed to have received assistance from their US counterparts.

Dadyan first rocketed to fame through a string of viral comedy videos before becoming one of the founders of Ukrainian band Hryby.



He later stormed into a solo career as Kyivstoner, while also appearing in films.

Before Putin unleashed his full-scale invasion in 2022, Dadyan spent years in Moscow and worked with Russian rap star Vasily Vakulenko, known as Basta.

His activities in Russia during the annexation of Crimea and the war in Donbas had already drawn fierce criticism in Ukrainian media.

But when Putin launched his widespread conflict in February 2022, Dadyan fled Kyiv with his young son and wife for the US.

He remained there for two years before saying publicly from 2024 that he was living with his family in Slovakia.



The rapper has continued making music while also pursuing e-sports and competitive gaming.

In an interview last September, Dadyan took aim at President Zelensky while making clear he condemned Moscow’s aggression and supported Ukrainians fighting Russia.

The alleged hit plot comes as Poland battles an intensifying wave of Russian espionage, sabotage and so-called “greyzone” warfare.



Polish security officials say the country is now facing daily hostile incidents, with cyberattacks having rocketed since Russia’s full-scale invasion.

The sinister campaign has already included the murder of Russian satirical artist Semyon Skrepetsky in Poland, sabotage of a crucial railway route linking Warsaw with the east and a Russian cruise missile crashing in the Lublin region.

Skrepetsky, a fierce critic of Putin, was gunned down on June 15 in Biała Podlaska in the Lublin Voivodeship.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

His attacker allegedly walked up and fired twice before stepping closer and unleashing three more shots at point-blank range as the stricken artist lay on the ground.

Now the thwarted plot against Dadyan has thrust Poland into the crosshairs of an increasingly brazen Kremlin espionage war.

News.title: Andy Burnham cannot afford to ignore huge public anger over release of PC Harper’s killers any longer
News.content:
PM’s deaf ears

MORE than one million people have now signed the petition demanding the remorseless killers of PC Andrew Harper stay locked up.

Andy Burnham cannot afford to ignore such a massive swell of public outrage.



The still new Prime Minister says he is “increasingly confident” he can find a fix to stop them being freed under Labour’s catastrophic early release scheme.

That isn’t good enough.



For as long as thugs Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers have hope of getting out, PC Harper’s family will still suffer.

This has become a huge first test of Burnham’s leadership and he is fluffing it.

So far, he has presided over a shambles that has sown anguish and confusion.

There are only a few short weeks for the PM and his officials to get their act together and free up jail places before the mass release of hardened criminals.

Prison experts are already warning of a wave of rape and murder to come.

If Burnham continues to get this wrong, he will pay a heavy political price.



Bungle? You bet

DOES anyone in Labour understand the real reasons behind the decline of our High Streets?

Andy Burnham went on a tour of the country this week promising to listen to voters’ concerns.

Bizarrely, he then decided betting shops were the root of all evil and has set about cutting the already dwindling number of them.

Even in his own constituency there is widespread bafflement at his attack on bookies and the bizarre comparison with vape shops.

As one punter in Ashton in Makerfield said of the Government yesterday: “They don’t know what they are doing. No one forces anyone to have a bet.”



Burnham claims to be a champion of sport and the working classes.

But if he is capable of misjudging the mood in his own back yard, what chance have the rest of us got?

Zero sense

THE Green lobby has been out in force claiming the heatwave-fuelled wildfires in Stourbridge and the East Sussex train derailment prove we must spend £400billion on Net Zero.

Few argue with the need for Britain to adapt to changes in the climate.

But it’s insane to chuck so much taxpayers’ cash at renewable schemes that don’t work.



Solar panels often don’t operate in extreme heat and wind farms don’t work when it doesn’t blow. Electricity from both cannot be stored.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Until these systems become more reliable, we will need the oil and gas currently sitting untouched under the North Sea.

That’s not climate change denial. It’s basic common sense.

News.title: Donald Trump is having a terrible summer… now he’s staring down a make-or-break test without one of his best players
News.content:
DONALD TRUMP is having a terrible summer.

The President’s “six-week” war in the Middle East is now entering its sixth month and the Iranians are playing the once-famed dealmaker like a cat with a big ball of orange yarn.



Talks have ground to a halt, just as they did with Vladimir Putin over Ukraine.

The mad mullahs are openly mocking the President one day and trying to whack him the next.



No nuclear deal has emerged, and the Strait of Hormuz remains a daily tinder box with knock-on costs reverberating far beyond the region.

Western missile stocks are depleted to a dangerous degree, and while petrol prices have stabilised a bit, US debt was sold off at a 25-year high on Thursday.

And voters are feeling the pain, with mortgage interest rates hitting 6.69 per cent this week, the highest since Joe Biden was in office.

Promises of a “springtime boom for the US economy” have drained away quicker than Trump’s botched attempt to “beautify” DC’s famous reflecting pool by hiring some pool guys he knew.

I won’t be the first, or last, to see the obvious metaphor in the leader of the free world having to dodge a potential rocket attack by hiding in a catering truck as he was squirrelled off Air Force One. But it sums up how the President got himself into this mess.

Relying on Israeli intelligence of a perceived threat, trapped, literally, in a situation of his own making, while a hostile media screech and mock.



And just when he probably needed her the most, Karoline Leavitt — the pint-sized pugilist who has become the second most famous blonde in the White House with her combative outings at the press podium — threw in the towel.

Pals insist it had nothing to do with the fact the mum-of-two was left on the Air Force One in Turkey, when the President was removed by the Secret Service, leaving the rest as potential sitting ducks.

But the timing of her announcement — in the same week as the Ankara airport farce rocked Washington — has certainly been the source of much chitchat over here.



Leavitt was at the President’s side for arguably the most glittering portion of his now decade-long foray into politics.

Pushing the lawfare narrative outside yet another courtroom as Trump’s enemies on the Left tried to jail him rather than fight him at the ballot box proved to be political catnip.

And she sacked off her first maternity leave in the aftermath of Trump dodging death in July 2024.

Even diehard Trump-haters have given up trying to argue she is anything but a commanding presence in the briefing room, and an ace in his pack.

But now he’s staring down a make-or-break electoral test without one of his best players.



With the countdown to November’s midterms now weeks rather than months, by now White House strategists wanted to be talking up domestic wins, not bogged down in what is looking like the latest “forever war”.

And it could get much, much worse in the coming weeks.

The usually suave Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent looks like he hasn’t slept for days, after he raided billions from America’s foreign currency reserves to help prop up the flailing Japanese yen.



A casualty of the global instability that Trump’s war in Iran is reaping on the world, the Japanese have the US by the short and curlies again.

Holding more than a trillion dollars of US debt, threats to start a fire sale of bonds unless the US Treasury helped Tokyo stabilise their currency by buying lots of it saw Bessent forced into action.

It’s not immediately clear it will work for very long, however, with a massive risk of huge interest-rate rises in an election year if it does not.

The irony is, if it were not for Iran, Trump might be looking at some good ground to fight the midterms due to the US Left taking a look at what Jeremy Corbyn did to Labour in Britain, and saying, “We will have some of that.”

Hard-left candidates have been selected in key Senate races, only for it to emerge they fathered children with their second cousin, like the odd chap in Maine, or the candidate who believes God is trans and barbecue is dangerous — in Texas, of all places.



Or take Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who says American football is “toxic”, wants to ban fireworks on the 4th of July and cancel Thanksgiving.

But some of Trump’s supporters seem more interested in tearing strips off each other, perhaps with some sympathy for the increasingly prominent Democratic Socialists of America due to a shared passion for hating Israel.

While Trump’s been quick to scream about communism and socialism, it is far from clear voters will heed his warnings.

It appears JD Vance, the Vice President seeking to get his own rocky few months back on track and who has long warned the administration should focus on the “home front”, does not believe so yet.

He told Fox News: “My warning to my fellow Republicans is you don’t stop socialism by throwing slogans at people about the free market. You stop socialism by making people’s lives better.”



Ouch. Especially with just 12 weeks to polling day.

IT’S Passport to Piddington!

The leafy Oxfordshire hamlet of just 370 has voted to leave the United Kingdom over Andy Burnham’s punish-the-posh strategy of tipping 1,250 boat migrants in their backyard.

As council leader Tim McNally explained to The Sun: “We are going down to the US Embassy and will bring our declaration to them.

“Donald Trump loves old, quaint English villages, but he’s not so keen on migrants,” chimed in his colleague Joe Marshall.



Given that their referendum faces some fairly steep legal issues, I fear the patriots of Piddington may have to up their game.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In 1822, the fine folk of Hastings, East Sussex, in a tax dispute with the Crown, declared an 8.5-acre patch of the town the 24th state of the newly created United States of America.

They raised the Stars and Stripes and held out for a whopping 12 years before the government sent in the heavies.

News.title: Bus drivers demand air-con on vehicles as they go on strike & warn extreme heat may lead to fatal crashes
News.content:
BUS drivers went on strike yesterday as they warned that extreme heat in their cabs could lead to fatal crashes.

About 1,500 Arriva North London drivers with union Unite started two days of action, one of 11 planned by mid-October.



They want more air-con in buses.

Driver Peter Skinner, 56, said: “I know a lady at another garage who passed out as she stepped out of a cab.



“She was pregnant.

“How long before that happens at the wheel?



“Think of the carnage of a 14-ton bus with 80 people in it.”

Peter Crane, 62, showed a photo of his cab temperature reading 44C (111F).

He said: “We’re so fed up, we get into the bus, and it’s absolutely boiling.

“It makes you drowsy. It makes you feel a bit uncomfortable. You’re sweating, you’re sticky.



“It’s like, you get off a plane, you go to Greece or Spain or something.”

“It’s like being in a greenhouse. That’s my life. You can’t walk out. It’s not like an air-conditioned office. Not like our bosses, our directors, who are driving by with what we need, air-con in a car, it’s cool.

“We just want the same thing. Why can’t we have air-con? Why can’t we be comfortable and safe?

Unite said driving conditions this summer have been some of the worst ever, despite union warnings 18 months ago.

Arriva London said: “We are continuing to upgrade air-con and new buses.”

News.title: Andy Burnham accused of ‘bypassing’ locals to fast-track new migrant camps at army bases
News.content:
PM ANDY Burnham has been blasted for “bypassing” local communities’ opinions to open migrant camps.

Planning permission for two controversial sites at disused Army bases are to be signed off by Housing Secretary Angela Rayner instead of local planning committees.



The fast-tracked process can be used for projects deemed to be of national importance — but multiple MPs have branded the move undemocratic.

There is no requirement for a formal public consultation, but applications must still “engage with the community”.



It comes after the PM said middle-class areas needed to “play their part” and take in more asylum seekers, even if that is more costly.

Nick Timothy, the Tory MP for West Suffolk, near the RAF Barnham site, said the process was being used to “cut out local people”.

Terry Jermy, the Labour MP for South West Norfolk, said: “The risk for the current government is that we are quite rightly focusing on devolution and power to local communities and this process would seem to be the opposite to that.

“There’s a contradiction in our approach.”

Calum Miller, the Liberal Democrat MP for Bicester & Woodstock, called it “an affront to democracy”.

He added: “The government is deliberately bypassing the views of local representatives and people to ram this through.



“Andy Burnham has said that the era of Whitehall dictating to communities is over. This is his chance to show that he means it.”

A government spokesperson said it was “ensuring members of the public will be able to submit their views” and pointed to their commitment to ending the use of asylum hotels.

News.title: Soldiers to be sent in & help firefighters battling blazes sweeping tinderbox Britain as crews struggle with incidents
News.content:
SOLDIERS will help 999 crews tackle wildfires as they struggle with dozens of devastating outbreaks.

PM Andy Burnham announced the move as his Government declared a temporary ban on the sale of disposal barbecues blamed for a series of blazes this summer.



Around 100 military personnel are being sent to provide support after South Wales Fire and Rescue Service said it was dealing with 30 fires affecting areas including Blaenavon and Porth.

It requested military assistance to provide “additional logistical and defensive tactical support” after days of intense operational demand.



Mr Burnham said: “That support is critically needed.”

Fire and rescue services in differing parts of the country have already been sharing crews.



But the PM said the sheer number of incidents meant the usual system risked being stretched.

At 7pm last night, the Government sent a rare emergency alert to every mobile phone in England and Wales, warning of the risk of activities that could spark flames.

Mr Burnham said the request came directly from fire services. But some mocked the message’s tone. Tory MP Neil O’Brien wrote: “Thought WW3 was about to kick off but it is just a message saying not to set stuff on fire. Bizarre.”

Meanwhile, the temporary ban on selling the disposable grills was announced by the Business department, which ruled they “cannot be considered a safe product”.



As 999 teams continued to tackle wildfires, the Prime Minister said: “Britain is a tinderbox right now.

“Setting a fire in any outdoor setting of any kind is a risk to other people’s homes. It’s a risk to other people’s lives. Don’t do it. Please don’t do it.”

Mr Burnham had first suggested a ban on Wednesday — but did not go through with it until yesterday, the day after fires tore through homes in the West Midlands.



He also argued the UK must face up to the “changing climate” and transition to “more clean energy”.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the ban in England, Scotland and Wales was a “common-sense step to protect lives and the environment”.

All retailers will receive guidance on the change, which will be kept under review. Some supermarkets had halted sales voluntarily.

The rule came after an emergency Cobra meeting and was announced while the PM visited residents forced to flee their homes as an “apocalyptic” inferno ripped through their street.

“Up to 300 had to be evacuated due to the ­ferocious blaze, which engulfed around 40 acres of land close to Stourbridge Golf Club, West Midlands, on Thursday.



It left at least 19 people in hospital, including a child and three firefighters, as residents fled with only minutes to spare.

Nineteen houses have been destroyed and 18 damaged, West Midlands Fire Service said.

Last night, some locals blamed teens celebrating A-level results.



A TikTok craze sees some youngsters torching study notes.

Around 100 firefighters had ­battled flames which raced through tinder-dry grass and woodland before reaching properties.

Devastated families returned to find homes reduced to charred shells and all possessions destroyed.

Among the worst hit were Gordon and Pauline Addis, and Gordon’s daughter Jo Egan, whose two semi-detached cottages were devastated after flames swept across fields behind them.

Gordon and Pauline managed to escape with their dog Chester, but the family was unable to reach Jo’s two cats, Hooper and Brody, who are feared to have died.



Gordon, in his 70s, suffered burns to his arm and neck and was taken to hospital before later being discharged.

His daughter Gina Addis said: “The fire spread rapidly from the fields behind and they were lucky to escape with their lives. Both houses have been devastated beyond repair . . . everything is gone — their belongings, their memories and the places they felt safe.

“We also believe that my sister’s two beloved cats have sadly ­perished, which has added even more heartbreak to an already ­devastating situation.”



One resident commented: “The fire was apocalyptic. I’ve never seen anything like it in my life.”

Members of a riding school said their “legs were burning” as they raced to rescue eight horses.

And local Emmerald Morrall described eight hours of “absolute chaos, panic and fear”.

She said: “The street was full of bewildered people, dogs panting in the heat. It was like a disaster movie.”

Thursday’s drama was not restricted to Stourbridge, with a series of wildfires across the nation.



Crews battled 11 major incidents, including in Birmingham and Stoke-on-Trent.

Two people have been arrested on suspicion of arson.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Meanwhile, Mr Burnham will today pledge a £65million funding boost to help farmers after the ­driest July on record.

Visiting a farm in the South West, he will say: “The ability to grow our own food is national security, and I will treat it that way.”

News.title: Cambridge Vice-Chancellor ‘desperately saddened’ after former Professor Jason Arday found dead at home
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

PROF TRIBUTE Cambridge Vice-Chancellor ‘desperately saddened’ after former Professor Jason Arday found dead at home

CAMBRIDGE Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice has been left “desperately saddened” after former professor Jason Arday was found dead.

Dr Arday, 41, was discovered “unresponsive” at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.



He was later pronounced dead at the scene.

Professor Prentice has now paid tribute to the former Cambridge academic following his death.



She said: “We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news.

“Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”



Education Secretary Lucy Powell took to X to say she was “deeply shocked and saddened” to hear of Dr Arday’s death.

She offered her “heartfelt” condolences to his friends and family.



Cops were called by the London Ambulance Service at 3.12pm on Friday.

A Met spokesman said: “Sadly, a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene.

“His next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by officers.

“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.

“The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s Central South Command Unit.



“A file will be prepared for the coroner.”

In a statement issued through his publisher Simon & Schuster UK, his family paid tribute to him as an “amazing” and “gentle man”.

His family added that Jason always wanted to “see the best in everyone”.

The statement added: “We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son.

“We won’t comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now.”



It comes after a turbulent few weeks for Dr Arday, who was at the centre of a high-profile dispute having been accused of plagiarising from other students for his PhD thesis.

On August 5, Dr Arday resigned as professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge.

Last week, Cambridge launched an investigation into Dr Arday’s appointment and tenure at the university.

Dr Arday, who became the university’s youngest black professor in 2023, also came under fire after critics accused him of stealing research.

An initial investigation into the professor’s “appointment and tenure” was launched last week.

Dr Arday resigned just a few hours after the university announced the investigation, citing the “unrelenting level of public scrutiny”.

News.title: Jason Arday, ex-Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row, found dead
News.content:
Jason Arday, the former University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row, has been found dead.

Emergency services said a man was found "unresponsive" at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.

Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week after allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He had denied the claims.

Arday's family said in a statement that they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

On Friday, police officers were called by the London Ambulance Service. A 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene and his next of kin have been informed, the Metropolitan Police said.

In a statement, the Met Police said: "At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious."

Cambridge University vice-chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice said: "We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news".

"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time", she said.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" to hear about the death and she urged people to "remember there are real people with loved ones involved".

Arday, 41, had denied any plagiarism - but admitted errors in his work - and last week said the recent controversy about his work had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in Prof Arday's work.

There were also questions around Arday's claims that he ran 30 marathons in 35 days, and 300 miles in three days for charity, which Arday said had raised more than Â£5m for charity, as well as running 600 miles on a treadmill in six days.

Arday said some errors in his early academic work was because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. Similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics, he said.

"We're talking about academia here. I didn't murder somebody. I think the cruelty that I've experienced and the positioning of me as this kind of liar and fantasist is totally unacceptable," he told the Times newspaper, external earlier this month.

Arday's appointment as Cambridge's youngest ever black professor at the age of 37 in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment.

Announcing his resignation last week, Arday said the "personal cost" of the scrutiny of him had become "too great".

He said: "While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement.

"The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

He stressed that his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

Cambridge initially said claims of plagiarism regarding Arday's thesis and some journal publications had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University (LMJU) and the journals in question.

LJMU - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.

Earlier this week, Cambridge announced an independent investigation into his appointment.

In a letter to university staff at the time, Prof Prentice said: "I fully understand the concerns being raised across the university and well beyond it, regarding Jason Arday's appointment and I share them...

"That investigation, as you say, should be thorough and transparent, and will be carried out independently by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge."

Arday originally worked as a PE teacher before earning his doctorate at LMJU and going on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.

Glasgow university also announced a review into Arday's previous academic work.

When news of his death emerged, the university said in a statement it was "shocked and saddened" by the death of a former colleague.

"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with his friends and family at this desperately sad time." it added.

Durham University, another of Arday's former employers, described him as "a kind and warm person, who actively sought to promote opportunities for PhD students".

Last weekend, Arday cancelled an event promoting his forthcoming memoir.

Publisher Simon & Schuster previously said that the book, Great And Unfortunate Things, would be published in the UK on 27 August. It was released in the US earlier this week.

The book tells the story of his life from being non-verbal until the age of 11 and unable to read or write until 18, then going through a series of "improbable triumphs and heartbreaking setbacks", before being appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge.

News.title: Fires prompt national alert as 19 homes destroyed
News.content:
Fires across England and Wales have prompted a national government alert warning people not to light anything that could spark a wildfire.

The warning on Friday evening came as it was revealed 19 homes were destroyed and a further 18 damaged in a huge fire in Stourbridge, West Midlands, that spread rapidly through grass and woodland on Thursday before damaging homes.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told members of the public to take the warning "seriously", adding it was triggered at the request of firefighters.

West Midlands Fire Service chief fire officer Simon Tuhill said the Stourbridge blaze was one of the most significant incidents the service had ever dealt with.

It was one of several fires being dealt with across England and Wales on Friday.

In Wales, a major incident was declared near Llandovery, Carmarthenshire, after dozens of homes were evacuated and roads closed

In Hampshire, firefighters spent a sixth day tackling a wildfire in the New Forest, Hampshire, which broke out on Sunday.

Sixteen emergencies were tackled by Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service on Thursday afternoon, including a fire at Mousehold Heath, off Gurney Road in the city.

Elsewhere in the West Midlands fires caused extensive damage in Warstock and Kings Norton, Birmingham on Thursday. A 55-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of arson with intent to endanger life .

In Stoke-on-Trent on Thursday four homes in Sandyford were destroyed, with other properties damaged. Two people were arrested on suspicion of arson. Six firefighters were taken to hospital due to smoke inhalation and heat exhaustion.

In Willenhall, West Midlands, at least three homes and several gardens were destroyed in fires on Stonehouse Avenue and Harry Perks Street.

Investigators said they were working with other emergency services to establish how the Stourbridge fire started, with police saying they were keeping an open mind.

Some of the worst-affected areas have been cordoned off and many residents who were evacuated, including the Bishop of Dudley, the Right Reverand Martin Gorick, have not been able to return home.

News.title: Temporary ban on sale of disposable BBQs over wildfire risk
News.content:
"We have a fire and rescue service across the country that isn't properly set up to deal with these incidents," Burnham said.

"We don't have the capability in the way that we should have to fight these fires.

"There's thousands of firefighters out there today doing back-breaking work, in full kit, in the most difficult conditions", he added.

He said the UK must face up to the "changing climate" and transition to "more clean energy".

His comments came ahead of the appointment of Baroness Blake of Leeds as fire minister.

Friends of the Earth urged the prime minister to tackle the "root cause" of the "climate emergency" that is fuelling this summer's extreme weather events.

"Without urgent action to curb the carbon emissions driving this crisis, future heatwaves, droughts and wildfires will only get worse and the ability for future generations to adapt will disappear" the environmental group warned.

Burnham was speaking during a visit to Stourbridge to see the impact of a devastating blaze.

As the UK experienced its hottest day of the year on Thursday, residents fled their homes when fires spread through dry grass and tore through houses.

West Midlands Ambulance Service said it treated 54 casualties at eight different fires across the region. Nineteen people were taken to hospital for treatment.

In 2025, fire and rescue services in England and Wales broke a new record when they responded to nearly 1,000 wildfire incidents, with the NFCC warning at the time that climate change is increasing their risk and severity.

The conditions the UK is experiencing so far this summer also mirror the warnings given by climate scientists that human-induced climate change would lead to more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as potential summer droughts.

In England, the Rugby Football Union has delayed the start of the community rugby season because of concerns about player welfare and pitch conditions because of the drought conditions.

News.title: Mangione admits killing healthcare CEO and pleads guilty to federal charges
News.content:
Mangione had initially pleaded not guilty in both the federal and state cases against him for the shooting death of Thompson.

At a hearing in Manhattan federal court on Friday, Mangione's lawyers announced that he intended to plead guilty to the two federal charges against him.

Wearing a beige prison outfit, Mangione appeared solemn and serious throughout the hearing.

Reading a statement aloud to the court, he admitted to planning the attack ahead of time, crossing state lines with the intent to kill and using a gun he printed on a 3-D-printer and equipped with a silencer and magazine.

He told the court he was driven to kill Thompson because of his experience with the healthcare system "after years of enduring severe pains from a broken back".

Mangione stated that he had learned UnitedHealthcare would hold an annual investor conference in Manhattan in December 2024.

He then travelled to New York for the event, he told the court.

He also said he emailed UnitedHealthcare prior to the conference "posing as an investor" and asking questions about the event.

"I emailed UnitedHealthcare with the intent to shoot Brian Thompson," Mangione said in his statement. "On the morning of Dec. 4, 2024 I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan in his back."

The sentencing for the federal charges is scheduled for 18 December.

Thompson's family said in a statement that they will continue to seek justice in both New York state and Pennsylvania, where Mangione was arrested.

"While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable.

"Now we look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime," the family added.

Prosecutors have recommended Mangione serve between 24-30 years in prison. But Judge Margaret Garnett said in court that she ultimately decides his sentence.

Garnett explained to Mangione that the recommendation is not binding and that the maximum sentence is life in prison along with financial penalities. There is no parole in the federal system.

News.title: Derailed Essex to London train leads to travel chaos
News.content:
Martin Frobisher, of Network Rail, said the summer's hot weather had "presented exceptional challenges to the railway".

In an interview with the BBC Transport Correspondent Katy Austin, Frobisher also confirmed speed restrictions were not in place in either Wickford or Lewes.

On the possible impact of the hot weather, he said "yes, that's one of the things that we're looking at.

"We've got our investigations underway. We've got technical engineers on site, our best experts who are on site with the Rail Accident Investigation Branch.

"They're looking very thoroughly at what's happened. And based on that, we will act on what we learn."

However, he added it was "too early to speculate on the full findings".

The investigation would specifically assess "whether or not this was weather-related", said Mark Francois, the Conservative MP for Rayleigh and Wickford.

The Department for Transport stressed Britain's railways were "among the safest in the world" as it reacted to the incident.

It said derailments were "incredibly rare" events.

An East of England Ambulance Service spokesperson said: "Our crews assessed 62 patients who were on board the train.

"Following assessment, all patients were discharged at the scene.

"We also assisted with the evacuation of a second train that was unable to continue its journey due to the derailment.

"There were no casualties among those on board."

A spokesperson for BTP also confirmed there were no reported injuries.

News.title: Chris Mason: Where does this unorthodox by-election victory leave Nigel Farage?
News.content:
It is a question prompting at least some debate within the party.

"When he goes down this angry route he doesn't help himself," the prominent Reform activist Tim Montgomerie told Radio 4's The World At One.

Montgomerie, the founder of the ConservativeHome website, defected to Reform two years ago. He praised Farage's political ability but added: "It's very frustrating how he's behaved today. He needs to get a grip of this problem."

Montgomerie argued Farage and Reform were at their best when they were more positive rather than "inward looking" and focused on "grievances."

The "grievances," as Montgomerie puts it, are real and legitimate, say Farage's friends.

In the short term at least and from a point of weakness I have previously written about, the by-election allowed Farage to get on the front foot and to frame an argument, as he saw it, as the people versus those out to get him.

Rubbish, say his critics, the rules apply to all MPs and the undeclared Â£5m gift from the billionaire businessman Christopher Harborne, in the months before Farage became an MP, should have been registered, they insist.

Talking to GB News in the early hours of this morning, before the result, Farage repeated a concession, of sorts, about this: "If I made one sin, it's that I haven't filled in a piece of paper.

"I've broken no law, I've broken no tax law, I've taken no public money. I don't even own a motor home. Maybe I haven't filled in a piece of paper. I'm confident I'm right - we'll see where we go."

He has long maintained he sought legal advice about whether he needed to declare the money and had been told he didn't.

The wider question is where Nigel Farage and Reform find themselves in the big picture politically and whether their current approach is a wise one.

There is early evidence of something of a Burnham bounce for Labour, which has disrupted Reform's long standing lead in the opinion polls.

And the Conservatives appear more chipper and competitive than a year ago too.

Then there is the rise of Restore Britain, run by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

Let's be clear: none of the political parties are wildly popular at the moment, but Reform's support has shrivelled a bit and their rivals are more upbeat.

The landscape for the new political season at Westminster is taking shape, ahead of MPs returning to the Commons in a few weeks.

Labour with a spring in its step, for now at least. Reform punchy but feeling under the cosh and plenty of the others scrapping for attention too.

It will be a fascinating few months ahead.

News.title: Britain's Finlay Tarling dies in Volta a Portugal accident
News.content:
British cyclist Finlay Tarling has died aged 19 after an accident during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany-Ineos rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on the road and track.

In a statement provided to local media, Major Tiago Machado of the National Republican Guard said there had been "a collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle" and that an investigation was under way.

The Welshman was competing for the NSN Development Team when the incident occurred on the 166.8km route from Melgaco to Fafe.

In a statement, NSN said: "We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.

"Fin was a much loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

"Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend."

In a post on X, the race organisers and the Portuguese Cycling Federation expressed their "most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his team-mates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones".

It added that the racing was stopped and the scheduled podium ceremony would not take place as a sign of "respect and mourning".

Portuguese president Antonio Jose Seguro added that Tarling's death had "plunged the peloton, the tournament and the host nation into mourning".

British Cycling's performance director Stephen Park, added: "All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal.

"Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man.

"Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh at this tragic time."

News.title: Bezos-backed consortium buys a third of Liverpool FC
News.content:
Liverpool's owners have agreed to sell about a third of the club to a consortium including billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

In a statement, Fenway Sports Group (FSG) confirmed it had entered into a "definitive agreement" for the sale of a "strategic minority investment" to 1892 Holdings.

The group is led by British-Indian millionaire businessman Amit Bhatia and also includes billionaire Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.

Bhatia is set to become Liverpool's vice-chairman, and will join an expanded board pending regulatory approval.

The son-in-law of Indian billionaire businessman Lakshmi Mittal, he had been a director and co-owner of Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before relinquishing his stake in the club last month.

American businessman Bezos, founder of e-commerce giant Amazon, is the fourth-richest person in the world, with an estimated net worth of $256bn (Â£192bn). This marks his first foray into sports ownership, although he will not join Liverpool's board.

However, Bryan Baum, founder of venture capital firm K5 Sports - through which Bezos is investing - will join the Anfield board, alongside Saverin's wife Elaine. Bezos is the biggest investor in K5 Sports.

BBC Sport has been told that the transaction will have no impact on the club's approach to the transfer window, and that there is no new or separate transfer budget associated with the investment.

The agreement includes an option for the consortium to increase its investment in the future. That suggests the group will be in pole position to become majority shareholders if Fenway wants to sell up, but according to one source, no commitments have been made to do so.

The deal is said to value the club between Â£5bn and Â£6bn.

News.title: Prisoners charged over attack on Sara Sharif's father
News.content:
Two prisoners have been charged with the attempted murder of fellow inmate Urfan Sharif who was jailed for killing his daughter Sara Sharif.

Steven Sansom, 47, and Adam Watson, 39, have also been charged with other offences relating to the incident in Belmarsh Prison on 1 January 2025, the Crown Prosecution Service said.

The men will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court for a first hearing on 26 August.

Sharif, 43, and Sara's stepmother Beinash Batool were sentenced to life imprisonment after being convicted at the Old Bailey for murdering 10-year-old Sara at their home in Woking, Surrey.

Sharif reportedly suffered cuts to his face during the attack, and received medical treatment at the prison.

Daren Streeter, deputy chief crown prosecutor at CPS London, said: "Our prosecutors have worked closely with the Metropolitan Police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and pursue criminal proceedings."

Sara was hooded, burned and beaten during a "campaign of torture" that lasted two years before her body was found at the family home in August 2023.

During the trial, Justice Cavanagh told the court "the degree of cruelty involved is almost inconceivable".

Urfan Sharif was sentenced to a minimum of 40 years in prison for murder, while his wife Beinash Batool, 30, received a minimum of 33 years.

Sara's uncle, Faisal Malik, 29, was sentenced to 16 years' imprisonment for causing or allowing her death.

The three fled to Islamabad, Pakistan, with Sara's five siblings, the day before her body was found, prompting an international manhunt.

They hid out there for four weeks before returning to the UK, where they were arrested.

News.title: Two dead after light aircraft crash
News.content:
Two people have died following a light aircraft crash in north Wales.

The aircraft was found in a remote location close to Trawsfynydd, Gwynedd, with the two people on board pronounced dead at the scene, North Wales Police said.

The force received reports shortly after 12:00 BST that a light aircraft travelling from an airfield in England had not arrived at Caernarfon Airport as scheduled.

Multi-agency air and ground searches were carried out until the aircraft was found.

A team of investigators have since been deployed by the Air Accidents Investigations Branch (AAIB).

News.title: Stephen Bear jailed over sex offender breaches
News.content:
Reality TV contestant Stephen Bear taunted police by "bragging" he was on a beach in Brazil while he breached his requirements as a sex offender, a court has heard.

He was not on the run during the trip last year, but under the rules of his registration requirements he was ordered to tell authorities about foreign travel.

Bear, 36, admitted five counts of failing to comply with the register notification requirements at Thames Magistrates' Court and was sentenced to 24 weeks in prison.

He is already in prison having been jailed on Thursday after admitting breaching a restraining order that banned him from posting online about his ex-partner Georgia Harrison.

News.title: Weekend cancellations after East Sussex train derailment
News.content:
Rail services on a busy line in the South East are being cancelled this weekend after a train carrying 150 people derailed in East Sussex.

Two passengers suffered serious injuries and 18 others were also hurt when three carriages of the train came off the tracks near Lewes on Thursday. Police have since said none of the casualties had life-threatening injuries.

Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) inspectors are at the scene gathering evidence, examining infrastructure and reviewing CCTV, signalling and train data.

The derailment was followed by another incident in Essex on Friday, when a Greater Anglia train came off the tracks near Wickford.

Train operator Southern Rail said trains between London Victoria and Eastbourne will be cancelled this weekend as the line between Haywards Heath and Lewes has been closed indefinitely in both directions.

Southern says Cooksbridge and Plumpton will also not be served all weekend, with rail replacement buses operating.

Eastbourne is expected to get a bumper number of visitors this weekend when the seaside town hosts its popular Airbourne air show.

The rail company has advised people to travel to Eastbourne along the coast via Brighton.

It has also urged commuters planning to travel on Monday to check for updates on its website, external on Sunday evening.

News.title: UK diplomats no longer get hardship bonus for being posted to Buenos Aires
News.content:
British diplomats in six locations around the world, including Buenos Aires and Santiago in South America, will no longer get hardship payments for working in dangerous cities.

Bonuses and respite breaks are granted to those working in cities considered risky, like Beirut in Lebanon, or with high crime, such as Pretoria in South Africa, or high air pollution in cities including New Delhi and Beijing.

The UK government has removed Santiago, in Chile, Panama City in Panama, Pyongyang in North Korea, Bamako in Mali, and Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in addition to the two south American cities, according to the latest list published last week, external.

The 144 locations still on the list include many trouble spots but also popular holiday destinations such as Bali and Rio De Janeiro, prompting criticism from the Conservatives.

Tory chairmanÂ­ Kevin HollinÂ­rake said civil servants receiving extra pay for working in such areas is unfair on the taxpayer.

The Foreign Office has given civil servants extra payments for working in areas where there is a high level of danger, or high risks to health, for the past 30 years.

They are meant to compensate staff and families for the additional costs and challenges of living overseas in difficult locations and are reviewed regularly.

Factors and risks covered by the allowance include security measures, climate, natural disaster, isolation and other impacts on quality of life.

Amounts are not routinely published but in 2009, the last time a breakdown was released, the highest payments for civil servants and their spouses were for postings to Karachi, Pakistan, which was worth an extra Â£26,647, or Â£14,804 in Abuja, the capital of Nigeria.

The hardship payment for being posted as part of a couple to Buenos Aires was Â£1,517 and Santiago was Â£777, according to the 2009 Diplomatic Services Allowances, external.

Answering a parliamentary question from Tory peer Lord Moylan, external, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield said assessments of hardship take into account factors that mean members of staff are required to take additional breaks for the benefit of their physical or mental health.

He added: "These arrangements are not new, and indeed have applied consistently under successive governments for a number of decades."

Bangkok, Cape Town, and Kuala Lumpur are still among the cities that qualify for hardship payments, alongside Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Muscat.

Hollinrake said it was unfair that taxpayers were "footing the bill" for these destinations and pledged to cut the size of the civil service if Conservatives were returned to power.

"Whilst businesses and families are paying higher taxes to fund this government's policies, civil servants are being sent on taxpayer-funded jollies to places like Bali, Cape Town and the Maldives," he said.

"This kind of nonsense has no place in government."

But the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office defended the scheme, with a spokesperson saying: "British diplomats serve their country around the globe, including in some of the toughest and most challenging physical and political environments in the world.

"We have a duty of care to ensure our staff are properly supported, and compensation and other provisions reflect the circumstances of the posting, as it would be in any private sector job."

News.title: Woman cleared of owning XL bully which fatally bit man
News.content:
A woman has been cleared of owning an XL bully dog that bit her partner's father, causing him to bleed to death.

Chanel Fong, 33, was accused of owning the dog, Cookie, which was dangerously out of control and of an alternative charge of being the person in charge of the animal at the time of the attack.

She was found not guilty of both by the jury at Caernarfon Crown Court.

Her partner's father, Keven Jones, 62, from Chester, died from severe blood loss after being bitten on the leg.

The attack took place before XL Bullies were added to the banned dog list.

The court heard Keven Jones had been in poor health and had been taking methadone and blood thinning medication, and had been staying at Fong's Wrexham home in May 2022.

Fong said the dog belonged to her partner Joshua Jones, who was not present when his father was bitten, although the prosecution claimed she was Cookie's joint owner.

The court was told there had been a number of dogs at the home on Holt Road in Wrexham, including two XL Bullies, called Fire and Rogue.

Rogue was Cookie's mother and in season at the time, so had to be kept separate from other dogs.

At about 11:30 BST on 23 May, Jones told Fong he would get Cookie and another dog in from the garden, but he was then heard shouting at Cookie to "get off" him.

The court heard Fong also called into the garden for Cookie to get down, which is when Jones came towards her "wobbly".

He pointed to his leg, which was pumping blood, and he said to Fong, "he's got me there".

Fong called the emergency services and attempted first aid, including applying pressure to the wound, but Jones could not be saved.

A post-mortem examination said he had died from extreme blood loss caused by dog bites.

Cookie was later humanely euthanised.

News.title: Sign of life as bright orange 'fire fungus' grows at park ravaged by wildfire
News.content:
A fungus that grows in places damaged by fire has been found at the site of a major wildfire in the Cairngorms National Park.

Forestry and Land Scotland (FLS) said the bright orange, pyrophilous (fire-loving) fungus could be the first sign of nature's recovery at Glenmore near Aviemore.

A wildfire started in the area on 15 July and the incident, which has burned through thousands of acres of woodland and moor, continues to be monitored for hotspots.

FLS said the fungus was among the "first colonisers" of burned ground and played a role in breaking down carbon and preventing soil erosion.

News.title: Mother jailed for killing baby by burning her with a hairdryer
News.content:
A mother who killed her baby daughter by burning her with a hairdryer has been jailed for six years.

Courtney Gartshore, 28, used the appliance to subject three-month-old Dahlia-Rose to "significant and sustained heat" on her head and body.

Emergency services were called to the scene at a property in Peterhead, Aberdeenshire, in September 2023, but the child had died.

Gartshore was convicted of culpable homicide - the closest equivalent to manslaughter in Scots Law - following a trial at the High Court in Aberdeen in July.

Warning: This article contains details readers may find upsetting

Sentencing Gartshore at the High Court in Edinburgh, judge Simon Collins KC told her, external she had inflicted "severe and disfiguring" burns on her daughter.

He said: "Given Dahlia-Rose's very young age, and the horrifying way that she died, this is a uniquely disturbing and distressing case.

"But it is tragic as well as terrible. And that is because the evidence suggested that the accused loved Dahlia-Rose, yet will have to live the rest of her life with the knowledge that she was responsible for her death."

Food and Drug Administration officials traveled to Mexico this week to inspect Taylor Farms’ operations there as part of the agency’s investigation into the nationwide cyclospora outbreak, according to a new report.

FDA investigators examined the processing facility where lettuce linked to the cyclospora outbreak — caused by a microscopic parasite that can trigger explosive diarrhea — was handled, sources told The Washington Post.

Investigators sought to reconstruct the conditions in which the leafy greens were grown and gathered, reviewing weather records and satellite imagery and gathering testing materials. They are also expected to inspect the site’s fields.

Former health officials and food safety experts said the agency should have traveled to Mexico sooner, rather than waiting weeks after public health officials linked the company’s shredded lettuce to the outbreak. It was reported earlier this week that inspectors hadn’t visited the Mexico location in the last seven years.

Some warned that evidence of the conditions that may have enabled the contamination could already have disappeared, further complicating the investigation. Taylor Farms said it suspended all production at the facility on July 18, and more than three million pounds of lettuce tied to the site has been recalled.

open image in gallery FDA officials visited Taylor Farms’ Mexico operation this week in connection to the current cyclospora outbreak, according to a new report ( Getty Images )

“Ideally, as soon as [the FDA] traced it back to the source, they would be out there working with the facility and specifically working with Taylor Farms to do a root-cause analysis so that we can understand what happened,” Barbara Kowalcyk, the director of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security told the outlet. “That’s really what’s going to drive prevention going forward.”

Mexican authorities conducted their own inspection of the site from July 18 through July 20, according to the Mexican government.

CBS News reported this week that Taylor Farms’ facility in the Guanajuato state linked to the outbreak had not been inspected by the FDA since 2019.

Since May 1, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has received reports of nearly 14,000 lab-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis, the illness caused by infection with the cyclospora parasite. Upwards of 10,000 additional cases may require further investigation.

By comparison, 1,180 cases were reported domestically between May and August 2025.

Hundreds of people nationwide have been hospitalized, and two deaths have been reported. Michigan has emerged as an epicenter, with more than 13,000 cases reported in the state alone.

The illness is typically linked to consuming food or water contaminated with feces and can cause diarrhea, vomiting, nausea and fever. Symptoms can take weeks to emerge and generally resolve on their own, according to the CDC.

open image in gallery A Taylor Farms spokesperson previously told The Independent that the company ‘immediately removed all potentially implicated product from the marketplace’ when questions arose about the source of the outbreak. ( Getty Images )

In an August 13 update, the FDA confirmed that it had begun inspections at Taylor Farms de Mexico.

“The outbreak includes people who reported exposure to processed iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico served or purchased at various locations, including people who previously reported eating at Taco Bell,” the health agency said. “Most of these illnesses began before the Taylor Farms de Mexico iceberg lettuce recall on July 17, 2026.”

The agency said it is “confident” that all recalled iceberg lettuce tied to the outbreak is now off the market.

A Taylor Farms spokesperson previously told The Independent that the company “immediately removed all potentially implicated product from the marketplace” when questions arose about the source of the outbreak.

“Out of an abundance of caution we issued an even broader recall of all iceberg lettuce sourced from the region,” the spokesperson added. “We have also voluntarily suspended all iceberg lettuce sourcing and production from central Mexico.”

The Independent has contacted the FDA and Taylor Farms for comment.

The homicide rate in the United States dropped to the lowest it's been in 75 years, according to an FBI report on 2025 crime statistics released Friday, which also showed overall violent crime dropped 9.3% last year.

Experts note that national violent crime rates have been declining since 2022, and pinpointing an exact reason is difficult. They say multiple factors contribute to decreases in crime rates seen in the FBI report, which is based on data reported voluntarily by many but not all law enforcement agencies across the country.

“The homicide drop is historic and crystal clear. But right now, what’s driving it is about as clear as a glass of milk,” said Adam Gelb, president and CEO of the Council on Criminal Justice, a think tank based in Washington.

“Rates are falling in cities with very different public safety strategies, economic conditions, and political leadership," Gelb said. "The consistency across the map should make us cautious about handing credit to any one leader, party, policy, or program before the evidence catches up.”

President Donald Trump announced the decreases in the annual crime numbers during a visit to a New York police academy Friday.

Trump proclaimed his role in lowering violent crime rates, taking a swing at his predecessor and at so-called sanctuary cities, while touting what he said was his overwhelming support of law enforcement and his tough-on-crime moves such as deploying the National Guard in Washington and elsewhere.

“We ended the war on police, and we declared a very strong war on crime,” Trump said during the Long Island appearance.

Regardless of the contributing factors, criminologists who have been tracking violent crime and property crime in a few dozen cities had been predicting that the homicide rate might drop to 4 per 100,000 residents, which would have dropped the rate to the lowest since 1900, when those rates began to be tracked.

The rate came close when the numbers from thousands of departments were calculated, reaching 4.1 homicides per 100,000 people. That rate is tied with 1955 and 1956, according to Friday's report, as the lowest rate since 1900.

The report showed murder and nonnegligent manslaughter decreased 18.1% between 2024 and 2025, while overall property crime declined by 12.4% during the same period.

Motor vehicle theft, which had spiked in 2022 and 2023 following a social media challenge that helped people exploit a manufacturing issue in some models of Kia and Hyundai vehicles, dropped by almost 23% to the lowest levels in more than 20 years.

In an unusual move just a few months before the midterm elections as many Republicans continue to tout the drop in crime, the FBI report also noted that violent and other crime has continued to drop during the first six months of 2026. The federal agency normally waits until all of the yearly data is reported to suggest a drop in crime.

Groups like the Council on Criminal Justice have also said 2026 could see an even larger decline than 2025, with homicides dropping 18% in those cities during the first six months of this year, compared with the same timeframe in 2025.

Crime surged during the coronavirus pandemic, with homicides increasing nearly 30% in 2020 over the previous year, the largest one-year jump since the FBI began keeping records. Violent crime across the U.S. dipped to near pre-pandemic levels around 2022.

The FBI collects standardized crime data from law enforcement agencies across the country through its Uniform Crime Reporting Program, though not all agencies participate. The 2025 report includes data from more than 17,000 agencies, or more than 87% of the agencies in the FBI's program, serving communities including almost 329 million Americans.

Hours after Japanese war planes bombed Pearl Harbor and military installations across Oʻahu on December 7, 1941, martial law fell over the Hawaiian Islands.

The military took control of the territory almost overnight. And the FBI, which had a list of suspects, began arresting people, including American citizens who had committed no crime.

Within two years, in March 1943, the largest and longest-operating of Hawaiʻi’s 17 known wartime detention sites opened in a remote, sweltering gulch in central Oʻahu. It closed three years later.

The prisoners who lived at Honouliuli gave it a bitter nickname: Jigoku Dani, or “Hell Valley” in Japanese, for the heat that pooled, windless, at the bottom of the ravine.

This year marks 80 years since Honouliuli closed. On July 18, for the first time, the National Park Service opened its gates to the public in a pilot program. Free guided tours by a rotation of a dozen docent volunteers are held for up to 22 people once a month through the end of the year. More than 1,800 are already on the waiting list.

“I don’t want local kids growing up not knowing that this happened in Hawaiʻi,” said Christine Ogura, superintendent with the National Park Service, in charge of Honouliuli since 2021. “It didn’t just happen on the mainland.”

Selective Incarceration

Executive Order 9066 was signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on February 19, 1942. It gave the military authority to remove people from designated areas of the country, and became the basis for forcibly relocating and incarcerating roughly 120,000 Japanese Americans on the West Coast and farther inland. This mainland incarceration is the story many know.

While most of the more than 2,000 Japanese Americans arrested in Hawaiʻi after Pearl Harbor were shipped to camps on the continent, roughly 400 were held in Hawaiʻi – first at a camp on Sand Island, and eventually at Honouliuli. The location was chosen because of its close proximity to Schofield Barracks.

By the time it closed, the 160 acres of Honouliuli had also become the territory’s largest prisoner of war camp, holding close to 4,000 people at once.

Most of those POWs were not Japanese soldiers at all, but Koreans and Okinawans who were conscripted into Japan’s imperial army, as well as Italian, German and other European Americans, who were taken on suspicion of disloyalty.

At the time, almost 40% of Hawaiʻi’s population was of Japanese ancestry, so it would have been impossible to incarcerate them all. A large chunk of the labor force would have disappeared.

Instead, there was a selective choosing process: Those who were influential to Japanese communities, such as journalists, politicians and religious leaders, were taken as individuals, as opposed to families, like on the West Coast.

In total, less than 1% of those with Japanese ancestry were incarcerated in Hawaiʻi during the war.

Walking a stretch of red dirt trail recently, cleared of the shoulder-high guinea grass and haole koa that once choked the path, Ogura, the superintendent, gestured at the tangle of non-native brush still crowding the slopes beyond, lined with barbed wire on the side.

Ogura is Nisei, or second generation Japanese, and grew up in Hawaiʻi. She spent more than a decade working in wildlife conservation on the mainland before returning home for the job. She recalled reading about Honouliuli and realizing she had never learned this history.

“It could have been me,” she said, “because it’s people exactly like me – my mom, my grandparents — who were targeted.”

For decades after the war, almost no trace of the camp remained visible. The army tore down the buildings when it closed Honouliuli. The site’s location was essentially lost, known only through the memories of the dwindling number of people who had lived there.

That changed in the late 1990s, when the Japanese Cultural Center of Hawaiʻi began to search for the site. In 2002, working from old photographs and sketches made by the internees, they matched the terrain to a gulch in Kunia.

President Barack Obama designated Honouliuli a national monument in 2015.

“While the treatment of Japanese Americans in Hawai’i differed from the treatment of Japanese Americans on the U.S. mainland,” he said at the time, “the legacy of racial prejudice, wartime hysteria and failure of political leadership during this period is common to the history of both Hawai’i and the mainland United States.”

Congress designated it a National Historic Site in 2019.

‘We Want Their Story To Have A Purpose’

Among those who have spent years trying to keep the history of Honouliuli from disappearing again is Sharon Fujimoto-Johnson, a children’s book author, whose grandfather was incarcerated at the site. He was 29 and a U.S. citizen.

As a little girl, her father had given her a small collection of shells that his father had gathered while he was incarcerated. Those objects eventually became the seed of her illustrated book, “ Shell Song,” which traces his story.

When she finally visited Honouliuli in person last year with her younger daughter, she was struck by how deeply hidden the place still is.

“You hike down, and it’s so deep down in this gulch,” she said. “You look up and you can’t really see anything, just walls of mountain on both sides.”

Standing there, she thought of her grandfather arriving with no idea when, or if, he would ever leave.

“I could feel more strongly, maybe, just a sense of despair that could have been something he felt,” she said.

Her hope is that the park’s opening lets visitors reckon with the camp’s impact on many individual lives.

“So often the Japanese American incarceration is talked about in this lump sum, the story that happened to this group of people,” she said. “But I really feel like when it’s broken down into individual stories, that hits at a different level.”

Even as the first tours begin, much of Honouliuli’s physical record remains unexamined.

The tour route itself is modest for now. Beginning at the Hawaiʻi Plantation Village, a shuttle sponsored by Pacific Historic Parks drives through University of Hawaiʻi-West Oʻahu land before arriving at the entrance.

The trail runs down into the gulch, across the rehabilitated aqueduct, past a rock wall from the plantation days, and a low concrete slab that was once a mess hall where those incarcerated could meet visiting relatives, but only if they spoke English. The whole tour takes about 90 minutes.

A mural at UH-West Oʻahu illustrates native plants such as wiliwili, which the park hopes to someday restore at scale. For now, a few seedlings survive on their own along a rocky embankment at the site, a small sign of what native habitat once looked like before sugar cane, and later guinea grass, took over the valley floor.

Honouliuli was a part of the largest ahupuaʻa on island before James Campbell, an Irish real estate developer, purchased 41,000 acres of the ranch land in 1887.

“I’m one of the many that didn’t quite know the history, especially with it being pretty much in our own backyard,” said Brandon Akiona, a graduate student and docent volunteer who led the first public tour last month. “It wasn’t really covered in school.”

His own great-grandfather, he learned only recently, had been incarcerated at Sand Island, and then on the mainland.

“Essentially, the time was taken away from them for nothing,” he said. “We want their story to have a purpose and for their experiences to be heard.”

At the site, tiny yellow ʻilima flowers blossom in the foreground of a view of Pearl Harbor, which can be seen overlooking the gulch, a visual reminder of how the U.S. entered the war.

“But what I think my park does to complement that,” Ogura, the superintendent, said, “is to show the true impact of that day on local communities.”

___

This story was originally published by Honolulu Civil Beat and distributed through a partnership with The Associated Press.

News.title: Trump’s plane is filled with ‘boxes and boxes of McDonald’s,’ RFK Jr reveals
News.content:

Donald Trump fills his plane with his favorite fast food despite it being at odds with his administration’s “Make America Health Again” agenda, according to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

“When you get on his airplane, it’s just boxes and boxes of McDonald’s,” Kennedy said on an episode of the Net Positive with John Crist podcast released to YouTube Wednesday.

Trump’s love of McDonald’s is well-known. Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters revealed the president’s go-to order on the Chamber, Changes & Conversations podcast last October: “He had hot fries waiting for him from McDonald’s...Then he had a Filet-O-Fish, a Quarter Pounder, a Big Mac and I think he combined two of them.”

When he was running for president in 2024, he hosted a campaign event at one of the fast food locations in Pennsylvania, where he worked as a fry attendant.

Kennedy was pictured on Trump’s private plane with a tray of McDonald’s shortly after the then-president-elect tapped him to lead the Health and Human Services Department.

open image in gallery Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has revealed that President Donald Trump has 'boxes and boxes of McDonald’s' on his plane ( Donald Trump Jr. via X )

In the photo, Trump is all smiles as he sits in front of a table filled with fast food surrounded by Kennedy, tech billionaire Elon Musk, House Speaker Mike Johnson and his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., who was holding a box of fries.

“Make America Healthy Again starts TOMORROW,” Donald Trump Jr. posted on X in November 2024, alongside the photo.

The MAHA movement, led by Kennedy as health secretary, scrutinizes ultra-processed foods. HHS recently announced food policy reforms that target the issue.

In an effort to better see what substances are entering the food supply, the Food and Drug Administration has issued a proposed rule requiring manufacturers to notify the agency when they conclude that the use of a substance added to food is “Generally Recognized as Safe.”

HHS and the Department of Agriculture also have submitted the federal government’s first proposed definition of ultra-processed food for final review. A definition would keep research on the link between ultra-processed foods and chronic diseases more consistent, HHS explained.

open image in gallery Kennedy was asked if he ever quietly tells Trump that having loads of junk food on his plane isn’t helping the ‘Make America Great Again’ movement, but he said he’s ‘not a scold’ ( AFP via Getty Images )

“Nearly 60% of the American diet is made up of ultra-processed foods, and childhood obesity now affects more than one in five American children,” Kennedy said in a statement Monday. “We cannot reverse America’s chronic disease epidemic without transforming our food system.”

Crist asked Kennedy on his podcast if he ever quietly tells Trump that having loads of junk food on his plane isn’t helping the MAHA movement. “I’m not a scold,” Kennedy replied.

Kennedy has been more vocal about his opinion of Trump’s diet in the past.

“The stuff that he eats is really bad,” he said on The Joe Polish Show in November 2024.

“Campaign food is always bad, but the food that goes onto that airplane is like just poison,” he said. “You don’t have the choice; you’re either given KFC or Big Macs. That’s when you’re lucky, and then the rest of the stuff I consider kind of inedible.”

Keely Hodgkinson came up just short of a coveted European 800 metres title hat-trick after Swiss favourite Audrey Werro won their hotly-anticipated showdown in Birmingham as the British Olympic champion settled for silver.

Hodgkinson started quicker, but was overtaken by Werro on the back straight was never overtaken after the first 200m.

Double-defending champion Hodgkinson was just behind as they rounded the final bend, but Werro would not be caught and crossed the finish in a championship record one minute, 54.81 seconds.

open image in gallery There was disappointment for Keely Hodgkinson on home soil ( PA )

Hodgkinson claimed silver in 1:55.01 and the Netherlands’ Femke-Broeders Bol took bronze in a national record 1:55.54.

"A bit of mixed emotions,” Hodgkinson told the BBC. I think with that level of competition, any medal is a really good achievement and another one to add to my collection so I can never be disappointed with that. But I'm defending champion so I wanted to do that.

"I knew it was going to come down to the wire but I really thought I was going to win today. But it wasn't meant to be. I didn't do anything wrong, it was just one of those things.

"I've said all year it's really motivating to be in such a competitive event. I love it, I think it brings out the best in me. Championship racing that's what it's all about, you don't know how it's going to go and some people can have a good day or a bad day. I think I had a pretty good day today but it just didn't go how I wanted it to."

More follows....
