Spurs are set to take a lower fee for Romero than what they received for teenage defender Luka Vuskovic, who joined Brighton in a club-record £50m deal earlier this summer.

Speaking on Sky Sports' Tottenham summer special podcast, Sky Sports News' Michael Bridge said of Romero's exit: "Spurs are not going to get the value for a player of his ability.

"Luka Vuskovic, who didn't make any competitive appearances for Spurs, will be sold for more than what the club's captain will go for because he's gone to a Premier League club.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Romero's last game for Spurs ended in tears as he suffered a season-ending injury in the loss at Sunderland

"I think it's best for all parties that Romero leaves. I think 99.9 per cent of Spurs fans would agree with that.

"On his day, there aren't many better - he doesn't make any mistakes for Argentina, but in terms of Tottenham it just feels like it's his job.

"He adores Argentina, and there's nothing wrong with that, but it feels as if Tottenham is a bit of a chore for him and it's gone a bit too much that way."

Could Romero have joined Arsenal?

Earlier this month, one source had told Sky Sports News that Arsenal had looked into Romero as an option to bolster their centre-back options.

However, it never progressed beyond interest, with Spurs reluctant to let their captain join a Premier League side, let alone their fiercest rivals Arsenal.

"There was talk that Romero would have happily accepted a move to Arsenal," Bridge told Sky Sports' Tottenham summer special podcast.

"There were no club-to-club talks on this, but when you hear that then that's the final nail for Tottenham supporters."

The north London rivals tend not to do transfer business with one another. The last transfer negotiated between the two clubs came 49 years ago when goalkeeper Pat Jennings joined Arsenal from Spurs in a deal worth a reported £45,000.

O'Hara: Time for Romero to move on

Also speaking on Sky Sports' Tottenham summer special podcast, ex-Spurs midfielder Jamie O'Hara said of Romero: "He's a bit of a liability. When he plays, he costs us games, points and red cards.

"I just think his attitude towards the board and the way he was, I just think it's, 'All right, thank you, and we're going to move on'.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie O'Hara called for Tottenham to sell Romero

"We've finished 17th the last two seasons, and he's been involved. He was captain last season, and the way he acted at the end of the season, when he got injured, and we all saw him crying, that wasn't for Tottenham; it was more for Argentina and his World Cup.

"And then he goes to Argentina on the last day of the season, and everyone's like, 'Where's Romero?' So that situation for me needs to be put to bed. I don't think we need any of that bad publicity around us.

"Get as much as we can for him; let him move on. We've got back-up now with Van Hecke and Senesi, so thank you, see you later."

Spurs are set to make a loss on Romero, who joined from Atalanta for around £42m in the summer of 2021.

O'Hara said of Atletico's £34.2m deal for Romero: "The problem is there's a premium for English clubs, who will pay over the odds for people with European clubs inflating the fee.

"The problem is if you're going to go and sell him to Atletico Madrid, they haven't got the money.

"If we were selling him to Man Utd, we could probably get £60m-70m for him. But the problem is if you sell a player to Europe, they just don't have the money that the Premier League clubs have, so you have to accept that it's going to be a lesser fee than what maybe you think you can get for him.

"He wants to go to Atletico Madrid. He just feels like an Atletico Madrid player. I just feel like you've just got to take that one on the chin and move on from it."

Romero's exit signals new era at Spurs

Image: Romero is set to leave Spurs after five years at the club

Speaking on Sky Sports' Tottenham summer special podcast, Sky Sports News senior football news editor Lyall Thomas said: "Quite a top figure in the football industry said to me, 'Go and watch Romero's role in the second goal in Spurs' 3-0 defeat to Nottingham Forest at home last season'.

"I watched him, and it was arms in the air, not tracking the player back who ended up scoring, which contributed to the goal.

"That was Spurs when they needed their captain the most, and he just wasn't there in that moment, so that says it all.

"It's time to move on from that era of Spurs and into the new era.

"This has been shown by some of the players they've brought in, which is not just to have an impact on the field but to have an impact on the dressing room and sort that area of the club.

"It's a move that suits Romero to go and work with his compatriot [Diego] Simeone. I can imagine they will suit each other down to the ground. It just fits. The planets are aligned on this one."

Sports.title: Liverpool takeover Q&A: What do we know about Bezos' consortium?
Sports.content:
Liverpool's owners Fenway Sports Group have sold a stake in Liverpool Football Club to a consortium including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

The world's third richest person is part of the group fronted by former QPR co-owner Amit Bhatia. Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is also part of the syndicate.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports Vinny O'Connor explains why FSG have sold a minority stake in Liverpool to the Bezos-backed consortium

According to Sky News, the consortium has agreed to buy a roughly one-third stake in the club in a deal that values Liverpool at more than 7bn (£5.2bn). Closing of the transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.

We take a look at some of the key questions surrounding what the deal could look like...

Who are Bezos and Bhatia?

Bezos is one of the most famous businessmen in the world and the owner of e-commerce giant Amazon, which he founded in 1994 out of his Seattle garage.

His other investments include aerospace company Blue Origin and venture capital firm Nash Holdings, which is the ownership vehicle for The Washington Post.

Bhatia is a 46-year-old British Indian entrepreneur, who has an investment banking background.

Image: Amit Bhatia is the former co-owner of Queen's Park Rangers

He currently manages a multi-asset investment firm called AyBe Capital which invests in range of diversified sectors including technology, media, property and real estate, consumer retail and health.

Bhatia is married to Vanisha Mittal Bhatia, who is the daughter of Indian billionaire Lakshmi Mittal.

He leads and manages 1892 Holdings, the consortium that has agreed the minority investment in Liverpool with majority owners Fenway Sports Group.

What are they worth?

Forbes estimates that Bezos' personal fortune is in the region of $281bn (£209bn), making him the third-richest person in the world behind Elon Musk and Google co-founder Larry Page.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky News' Mark Kleinman discusses Amazon founder Bezos' involvement in the consortium

It's unclear how much Bhatia himself is worth. But his father-in-law, billionaire steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, is worth an estimated £23.2bn according to Forbes. That makes him the 72nd richest person in the world.

What are their sporting interests?

Bezos is a big American Football fan and has previously been reported to have explored bids for the Washington Commanders and the Seattle Seahawks.

He is not known to hold a significant stake in any other sports team or enterprise currently.

Image: Bezos is known to be a big American Football fan

Bhatia was just 28 when he joined the board of directors and became vice-chairman of QPR in 2007 after the Mittal family bought a 20 per cent stake in QPR, joining Bernie Ecclestone and Flavio Briatore as investors in the London club.

He spent five years as QPR chairman between 2018 and 2023 and stayed on as a director and co-owner until earlier this week when he transferred his stake in the club to majority owner Ruben Gnanalingam.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player We take a closer look at Amit Bhatia

Through AyBe capital, Bhatia is an investor in TGL - Rory McIlroy and Tiger Woods' golf league which fuses golf and technology and features six teams with some of the best players in the world in a season-long competition.

His firm also invests in Switch Hitter, which is a media brand founded by Kevin Pietersen, delivering exclusive interviews and content with the world's top cricketers.

Image: Rajasthan Royals were one of the most sought-after IPL cricket franchises

Earlier this year, Bhatia's father-in-law acquired a 75 per cent stake in the Rajasthan Royals Indian Premier League cricket franchise.

Why have FSG decided to sell?

FSG were under no pressure to sell but did indicate in 2022 that they were open to new investment in Liverpool, with the sale of a small stake to Dynasty Equity completed the following year.

Liverpool have enjoyed huge success under FSG, lifting every major trophy available to win.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Football finance expert Kieran Maguire explains what a 'strategic minority stake' is

FSG may think it is mission accomplished somewhat as far they are concerned, and therefore were amenable to fresh investment. They also stand to make a huge profit on their initial investment, with the deal for a 30 per cent stake worth more than five times what they paid for the entire club back in 2010.

How much have the consortium bought?

The consortium is acquiring a roughly one-third stake in the club.

Could the Bezos-backed group take over Liverpool?

Liverpool's new minority investors have an option to become majority shareholders of the Premier League club for a valuation of around $8bn in the next 12 months, according to Sky's US partner CNBC.

Sky Sports News has been told the agreement announced today includes a framework for future investment from the Jeff Bezos-backed consortium.

However, sources have stressed that the existence of such an agreement is not a guarantee of any future transaction.

Liverpool's statement says FSG continues to retain majority ownership and operational control of the club.

What is the club valued at?

Liverpool are the fourth most valuable club in the world. The consortium's investment in Liverpool values the club somewhere in the region of £5.2bn ($7bn), making it one of the sport's richest-ever deals.

Who owns Liverpool?

FSG have complete operational control of Liverpool, but private equity firms RedBird Capital and Arctos Sports Partners hold minority stakes in the club. Dynasty Equity are also passive investors in Liverpool after injecting £164m into the club in 2023 in a deal valuing Liverpool at more than $4.5bn.

Image: The Anfield home of Liverpool Football Club

How much did FSG pay for Liverpool?

FSG were known as New England Sports Ventures when they paid £300m for Liverpool in October 2010 after a tumultuous period under former owners Tom Hicks and George Gillett.

When will the deal go through?

The deal - which was first reported on at the end of last month - has accelerated at a rapid pace. Now that everything has been agreed, the closing of the transaction will happen after regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions are met.

Who else is involved?

Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin and his wife Elaine are also part of the syndicate of investors. Saverin, 44, was part of a consortium which assembled an unsuccessful takeover bid for Chelsea during the 2022 auction triggered by Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine.

Sports.title: Glave: From 2022 in a back brace to European champion - 'Delayed but not denied'
Sports.content:
Britain's Romell Glave: From two serious back injuries and 2022 in a back brace to European 100m champion - 'Delayed but not denied'

Romell Glave chats exclusively to Sky Sports following his 100m European Athletics success

"2026 was my year of redemption," Romell Glave exclusively tells Sky Sports two days on from when he stood on the podium draped with a 100m gold medal at the European Championships.

The 26-year-old's story and journey to the point of becoming European champion in athletics' marquee event is a remarkable one. "Delayed but not denied," Glave says, with a twinkle in his eye.

Born in Manchester, Jamaica, Glave moved to the UK at the age of 15, joined Croydon Harriers, and by the age of 17 was the fastest 100m sprinter on the planet for his age group, clocking a time of 10.21.

Injuries hit regularly and harshly over the intervening years. So much so that he spent the majority of 2022 in a back brace having fractured vertebrae - issues first occurring when he was forced to train on grass due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

His back injury meant he was only able to make his European Championship debut for Britain in 2024, aged 24.

At that competition, Glave qualified for the 100m final and claimed the bronze medal in a tight race, but though a quest for more followed, he then fractured and inflamed his back for a second time, forcing him to miss out on the Olympic Games in Paris.

In 2026, he returned with a vengeance to succeed. He won gold in the 60m at a World Indoor Athletics meet in Stockholm - defeating Olympic silver medallist Kishane Thompson. He broke the 10-second barrier legally for the first time when he ran 9.98 to win the British title in June, and lowered his personal best again to 9.97 in London the following month.

All his work then culminated in European Championship 100m gold in Birmingham on Tuesday.

"It's been a journey and a half and also a total rollercoaster," Glave tells Sky Sports. "And I know success was a long time coming.

"I just needed to stay healthy because I knew that with the support I've had for the last three years since I had my back fracture, from medical staff like Nick Allen and Peter Horobin who have been there for me, I had a great chance.

Glave was the world's fastest 17-year-old but injuries held him back up to now

"To be able to stand here as a European champion means a lot. It's testament to the hard work they put in to get me to the line and also to keep showing up for me because without them, I don't know if this would be possible.

"It's been a euphoric moment for me, an unreal feeling. Just a feeling of relief the job is accomplished. This is why we do this sport, it means so much to me."

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

'2026 was my year of redemption - nothing was stopping me from succeeding'

Hit by one injury knockback after another, many athletes may even have called it quits.

Instead, Glave tackled 2026 with an intensive determination to succeed. So much so that even when doubts, nerves or physical issues crept in he was able to channel them out.

It was notable watching the start line to the 100m final just how relaxed Glave appeared, a state very difficult to achieve ahead of an event that means so much and that he would have worked so hard towards. But this was an athlete totally in flow.

"I would say I came into this season just to show a bit of redemption after the loss of years, loss of seasons to injury," Glave says.

"But to also start this season with a very resilient mindset of: 'I want to go for everything.' I was a 2024 bronze medallist at the European Championships and missed the gold medal by a small margin. So why not dream bigger and upgrade my medal to gold?

"That was the aim and objective for the season, from the start of the season. To be European champion and to be able to walk away from from that 100m being crowned king of Europe. It's an amazing feeling.

"It brings me calmness. I've been dreaming of this moment and to be able to live it, it's very surreal.

Glave and British team-mate Jeremiah Azu finished first and second in the 100m final

"Over the last few days, I have had discomfort in my abdominal muscles, but I was not going to let that stop me from obtaining my objective.

"I was able to go out there, regardless of how I was feeling, the discomfort I was enduring, and just focus on the job that was presented in front of me. I got the job done.

"I was ready for this moment, this occasion. I was ready mentally, most importantly, regardless of how I was feeling emotionally or physically, I wasn't going to let that take away the moment from me because I prepared all season long for it.

"This season was all about redemption, that's the theme, and speaking to my sports psychologist, we've been working on all of those formulas to make sure I'm preparing the best way possible to get through."

Glave has tackled 2026 in sensational fashion after a devastating turn in 2024 saw him miss the Olympics

'2024 back injury left a void in my heart'

Thinking back, Glave lays bare the inner turmoil he experienced having battled through one serious back injury, won a European Championship bronze, but then suffered with his back again to miss an Olympics Games and virtually have to start his career all over again.

"It was very disappointing. After the 2024 European Championships, I could feel I was on that momentum, because the trials were two weeks afterwards.

"My first session back after I was crowned European bronze medallist, I picked up the injury and it was a very sad moment for me. My mind went to missing the Olympics, because everyone trains towards going to that.

"And to get a European bronze and have that momentum going into the Olympics, that's what everyone wants. To cut the journey short at that moment, it left a a void in my heart. I'm never going to get that moment back, that's gone."

Glave had to endure a career filled with serious injuries and setbacks

One man Glave has repeatedly singled out in the aftermath of his success has been coach Michael Afilaka, someone he describes as more than just his sprint coach: "a mentor, life coach, a man of wisdom and integrity."

Indeed, referencing his working relationship with Afilaka from serious injury to European champion proves very emotional for Glave.

"He's been doing this for over 20 years and is a private person, but God presented him to me on this journey. Having him beside me has been a life-changing decision.

"During those darkest times of my life, he's the only that is there. His belief, his dedication to continue to show up for me, I haven't really seen that before. I haven't really seen it in my life, in the way he has shown up.

"It's very emotional just talking about it every time, because he didn't have to do it, but because of his persona, he wants the best for me."

Glave spoke emotionally about the time and support coach Michael Afilaka has afforded him

'The next goal is world domination'

In terms of what's next, Glave is clear. He wants to challenge on a world level at the top of the sport.

"World domination is now the main goal, but just to have this stepping stone as European champion, I'm focusing on one step at a time.

"This season is like a stepping stone of what is to come for Romell Glave. I'm in a historic British team and now have the ultimate chance as well.

"So to be there and show up in a field of world-class athletes, that's the main objective now. To perform against those athletes, the world's best."

Sports.title: Stokes' Durham progress with Flintoff unable to repeat hundred heroics
Sports.content:
A Durham side featuring Ben Stokes thrashed Lancashire by 162 runs to reach the One Day Cup semi-finals with Rocky Flintoff unable to repeat his hundred heroics from earlier in the week.

​​​​​Flintoff, the 18-year-old son of England great Andrew Flintoff, cracked a 65-ball century for Lancashire against Somerset in the final round of group games on Tuesday as he registered his first senior professional ton.

However, the teenager was out for 22 from 39 balls versus Durham at Emirates Old Trafford - one of four wickets taken by Afghan leg-spinner Shafiqullah Ghafari - as Lancashire were bundled out for 187 chasing 350 for victory.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look as Rocky Flintoff, son of former England captain Andrew, hit his maiden senior professional century for Lancashire against Somerset with 123 off 76 balls

Quiet day for Stokes but Durham hammer Lancashire

Former England captain Stokes took one wicket, that of opening batter Harry Singh for 11, as he returned figures of 1-32 from four overs after earlier hitting one six in a knock of 11 from nine balls in Durham's 349-8 in Manchester.

Durham - who will now face Middlesex in a semi-final at Radlett on Sunday - saw David Bedingham strike 104 from 89 balls and Ollie Robinson make 76 from 57 deliveries.

The pair shared a fourth-wicket stand of 149 before Robinson's dismissal brought Stokes to the crease.

In reply, only 17-year-old Joe Moores (51 off 42), who stitched a 59-run stand with Flintoff, made a score of note.

Verreynne put on 54 with George Munsey (25 off 28) for the fourth wicket and then 154 with Haynes, although Verreynne's dismissal in the 41st over with 65 runs needed triggered a wobble of three wickets for four runs as Farhan Ahmed (2) and Olly Stone (0) fell to Coad, leaving Notts tottering on 213-7.

Haynes, though, found excellent support in No 9 Dillon Pennington (22no off 18), who cuffed the winning four having earlier taken 4-49 with his seam bowling, including Yorkshire top-scorer Will Bennison (91), in the hosts' 273-9.

Sports.title: Gay bags pair in Test warm-up as Pakistan captain Babar suffers injury scare
Sports.content:
England opener Emilio Gay bagged a pair and Pakistan captain Babar Azam suffered an injury scare on an eventful second day of the Test match-warm up in Beckenham.

Gay, having been dismissed by Mohmmad Abbas on day one while batting for a County Select XI against Pakistan, snicked Mohmmad Ali behind on Friday to fall for a seven-ball duck.

The Durham batter had suffered a shoulder injury playing for his county in the One Day Cup earlier this month but his appearance in this game has probably allayed any fears over his fitness for the first Test at Headingley from next Wednesday, live on Sky Sports.

Babar, meanwhile, was struck on the right hand by a delivery from young Hampshire seamer Manny Lumsden and retired hurt on five from 17 balls.

A statement from Pakistan later said that the skipper would sit out the remainder of the game as a precautionary measure but that he will participate in the team's practice session in Leeds on Monday.

Image: Pakistan captain Babar Azam will play no further part in the Test warm-up after being struck on the hand

Babar - whose side also play England at Lord's (from August 27) and Edgbaston (from September 9) - struck one four in Beckenham batting in the No 4 spot.

Pakistan plummeted from 164-2 to 238 all out, in reply to their hosts' initial 305 all out, as they surrendered a 67-run deficit on first innings.

England spinner Shoaib Bashir, hoping to be included in his country's XI at Headingley, bagged figures of 4-76 from 20.2 overs, dismissing opener Imam-ul-Haq (37), middle-order man Salman Ali Agha (14) and then Aamir Jamal (8) and Ghazi Ghori (27).

Abdullah Shafique (61) top-scored for Pakistan, while Lumsden and Northamptonshire's Saif Zaib picked up two wickets apiece for the County Select XI.

The home team extended their advantage to 195 runs by stumps after closing on 128-3 with James Rew (40), Caleb Falconer (52no) - the Middlesex youngster notching his second half-century of the game - and Zaib (24no) chipping in once Gay and opening partner Tom Haines (12) departed cheaply.

Sports.title: SunRisers into Hundred women's final with tense win over Brave
Sports.content:
SunRisers Leeds booked a meeting with Trent Rockets in The Hundred women's final after a tense five-wicket win over Southern Brave in the eliminator at The Kia Oval.

Set a modest 115 to win, SunRisers had looked in trouble at 54-3 after 47 balls - their dynamic Australian duo of Phoebe Litchfield (4) and Annabel Sutherland (17 off 12) both dismissed - and again at 95-5 after 78 when the impressive Issy Wong (3-21) took two wickets in two balls.

Wong, who had earlier claimed the key wicket of tournament leading run-scorer Litchfield, also bowled Lauren Winfield-Hill (37 off 37) and saw off SunRisers skipper Dani Gibson, lbw first ball.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Issy Wong took three wickets during The Hundred eliminator between SunRisers Leeds and Southern Brave

But India's Deepti Sharma kept a calm head, her unbeaten 28 off 22 ultimately seeing SunRisers over the line with 11 balls to spare and into Sunday's final at Lord's.

Score Summary - SunRisers Leeds vs Southern Brave Southern Brave 114-7 from 100 balls: Lizelle Lee (32 off 25 balls); Hannah Baker (2-13), Annabel Sutherland (2-31) SunRisers Leeds 116-5 from 89 balls: Lauren Winfield-Hill (37 off 37 balls), Deepti Sharma (28no off 22); Issy Wong (3-21)

The result was in keeping with the form guide, with the tournament's early pace-setters Brave losing a fourth straight match after starting with five wins from five.

SunRisers are defending champions - having won last year's women's competition under their previous name of Northern Superchargers - and have won five in a row going into the final against Rockets, who themselves have triumphed in their last six to clinch top spot in the women's table.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lizelle Lee sent one into the stands as Southern Brave made a strong start

Wong efforts in vain as Brave beaten in eliminator

Earlier, after SunRisers won the toss and elected to bowl first, Lizelle Lee got Brave's innings off to a decent start with a 25-ball 32 that contained five boundaries and a glorious straight six off Kate Cross (1-12) - the only maximum of the match.

The turning point came when Winfield-Hill pulled off an impressive stumping of the South African for the opening breakthrough off the impressive Hannah Baker (2-13).

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Hannah Baker took two wickets during The Hundred eliminator between Southern Brave and SunRisers Leeds

Baker also accounted for Charli Knott (25 off 21), bowled by the leg-spinner, while Sharma (1-24) went joint-top of the tournament's wicket-taking charts and Sutherland (2-31) snagged a couple late on off consecutive deliveries.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Annabel Sutherland was left agonisingly short of a hat-trick when Dani Gibson's mistimed catch went down, moments after two wickets in two balls

Cross' dismissal of Laura Wolvaardt (8) was the only Brave wicket, along with the run-out of Wong (4) off the last ball, not to fall to spin as Sophie Molineux's side fell some way short of a par score, despite the Australian's 22 not out.

Brave's hugely impressive attack of international bowlers just about kept them in the hunt, Lauren Bell (1-14) conceding just two off her first 10, which included the early wicket of Bryony Smith (2), before Wong cleaned up Litchfield to make it 13-2 after 17 balls.

Sutherland hit a breezy 17 off 12 before perishing to Sarah Glenn (1-25), while Winfield-Hill appeared to be playing a match-winning knock before Wong took two in two to find herself on a hat-trick.

At that stage, SunRisers still required 20 from 22 balls but Sharma and Jess Jonassen (10no off 5) comfortably steered SunRisers to victory and into the women's final.

'SunRisers can't afford those mistakes in final'

Analysis by Sky Sports Cricket's Natalie Germanos:

"A little hiccup from SunRisers at the end - those are mistakes they can't afford in a final, and certainly not against the Trent Rockets.

"They need to be careful in terms of reading the conditions.

"But otherwise, through the day, they didn't get a lot wrong."

Baker: I've never been so nervous in my life!

Meerkat Match Hero Hannah Baker, speaking to Sky Sports:

"I've never been so nervous in my entire life [as during the chase]! It's great to get over the line.

"With our power that we've got, we were always confident that we could chase that. Luckily, we got a bit of spin today.

"I spoke to Jonassen when we were out there and she told me to just hit my length - that's what I did.

"[Now we've just got to] relax, and get ready to go again."

When is The Hundred final?

SunRisers Leeds will face Trent Rockets in the women's final at Lord's on Sunday August 16.

The women's final is at 2.15pm, with the men's final at 6pm, live on Sky Sports Cricket.

Sports.title: RFU postpones start of competitive community rugby season in England
Sports.content:
The RFU has postponed the start of the competitive community game season until the week commencing Monday September 21 due to "concerns about player welfare and pitch conditions".

The RFU had already contacted clubs, schools and colleges, players and coaches to remind them of the existence of guidance surrounding the management of rugby pitches in drought conditions and the Natural Turf Pitches (NTP) Surface Risk Assessment to assess whether a pitch is safe to use and to mitigate the risks of injury.

The prolonged dry weather in many parts of England has left many grounds across the country unsuitable for safe full-contact activity.

After gathering feedback from representatives across different regions and discussing the options within competition committees, the RFU has decided to delay the start of the competitive community game season nationwide.

Sir Bill Beaumont, president of the RFU, said: "We know this decision will be disappointing for the clubs, schools and colleges, players, volunteers and fans looking forward to the start of the season, and we do not underestimate the impact it will have across the game.

"This has been a carefully considered decision. After listening to views from across the community game and weighing up the options available to us, we believe that delaying the start of the competitive season nationwide is the right course of action.

"While we recognise that not everyone will agree with this decision, making it now provides greater certainty for clubs, schools and colleges as they prepare for the months ahead.

"On behalf of everyone at the RFU, I would like to thank all those who have shared their views and contributed to discussions in recent days.

"Player welfare and readiness have been central to our thinking throughout, alongside our desire to give the season the best possible opportunity to begin on a fair and consistent footing across the country.

"We also wanted to provide clarity as early as possible to help the volunteers, staff and organisations who work so hard behind the scenes to plan and prepare for the season."

Share

Sports.title: Europe’s top clubs threatened Club World Cup boycott before Fifa plan collapsed
Sports.content:
Europe’s leading clubs threatened not to participate in future Club World Cups unless Gianni Infantino withdrew his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, issuing their ultimatum hours before the plan was scrapped.

In a letter to the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, the influential European Football Clubs (EFC) group warned that its cooperation with future tournaments would hinge on Infantino backing down. It said the threat would hold unless a joint venture between EFC and Fifa – a framework for which has already been agreed – is completed before television rights can be sold for the 2028 Women’s Club World Cup.

The letter, dated 31 July and signed by the EFC chief executive, Charlie Marshall, said Infantino’s actions could constitute a “substantial breach” of the bodies’ existing memorandum of understanding (MoU) and suggested this could be grounds for its termination. It floated the idea that EFC and its clubs may push back against the international match calendar and its player release rules, which are crucial to ensuring national team tournaments can function. Infantino shelved the privately backed Football Forward Enterprise (FFE) in the early hours of 1 August after widespread condemnation.

Fundamental to EFC’s complaints was the impression FFE would bring all broadcasting, commercial and sponsorship rights under its own umbrella. The letter asked Fifa to confirm this and said it would take decisive action if these elements were not included in the long-proposed joint venture, whose creation is enshrined in the MoU and intended to involve managing the commercial side of global club competitions. It witheringly wrote that progress on the tie-in had “unlike the FFE proposal, made no meaningful progress over the past year”. EFC already has a similar joint venture with Uefa, named UC3, which was launched in 2025.

A potentially incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”

In theory the threat still holds although Fifa, in a response to EFC’s letter since Infantino climbed down, is understood to have promised a swift meeting to keep the joint venture on track. EFC’s position followed concerns raised by a vast number of clubs around Europe, who were angered by the lack of consultation around the design of FFE. One major European club expressed concerns in its own letter saying it would support EFC in any “firmer collective action” if necessary and called for “more rigorous and transparent governance processes”.

Any European withdrawal from Club World Cups would in practice mean those tournaments could not run. EFC and Fifa operated last year’s Club World Cup, the first to take place with 32 teams, using a short-term prototype for any future joint venture. No hosts have yet been announced for the new-look Women’s Club World Cup or the next edition of the men’s tournament in 2029.

View image in fullscreen Chelsea won the Club World Cup in July 2025 by beating Paris Saint-Germain in the final. Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty Images

EFC’s letter also raised the ongoing delay, first reported in February, in distributing £185m of solidarity money to clubs that did not participate in the Club World Cup. Transparency over the event’s financial performance was also requested.

“We ask that you urgently share the final surplus revenue generated by the 2025 Fifa WC, together with a full profit and loss statement, so that all revenues, expenses and costs can be properly assessed in line with our partnership in this competition,” it said. “The absence of information on this matter, as with the lack of a solution on CWC solidarity for over a year, is also of serious concern and disappointment to EFC and our member clubs.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It is understood there is increasing optimism that this issue is on the verge of resolution although a notional average £50,000 windfall for every global top-flight club, if the pot was divided equally, pales in comparison with the £84m reward long since banked by last year’s winners, Chelsea.

Referring to clubs releasing players for international duty EFC continued: “Our memorandum of understanding, set to expire on 30 December 2030, includes EFC’s and its member clubs’ acceptance of the international match calendar and the release rules. Both are directly relevant for Fifa’s non-European member associations and to any value FFE may have.” It said Fifa’s apparent commercial vision for FFE constituted a “serious breach of trust” and warned the MoU could be jeopardised.

The letter demonstrates the extraordinary level of leverage EFC, which is chaired by the Paris Saint-Germain president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, can claim over Fifa and its increasing influence on football’s future. The organisation, set up in 2008 as a lobby group for clubs around the continent, now has well over 800 members although only a minority hold full voting rights. Some stakeholders elsewhere in football’s ecosystem have expressed fears about the level of power it has assumed. A separate representative body, the Union of European Clubs, was created in 2023 to represent smaller sides but is not recognised by Uefa.

One potential consequence of EFC’s discussions with Fifa could, in the medium term, be its expansion into a group representing clubs around the world. More immediately, last month’s letter demanded that Fifa deliver on a previous promise to fully integrate Al-Khelaifi into the Fifa council, which is purportedly its main decision-making body.

Sports.title: Liverpool owner FSG seals £1.65bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff Bezos
Sports.content:
Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, has confirmed it has agreed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin. The deal is understood to be worth £1.65bn, valuing Liverpool at £5.5bn, and will see Bhatia become the club’s new vice-chair on an expanded board.

Bhatia, the son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, initiated and led talks with FSG on behalf of the 1892 Holdings consortium, a reference to Liverpool’s founding year. The former co-owner of Queens Park Rangers has received financial backing from the Mittal Family Trust, the K5 Sports fund, of which Bezos is the lead investor, and EE Capital, the family office of Elaine and Eduardo Saverin.

Elaine Saverin, wife of Eduardo, and Bryan Baum, co-founder and managing partner of K5 Global, will also join the Liverpool board. Bezos is considered a passive investor and will not have a seat on the board.

Despite the involvement of Bezos, the third richest man in the world with $272bn (£201bn), Eduardo Saverin, worth an estimated $33bn and the Mittal family, worth around $17bn, FSG will remain in operational control of Liverpool as well as majority owners. 1892 Holdings’ investment remains subject to regulatory approval, which could take up to 90 days, and will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. There is also no change to the leadership or day-to-day running of Liverpool.

FSG insist the deal is not part of an exit strategy from a club they acquired in 2010 for £300m after the near-ruinous ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett. The transaction does not compel FSG to sell more of the club to 1892 at a future date, or include obligations for 1892 to increase their stake, but it does give Bhatia’s consortium options to purchase more of Liverpool should the majority owners eventually decide to sell.

It is the makeup of Bhatia’s consortium, rather than any financial need, that FSG claim attracted them to the British-Indian businessman’s proposal. The FSG leadership team of principal owner John W Henry, chair Tom Werner and president Mike Gordon have spent almost a year getting to know Bhatia and believe the deal will create further opportunities for Liverpool in global business, technology and investment, including in the important markets of India and Asia.

View image in fullscreen The sale will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Gordon, who has resumed a more hands-on role at Liverpool following the departure of Michael Edwards as chief executive of football at FSG, said: “Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club’s long-term interests in mind. That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world.

“As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special. Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place, and we look forward to working together.”

With Premier League and Uefa financial regulations linking a club’s spending to turnover, the new investment will not have an immediate benefit for head coach Andoni Iraola and his Liverpool team. However, the commercial opportunities presented by the involvement of Bezos, Bhatia and Saverin will enable the Anfield club to grow their annual revenue significantly. Liverpool’s annual revenue increased to a record £703m in the year ending May 2025.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Speaking on behalf of 1892 Holdings, Bhatia said: “We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield.

“To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club’s continued success for years to come.”

Bhatia was involved in QPR for almost 19 years and took on numerous roles, from chair of the club to chair of the club’s community trust, until transferring his shareholding in July. He is likely to have a more visible presence at Anfield than fellow members of his consortium or FSG.

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 10: Fulham
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 15th (NB: this is not necessarily John Brewin’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 11th

Prospects

Marco Silva cutting the cord after five years by the river came as little surprise. If his time at Craven Cottage was successful in re-establishing Fulham as a Premier League club, he rarely concealed his ambitions to manage in European competition. He was frequently explicit in his disappointment that the club’s ownership did not meet him halfway by funding a stronger squad. Silva’s powers of rebadging and replenishing talent will be missed now that he has decamped to Benfica. Under him, Fulham played entertaining football, a collection of ugly ducklings showing their renewed worth for a club that, despite falling short of European qualification, looked upwards rather than downwards at the relegation battle. They were often a pleasure to watch, and ornery opposition for all-comers.

Álvaro Arbeloa is a very different type of appointment, with far less experience than his predecessor in frontline coaching terms, even if he arrives with Real Madrid on his CV. His arrival, though, has opened up a working relationship with the Spanish aristos, Gonzalo García and César Palacios arriving to work with a coach who helped them through the ranks in Madrid. By little coincidence, all three share the same agency as their representatives. There have been links with Endrick and Thiago Pitarch, two further young Real jewels, leading to a sense of Fulham becoming some form of Madrileño nursery, a Santiago Bernabéu on Thames. Should that play out, it would represent another sea change.

Silva preferred to work with hard-bitten pros. A couple of his leading men, Raúl Jiménez and Harry Wilson, have departed. The latter played the best football of his career last season but, like his manager, got a better offer elsewhere, from Leeds. Fulham’s latest approach is to source young players and polish them up. Can they have the same successes as mid-tier peers such as Brentford, Brighton and Bournemouth, where the approach is far more data-driven? Will supporters be looking upwards rather than downwards? A previously enigmatic club just got more enigmatic.

Off-field picture

In May, the club were runners-up at the football business awards, for stadium experience, as the Riverside Stand’s opulent hospitality completed its first full season in service. Fulham need the Riverside to deliver as a revenue stream, as financial results for the 2024-25 season showed a pre-tax loss for the year at £44.5m, and that was lowered by the sale of João Palhinha in July 2024. There has been no such windfall since. The Khan family ownership continues to back the club, its overall investment estimated at about £900m, with staff costs at 117% of turnover. Therein lies the reasoning behind Silva not receiving the backing he desired.

Owner-fan relationship

The most expensive season ticket at Craven Cottage comes in at £3,084 for access to the Riverside’s facilities, the highest in the Premier League. Shahid Khan and his son Tony, the vice-chair and director of football operations, are unpopular among committed supporters for price rises and pandering to tourism. Khan’s boat Kismet was named superyacht of the year in 2025, its main salon inspired by the Palace of Versailles, and can be chartered for more than $3m per week. Though the balance sheets confirm Khan’s outlay in funding a continued Premier League status, fans would prefer he recognised not everyone lives the high life.

The manager

Where Silva had an unremarkable playing career, Arbeloa featured among the elite, a World Cup and Champions League winner. He also had the ear of Florentino Pérez, the perennial Real Madrid president asking him to replace Xabi Alonso mid-season in the 2025-26 campaign. That did not pan out and he took his first job away from Madrid, where he was a well-regarded youth coach, in south-west London. Khan Sr’s comment that Arbeloa “believes in giving young players a chance” is pertinent for Fulham’s change in direction. Crucially, as befitting traditions at Craven Cottage, the new man from Salamanca believes in open, attacking football, offering some continuity from Silva’s reign.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Gonzalo García surges forward during Fulham’s Costa del Sol Trophy match against Málaga. Photograph: Joaquin Corchero/AFP7/Shutterstock

Gonzalo García’s reputation was made by his performances at last summer’s Club World Cup, where he won the tournament’s Golden Boot. Comparisons were made to Raúl, a considerable accolade at the Bernabéu. Goals followed in the Champions League against Juventus and Borussia Dortmund but García eventually lost out to the star system of Vinícius Júnior and Kylian Mbappé. His reputation in Spain is as a hard worker off the ball, necessary for a Premier League player. Last season, Rodrigo Muniz’s injuries meant the old soldier Jiménez shouldered the burden at centre-forward. García is younger and fresher but the hype surrounding his arrival gives him much to live up to.

Stat attack

Fulham had the oldest side in the Premier League last season, which may help explain why they had arguably the least intense press. Marco Silva’s side recorded the fewest high turnovers, which occur when a team recovers the ball to start a new open-play possession sequence in the final 40 metres of the pitch. Real Madrid are hardly known for being a high-pressing side but they comfortably outperformed Fulham on this metric. It will be fascinating to see how Arbeloa approaches this.

Set for a breakthrough

Jonah Kusi-Asare’s arrival last summer from Bayern Munich is further mining of a super-club’s youth department. Bayern inserted a buy-back clause for a player they picked up from AIK. The Sweden Under-21s player has been compared to Alexander Isak, and made seven substitute appearances last season – without scoring – before an initial loan became a permanent move. At 6ft 5in he offers a different profile of striker to García. Hayden Mullins, the former under-21 coach now Newport manager, saw the best of Kusi-Asare last season, the 18-year-old scoring five goals in six matches.

World Cup impact

García made his debut for Spain in a pre-World Cup friendly against Iraq but failed to make the eventual champions’ tournament squad. Antonee Robinson had a fine tournament for the USA until the co-hosts perished in the last 16 at the hands of a Belgium team featuring Timothy Castagne. Luc de Fougerolles, yet to play a Premier League game for Fulham, showed off teenage defensive talents in Canada’s run to the knockouts. To complete a successful quintet – saving the best till last? – Sander Berge had a fine tournament as Norway also reached the quarter-finals.

Sports.title: Arsenal open talks with Bayer Leverkusen over deal for Jarell Quansah
Sports.content:
Arsenal have opened talks with Bayer Leverkusen over a move for Jarell Quansah as they intensify efforts to bring in cover for William Saliba and Jurriën Timber.

The England defender, who left Liverpool last summer for an initial £30m and was part of Thomas Tuchel’s World Cup squad, has been identified as an ideal replacement for the France and Netherlands defenders, who will miss the start of the new season due to injury. While Quansah’s preferred position is in central defence, he was also deployed at right-back by Tuchel at the World Cup and was sent off in the last-16 victory over Mexico.

It is understood that Leverkusen are reluctant to sell the Warrington-born 23-year-old, who signed a five-year deal when he left Anfield last July, and would want at least €50m (£43m). Arsenal – who saw a bid of £30m for Aston Villa’s Ezri Konsa rejected earlier in the window – are not thought to want to pay that much but now could test the German club’s resolve by submitting a similar offer. Liverpool had a €70m buyback option on Quansah but that has now expired.

Arsenal are still believed to be interested in Konsa, who also filled in at right-back for England during the World Cup but is better known as a central defender. Villa value the 28-year-old at £60m.

Mikel Arteta said this week that Saliba’s back injury would take “some time to heal” and he was unsure about when he would be available again. Arsenal also have concerns over Timber, who pulled out of the Netherlands squad on the eve of the World Cup after failing to recover from a persistent groin injury that forced him to miss most of the run‑in last season.

“Jurriën is progressing really well,” Arteta said after Arsenal’s friendly defeat by Borussia ­Dortmund last Sunday. “He’s on the pitch, he’s doing quite a lot right now, but it’s still weeks away. I cannot tell you how much.”

Arsenal would still like to sign a new attacker before the end of the window and could allow Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus to depart in order to free up more funds. ­Galatasaray have offered £38m for Martinelli, although the Brazil ­forward has turned down a move to Turkey. Napoli have shown an ­interest in Jesus.

Ethan Nwaneri could also be sold, with Milan, Fulham, RB Leipzig and Borussia Dortmund among those who have been linked with the 19-year-old.

The future of Myles Lewis-Skelly is unclear after he was offered to Chelsea and Manchester United this week. Arteta refused to address the rumours after he scored in the friendly against Como – managed by Cesc Fábregas – on Wednesday.

“I’m not going to talk about speculation,” he said. “If there is speculation about our players, it’s a good sign. That means our players attract attention and are doing a good job.”

Sports.title: Chelsea expect Enzo Fernández to stay after Manchester City opt not to meet deadline
Sports.content:
Manchester City did not make a £120m bid for Enzo Fernández before Chelsea’s 5pm deadline on Friday but Enzo Maresca still expects a busy end to the transfer window, as the club seek incomings and outgoings. Chelsea, meanwhile, now expect the Argentina midfielder to stay at Stamford Bridge.

Maresca takes charge of City for the first time in a major match on Sunday against Arsenal in Cardiff in the Community Shield but is a long way from finalising the squad he will have for the season. Fernández, who played under Maresca at Chelsea, remains a target for City, who could still test the water despite missing the deadline.

“For sure there are things we need to do, how many I don’t know, can be one, can be two, depends also if players want to leave, so we can see,” Maresca said on Friday, having suggested City would not agree to Chelsea’s demands. “It’s 48 hours for the final, my first final in this club, I would like to win my first trophy, so my focus isn’t on players that can leave or players that can arrive, my focus is on the game.”

City have rejected two bids from Barcelona for Rodri but anticipate a third, and are expected to sell Tijjani Reijnders in the coming days. They are also in the market for reinforcements as they aim to challenge on four fronts. City are close to signing the 18-year-old Morocco international Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille but are willing to bring in others.

Rodri, who has a year remaining on his contract, returned to the club on Friday after his holiday which followed a triumphant World Cup, but Maresca would not be drawn on the midfielder’s immediate future with a third Barcelona offer expected.

“The transfer window is open, we can buy players, we can sell players, anything can happen. I just saw Rodri now in the building, I gave him a big hug, he looks good, so we’ll see what happens.”

Reijnders is set to join the Saudi Pro League side Al-Qadsiah after the two clubs agreed a £51m fee for the Dutchman, who moved to City last summer from Milan but wants more regular playing time.

“They all work every day, they all do sessions every day and at the end of the week they all want to play a game,” Maresca said. “When they don’t play they struggle to understand or they struggle to see the reason why, and I can understand that after one season some of them would like to play a little bit more. It’s a normal situation.”

James Trafford has already been sold to Leeds, while Omar Marmoush, Rico Lewis and Savinho are others who spent much of Pep Guardiola’s final season on the periphery and could be sold.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Rangers and the paradox of a painful exit that boosts their trophy chances
Sports.content:
AND NOW FOR SOME PERSPECTIVE

All new managers want to hit the ground running. But landing with a dull thud has never been a barrier to future glory, certainly not at Ibrox. Take Graeme Souness, whose start as Rangers’ player-manager put the ‘pish’ in ‘inauspicious’. On his league debut, away to Hibs, he was sent off in the first half after a revenge attack on the wrong mullet. Rangers lost 2-1 and were beaten in the third game as well. Graeme out! Rangers won the League Cup and finished the season as champions for the first time in nine years.

Dick Advocaat had a similarly awkward start in 1998. In his first game, played at Tranmere’s Prenton Park, Rangers went 3-0 down to Shelbourne in the first leg of their Big Vase tie. They went through comfortably in the end but lost the first league game a few days later. Dic- Advocaat out! Rangers had to settle for a domestic treble that season. Different times, when toys were played with for more than a few seconds before being launched from the pram with maximum force, followed a few seconds later by a handful of freshly sourced excreta. In 2026, alas, hot air and horse pucky are an acceptable substitute for reasonable discourse. And so, after failing to win any of his first four games as Rangers manager, Derek McInnes is “out of his depth” and a “dead man walking”.

Que Sera, Sera? Eff that! Turns out the future is ours to see after four games, two of them in a competition Rangers had no chance of winning anyway. Football Daily hasn’t a clue if McInnes is up to the Brobdingnagian challenge of managing Rangers, one that most tea-timely newsletters don’t really understand. But we do know that a culture of self-fulfilling poppycock, where ostentatious negativity is football’s version of the fatberg and many people would rather be right than happy, is a stain on our daily bread.

That said, what a roflcopter of a start! Given the events of last season, it was never going to be an equanimity-cultivating experience for a new Rangers manager to see Russell Martin’s start and lower it. Rangers have one point from two league games and are out of Bigger Vase after the most costly 1-1 draw against Polish opposition on British soil since Brian Clough called somebody a clown. Paradoxically, the aggregate defeat to Jagiellonia Bialystok – and subsequent drop into Tin Pot – has increased Rangers’ chances of winning a trophy under McInnes. Time will tell whether those chances have increased from 0.0000001% to 0.0000002%, from 9% to 9.4% or from some other figure to some other figure. Right now, the supercomputers know, and the bairns in the prams certainly don’t.
