Sports.title: How will the three promoted teams fare in the Premier League?
Sports.content:
Coventry

A quarter of a century after their last appearance in the Premier League – following financial ruin, ground-sharing in Northampton and Birmingham and even a spell in League Two – Coventry have finally completed their comeback story. But the bunting has been packed away and they now face the daunting task of proving they belong in the top flight.

Frank Lampard is not starting from scratch. Coventry’s success last season was a collective effort and a product of smart recruitment over the past few years. The result was a side that overwhelmed the Championship with a fearless front-footed approach without relying on a single scorer. Seven Coventry players scored seven or more league goals.

They led the division for shots on target; they ranked second for big chances created, touches in the opposition’s final third and touches in the penalty area; and they produced direct attacking speed and passes-per-sequence numbers comparable to those of some of the Premier League’s most direct sides, including Brentford and Bournemouth.

The title was wrapped up with three games to spare; they conceded the fewest goals in the division (45 in 46 games); and their 97-goal haul was the fourth highest in a 46-game Championship season, behind only Fulham in 2021–22, Bournemouth in 2014–15 and Reading in 2005–06. Given the success Fulham and Bournemouth have enjoyed in recent years, Coventry will hope that proves a good omen.

Continuity is going to be central to their hopes of survival. They are not following in the footsteps of Sunderland, who spent about £155m last summer. Coventry’s net spend was about £3.5m last summer and just 17% of minutes on the pitch last season went to newcomers. Their best business in the transfer window was holding on to players such as Jack Rudoni and Milan van Ewijk, who were attracting interest from top-flight clubs.

View image in fullscreen Coventry’s captain, Matt Grimes, and manager, Frank Lampard enjoy the Championship parade. Now comes the hard part. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

They have not gone wild this summer but they have invested. Coventry have signed the centre-back Aurèle Amenda from Eintracht Frankfurt, the winger Loum Tchaouna from Burnley, and the midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi from Nordsjælland while also securing permanent deals for Frank Onyeka and Carl Rushworth, who were on loan at the club last season. They have also brought back the former favourite Gustavo Hamer after his spell at Sheffield United.

Lampard’s biggest challenge will be adapting a style built to dominate in the Championship into one capable of surviving the Premier League. Their direct, attacking approach will be riskier against opponents who possess the pace, quality and tactical sophistication to punish a rushed pass or a risky vertical ball.

Coventry will not have the same territorial control or volume of chances they enjoyed last season either – they need players who can get them up the pitch. Haji Wright’s pace and ability to attack space should be valuable, but Ellis Simms, who tends to thrive attacking the penalty area, will need service.

Hull

The fact Hull are playing in the Premier League this season borders on miraculous. This is a side that survived relegation to League One on goal difference the season before last, entered 2025-26 under a transfer embargo, scraped into the playoffs by beating Norwich on the final day of the season, and scored a stoppage-time winner in the playoff final. No one backed them in their pre-season predictions and yet, under the guidance of the relatively unknown Sergej Jakirovic in his first season in charge, they defied the statistics.

If matches in the Championship last season had been decided by expected goals, Hull would have finished second bottom. The glaringly obvious problem was at the back. They conceded 66 goals, giving them the fourth worst defensive record in the Championship. Looking back at the last 15 teams to be promoted to the Premier League, only Southampton (who conceded 63 goals when they were promoted in 2023-24) have come close to that tally and they went on to concede 86 goals in the top flight, finishing rock bottom with just 12 points.

As if that weren’t bad enough, Hull were lucky to not concede more: opponents failed to convert 10 opportunities where they had at least a 50% chance of scoring according to xG – the most of any side in the league. Hull simply have to improve as fortune does not tend to stick around long when you’re in the Premier League.

There are some reasons for optimism, though. Their form against the top teams in away matches was impressive. They conceded just eight goals in their matches at the teams in the top 10; they did not concede in either of their games against Coventry; and they didn’t concede in any of their playoff matches.

View image in fullscreen Hull City players celebrate reaching the Premier League with a victory parade. Photograph: Bruce Rollinson/PA

Jakirovic showed an impressive knack of switching tactics depending on whom his side faced or how a game was evolving. His switch from their usual 4-2-3-1 formation to a back three with wingbacks in the second leg of their playoff tie against Millwall was perhaps the most telling example of this succeeding as they caught Millwall by surprise, winning 2-0 at the Den. If continuity is the key word in Coventry’s fight for survival then chaos seems to be Hull’s. You don’t really know what to expect from them. The striker Oli McBurnie pointed this out last season: “It’s probably hard to gameplan against us, because we play so many different ways against different teams.”

As well as their unpredictability, this team have heart. They defied all expectations to reach the top, overcoming a relegation battle, a transfer embargo and statistical odds. Jakirovic put their success down to the bond they have forged. “It was like a puzzle,” he said. “Maybe it was the best that it happened like this. This group of players became even closer. They had to stick together and help each other.” As Robert Earnshaw, who played for Derby in their disastrous 2007-08 campaign, has warned: “You can relegate yourself based on how you think. It was almost as if everyone gave up. It was 20 games to go and it was like: ‘We’re never going to do it.’” This Hull side have fight and that should count for something.

Ipswich

Two years ago Ipswich entered the Premier League as one of football’s feelgood stories. After they had had 22 years away from the top flight, Kieran McKenna took them back through back-to-back promotions, turning a squad largely built for League One into Championship contenders. The 2023-24 campaign was fuelled by fearless, attacking football, late goals and a sense of togetherness, with Ipswich finishing second behind Leicester and becoming the first side in 12 years to climb from League One to the Premier League in successive seasons.

McKenna’s side had an established core who had grown together and exceeded expectations but they were small fish in a very big pond, and the Premier League quickly exposed the gulf in quality. Ipswich won just four games, conceded 82 times and finished 19th with 22 points. Their immediate return to the top flight, fuelled by Premier League experience and parachute payments, means this is a very different promotion story – less about underdogs defying expectations and more about a club that is aiming to belong in this league.

Their recruitment in 2024 suggested they had one eye on a return to the second tier. They brought in leading Championship players who had potential but were not proven at the top: Omari Hutchinson, Jack Clarke, Liam Delap, Dara O’Shea and Jacob Greaves. The club’s CEO, Mark Ashton, says they have to be “a bit braver” this time around. Rather than focusing on potential, they want to sign battle-ready, established top-flight performers.

Florentino Luís and Sasa Lukic bring the physicality and ball-winning presence the midfield lacked in 2024-25, while Issa Diop adds Premier League experience at the back. At the other end, with no Ipswich player scoring more than 10 non-penalty goals last season, Emersonn gives them a physically imposing striker, while Daizen Maeda and Abdul Fatawu add running power and intensity. Crucially, a lot of these players have Premier League experience and, with O’Shea, Clarke, Greaves and Jaden Philogene remaining from the season they went down, this is a side that look more ambitious and ready to compete.

Their defence also looks far more equipped for the top flight. They had the second best defensive record in the Championship last season, keeping 17 clean sheets and conceding just 47 goals (10 fewer goals than when they were promoted in 2023-24). This is not the chaotic and entertaining side that got them to the Premier League two years ago, but a more patient team that know how to be pragmatic and aggressive.

The biggest negative is the departure of the man who guided them back to the Premier League, with McKenna stepping away from football. Gary O’Neil, his replacement, has experienced Premier League relegation battles with Bournemouth and Wolves but it will be difficult to replace the identity, relationships and collective belief McKenna spent five years building through three promotions in four years, and 105 wins in 222 games. O’Neil is inheriting a more expensive and talented side than Ipswich had two years ago, but he will have to hit the ground running and help a host of new players to adapt quickly.

This is an article by WhoScored

Sports.title: How 'Gladiator' Amy Hunt became Britain's newest sprint superstar - as self-styled 'track goddess' eyes fantastic four golds in Birmingham and nipping at the heels of the international elite
Sports.content:
See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The fingers told the story of Amy Hunt’s incomplete mission in Birmingham on Thursday evening. First, she showed two for the gold medals she has collected so far in her domination of European sprinting and then she held up four to signify a job half done.

Even in this city of bovine obsessions, there presumably isn’t a bull stubborn enough to wager against that target being met over the weekend.

On Saturday, she will team up with Dina Asher-Smith in the 4x100m, for which the British quartet are favourites, and they will go again in the mixed relay on Sunday. Given the male talent pool includes Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu, respectively the European gold and silver medallists, Hunt’s chances of delivering on her astonishing projections are more than strong.

By now, folk are aware enough of her remarkable talents, both for the winning of races over short distances and her willingness to accompany the golds with spoken nuggets. In an era when too many of her contemporaries hide their personalities behind thick shields, Hunt, 24, is the open book athletics needed; a Cambridge graduate who isn’t afraid to share idiosyncratic declarations of self-confidence and one who, repeatedly, has backed up big talk with big performances.

By Thursday night, with the 200m title added to the 100m gold won on Monday, she was channelling Russell Crowe’s Gladiator on the track with the cry: ‘Are you not entertained?’ It was later followed by a charming explanation to reporters that her father is so obsessed by the film that his parting words to his daughter, prior to each race, include another Maximus classic: ‘Strength and honour.’

Added to the 200m world silver medal Hunt in Tokyo last year, the honours are adding up. So too is the strength of conviction that Olympic prizes and Asher-Smith’s British sprint records could soon be under threat by the next British speedster off the rank.

Newly crowned double European sprint champion Amy Hunt is the open book that athletics needs

On Saturday, she will team up with Dina Asher-Smith in the 4x100m

Hunt signalled she is halfway to her target of four gold medals after adding 200m glory to her 100m triumph

It is an enticing thought, especially as we approach the halfway point of the LA Olympic cycle. But there are a couple of caveats at play – by timings, the best of Asher-Smith, 30, remains some way ahead of what we have seen so far from Hunt, and more pertinent, the places on an Olympic podium are further clear again.

Some context here: Hunt’s best at the 100m is 10.97sec, which was delivered in Stockholm earlier this year, and at the longer distance she clocked 22.08sec in Tokyo last year. Fast as the sporting world likes to move on, let’s not forget Asher-Smith went 0.15sec faster in winning the 100m world silver in 2019 and was 0.2sec quicker while winning 200m gold at the same championships.

Asher-Smith, a world-class athlete at her best and, more importantly, an expert at managing the rounds at a championship, is no soft target. In other words, Hunt will need to maintain this steep trajectory to even get close to breaking her national records.

The other conversation involves catching the world’s elite and perspective is needed – in 2026, when we have seen the best of Hunt in the 100m, she only ties 25th in the global list, more than 0.3sec off the top, and her standard for the 200m places her 10th, more than half a second off Julien Alfred.

The purpose of mentioning these deficits is not to dilute any hype, but an accurate scaling of where she stands when non-European bibs are in the race might be necessary. In doing so, it should also be recognised, with some excitement, that Hunt is not close to being the finished article. That is a good thing.

Adam Gemili, her former training partner and an excellent analyst of the biomechanics in sprinting, told the Daily Telegraph that he can foresee Hunt reaching the 21.6s in the 200m, her stronger discipline.

The long stride of a 5ft 11ins runner has a certain ring of Usain Bolt about it; the trade off is slower starts in the 100m, but there are those around UK Athletics who believe she can the top-end speeds of the best women in the world. On the latter, it was demonstrated in how she ran down the field in the shorter distance on Monday and again when she passed Asher-Smith on the straight on Thursday.

Hunt's best times are still slower than Dina Asher-Smith at her peak and improvement will be needed to catch the world's best

It is exciting that Hunt is not the finished article with Adam Gemili forecasting she can go 21.6s in the 200m

Those strengths offer fascinating possibilities, as does her comfort in the unique challenge of a championship, where the pressure is greatest and fatigue accumulates between rounds. As Hunt previously demonstrated by describing herself as an 'academic badass and track goddess', some athletes are more born to the spotlight than others. Lord Sebastian Coe, president of World Athletics, has been among the luminaries at the European Championships to identify that ease with her circumstances as a decisive trait.

Doubtless it will be tested in more extreme circumstances at the world championships next year, by which point more time will have been afforded to understanding Hunt’s peculiar issue with low blood pressure. She revealed it in the wake of winning the 200m, with the consequence that felt close to fainting during a race in London earlier this year. Less than ideal.

But Hunt has overcome all manner of problems to get this far. It should not be forgotten that after breaking the under-18 world record for the 200m, she spent years tormented by injuries. A ruptured quadricep while at university left her in such a state that she needed help from her mother to get out of the shower.

These days, she might require assistance carrying the medals and little else.

Sports.title: Revealed: Cristiano Ronaldo signed prenup agreement with new wife Georgina Rodriguez, as marriage certificate and full details of their wedding at £30m mansion emerge
Sports.content:
Revealed: Cristiano Ronaldo signed prenup agreement with new wife Georgina Rodriguez, as marriage certificate and full details of their wedding at £30m mansion emerge

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez got married at their new £30million mansion near Lisbon in front of just four witnesses and their children, it emerged today.

Cristiano's doting mum Dolores Aveiro and his three siblings Hugo, Elma and Katia, were not present at the intimate civil ceremony, which took place at 1.30pm on Tuesday.

Georgina's sister Ivana, Cristiano's long-time friend Miguel Paixao and a Spanish couple named as Jose Rodriguez Sangil and his wife Monica Goncalez Martinez were the only witnesses.

Registrar Maria Manuel Ferreira de Campos Folhadela de Oliveira travelled from the northern Portuguese city of Porto to Cascais to officiate the ceremony.

And the star couple, who married exactly one year to the day after they announced their engagement on social media, have decided to keep their prenuptial assets separate despite tying the knot after a decade-long romance.

Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez married with four witnesses in Cascais, Lisbon

The marriage certificate for Ronaldo and Georgina's wedding has now emerged

The couple posted photos of them wearing their wedding rings after the small ceremony

They signed a prenup agreement to define their property regime on August 10, a day before the ceremony, at a public notary's office in Lisbon.

Cristiano Ronaldo's representatives confirmed earlier this week the footballer and his long-time partner married on August 11 in an 'intimate' ceremony in Cascais after the couple posted photos of them wearing their wedding rings on social media.

It followed speculation which turned out to be false that they were due to marry at Funchal Cathedral in Cristiano's native island of Madeira on Saturday.

No details had emerged about where in Cascais they had wed or who exactly was at the ceremony apart from their children.

Overnight respected Portuguese newspaper Jornal de Noticias published a copy of the marriage certificate showing it took place at Cristiano's massive mansion in the upmarket residential area of Quinta da Marina.

And it also evidenced the fact so few people were invited there appeared to be no place for Cristiano's mum, who gave the union her blessing shortly afterwards by posting a heart emoticon on her son's Instagram in response to his wedding announcement, or the rest of his family apart from his children.

Jose Rodriguez Sangil was described as a Spanish jeweller by Portuguese press.

The marriage document listed Cristiano's full name and age of 41 as well as his birthplace and the names of his parents, including his late father Jose Dinis.

Cristiano's massive built-from-scratch mansion in Quinta da Marina was the venue

The home boats an impressive infinity pool, underground car park and a private cinema room

Ronaldo wore his wedding ring on his finger as he returned to training in Saudi Arabia

The same details were listed for 32-year-old Georgina, born in the Argentinian capital Buenos Aires, and referenced by her full name of Georgina Luisa Rodriguez Hernandez. They will both keep their pre-marriage names.

The marriage certificate was recorded as number 1,493 of this year but appears to have been listed at Porto's Registry Office instead of Cascais which is the municipality where the wedding took place.

Cristiano and Georgina are now back in Saudi Arabia where the Portuguese international plays his club football for Al Nassr ahead of the start of the new season tomorrow.

Sports.title: Paul Scholes names £60m Arsenal star they should 'get rid of' instead of Myles Lewis-Skelly amid Man United and Chelsea links
Sports.content:
Man United legend Paul Scholes believes Arsenal would be making a mistake if they sold Myles Lewis-Skelly this summer - and highlighted another player the Gunners should move on instead.

Lewis-Skelly, 19, enjoyed a breakout campaign in 2024-25, and while he struggled for gametime last time out, he played an important role in the end-of-season run-in.

However, with the £75million addition of Bruno Guimaraes adding to the likes of Martin Zubimendi, Martin Odegaard, Declan Rice, Mikel Merino and Eberechi Eze as options in central midfield, it has raised uncertainty over the 19-year-old's future.

Reports then broke earlier this week suggesting Arsenal had offered Lewis-Skelly to both Chelsea and Man United.

And, speaking on The Overlap Fan Debate, brought to you by Sky Bet, Scholes felt that if Arsenal sanctioned his departure it would be a big mistake.

‘I prefer Myles Lewis-Skelly in centre midfield to Zubimendi,’ Scholes said.

Paul Scholes believes Arsenal would be making a mistake if they sold Myles Lewis-Skelly

Lewis-Skelly has been linked with a move to both Chelsea and Manchester United this summer

‘I think Zubimendi struggled last year. If there’s one player you are going to get rid of, it would be him [Martin Zubimendi].'

Scholes also pointed to a wider issue if Arsenal were to sell their academy graduate, who can play at left-back and in central midfield.

He added: 'It reminds me a little bit of when Danny Welbeck left Manchester United. I hated it, didn’t like it.

'Now, Danny was a little bit older than Myles Lewis-Skelly, but when you’re losing your own players, it’s disappointing.'

Jamie Carragher agreed with Scholes' thoughts and admitted he was left shocked by the reports.

He said 'Do you think it’s from his side or the club’s side? That’s the thing that was a little bit strange about it. It felt almost like Arsenal offered Manchester United Myles Lewis-Skelly.

'It wasn’t Myles Lewis-Skelly saying I want to leave or his people putting something out. That’s where the shock came from.

'I still can’t believe it. Obviously, last season wasn’t great for him for the whole season, but when a young player has already put in performances like I’ve seen him put in at the Bernabeu...

'He was running the game at the Bernabeu from left-back and then his performance in the Champions League final in central midfield against Paris Saint-Germain.'

Scholes felt Arsenal should move on Martin Zubimendi instead of the young Englishman

Carragher continued: 'You can’t play at that level unless you’re pretty special at that age. All young players have ups and downs. Last season he didn’t play as much as he probably would have liked.

'But, as you just said, his ceiling is so high for the performances he’s already put in as a kid. I couldn’t believe that Arsenal would even think about letting him go.'

When pressed on Lewis-Skelly's future earlier this week, Gunners boss Mikel Arteta refused to give anything away.

'I’m not going to talk about any speculation,' he said. ‘If there is a speculation about our players, that’s a good sign. That means that we attract attention and they’re doing a good job.’

Sports.title: Amazon's billionaire founder Jeff Bezos officially buys minority stake in Liverpool - as consortium's £1.65billion investment with ex-QPR owner Amit Bhatia is confirmed in Reds statement
Sports.content:
Amazon's billionaire founder Jeff Bezos officially buys minority stake in Liverpool - as consortium's £1.65billion investment with ex-QPR owner Amit Bhatia is confirmed in Reds statement

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Liverpool owners Fenway Sports Group have officially sold around a third of the club to a consortium of billionaires.

It is a mega-money deal that sees the Boston-based FSG, who also own baseball behemoths the Red Sox, set for a £1.65billion payout.

The consortium is led by former Queens Park Rangers supremo Amit Bhatia, with Amazon founder Jeff Bezos also indirectly involved — though the third-richest man in the world will not have a seat on the board.

Bhatia will become the club’s vice chairman.

Also on the consortium is technology pioneer Bryan Baum and Elaine Saverin, the wife of Facebook co-founder Eduardo who was Mark Zuckerberg’s class mate and business partner.

Mike Gordon, FSG President, said: 'Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club's long-term interests in mind.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos is part of a group to have bought a minority stake in Liverpool

Boston-based FSG, who also own baseball behemoths the Red Sox, are set for a £1.65billion payout

'That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world. As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special.

Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place, and we look forward to working together.'

Sources close to the deal and FSG suggest the move will not impact day-to-day running of the club and the relationship between the hierarchy and Bhatia, who has been in discussions for some time to make said purchase, may flexibly evolve over the years.

FSG maintain the keys to the club and are the majority owners who can make decisions, though Bhatia and his 1892 Holdings will be consulted on big decisions.

Bhatia believes that the consortium is a perfect mix of experience, relationships, contacts and reach across global business which will see them network into India and Asia.

Bhatia said: ‘We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield.

'To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club's continued success for years to come.’

MEET THE KEY PLAYERS

JEFF BEZOS

Bezos is the third-richest man in the world, according to Forbes. In 1994, he read that web usage was growing at a rate of 2,300 per cent a year and wanted to open an online book store, so set one up in his garage in Seattle alongside his then wife Mackenzie Scott.

He changed the name from Cadabra to Amazon after the South American river as, at the time, website listings were alphabetised so an 'A' listing would be near the top. They slowly started selling more products and are now one of the most recognisable companies in the world.

Bezos is no longer the CEO of Amazon but retains the title of executive chairman. He is also the owner of the Washington Post and founder of Blue Origin which competes with Elon Musk in the modern-day space race. He flew to space in 2021.

The 62-year-old has dabbled in the idea of sports investment before. He was interested in buying the current Super Bowl winners Seattle Seahawks and fellow NFL team Washington Commanders but pulled out.

He married former American journalist Lauren Sanchez last year.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has dabbled with the idea of sports ownership in the past

EDUARDO SAVERIN

Saverin was born in Brazil with Romanian heritage. He moved to Miami at age 13 and attended Harvard University. He became friends with fellow undergraduate Mark Zuckerberg and the pair wanted to set up a website for students to communicate, making a $1,000 investment each.

The site was originally named 'The Facebook' and soon grew to other universities, later anyone in the world aged 13 or older. It now has more than 3billion users and its parent company, Meta Platforms, has a market value of around £1.12trillion.

Saverin is played by Andrew Garfield in The Social Network film based on the book Accidental Billionaires about his rise at Facebook. Weeks before Facebook became a public company, he moved to Singapore and renounced his US citizenship.

The 44-year-old is now head of B Capital, a venture capital firm.

Join the discussion How do you feel about foreign billionaires buying into historic English football clubs like Liverpool?

Eduardo Saverin was a co-founder of Facebook and is now head of venture capital firm B Capital

Amit Bhatia, the son in law of Lakshmi Mittal, previously worked for QPR for 19 years

AMIT BHATIA

Bhatia is a 46-year-old British-Indian with an investment banking background in sectors such as technology, media, property, real estate and health.

He formerly worked on Wall Street before founding a construction company aged 32, which has more than 5,000 UK employees. He won the young entrepreneur of the year award in 2013.

Bhatia married Vanisha Mittal in 2004 in a six-day wedding which the Guinness World Records recorded as the most-expensive ceremony of all time at £41m. Vanisha's father is Lakshmi Mittal, the world's 65th-richest man with £24.8bn as per Forbes.

Bhatia worked at QPR for 19 years and his company, AyBe Capital, owns shares in the cricket franchise London Spirit, former England cricketer Kevin Pietersen's YouTube channel and an indoor golf league founded by Rory McIlroy.

The tycoon recently played a round of golf with basketball legend LeBron James and is regularly on the course with Indian cricketing icon Sachin Tendulkar.

Sports.title: Finlay Tarling dead aged 19: British cyclist dies after serious accident during eighth stage of Volta a Portugal
Sports.content:
Finlay Tarling dead aged 19: British cyclist dies after serious accident during eighth stage of Volta a Portugal

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

British cyclist Finlay Tarling has died today after a tragic accident during the Volta a Portugal.

The Welsh rider, 19, was on the eighth stage of the race when the incident occurred on a 166.8km route to Fafe, in the north of the country.

In a statement, his team NSN said: 'We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.

'Fin was a much loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

'Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend.'

In a post on X, the Portuguese Cycling Federation spoke of their 'most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his team-mates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones'.

British cyclist Finlay Tarling died in a serious accident during a race in Portugal

The organisation added that the usual podium ceremony would not take place out of 'respect and mourning'.

Tarling's older brother Josh is a world champion cyclist on the track and a stage winner at last year's Giro d'Italia.

Portuguese newspaper RTP reported that the incident had allegedly been caused by a vehicle that was not involved in the race.

The report stated that the car had driven on the wrong side of the road and collided with Tarling, who had been behind the peloton.

The rider was reportedly given immediate medical attention but died shortly after the crash.

Portugal's president Antonio José Seguro said Tarling's death 'saddens the peloton, the race, and the country that welcomed him'.

He offered his 'deepest condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his teammates at NSN Development Team, and to the entire cycling community, joining in their grief with deep emotion'.

A statement from the International Cycling Union read: 'The UCI is deeply saddened by the tragic death of British rider Finlay Tarling, who passed away following a serious accident during today’s 8th stage of the Volta a Portugal.

'The UCI extends its deepest condolences to Finlay’s family, friends, and teammates.'

More to follow...

Sports.title: Enzo Fernandez expected to STAY at Chelsea for the entire season after club's £120m transfer deadline passes with zero bids from Man City and other suitors
Sports.content:
Chelsea expect Enzo Fernandez to stay for the entirety of this season after a deadline to trigger his exit for £120million passed without incident on Friday.

Manchester City and other interested parties did not lodge a bid for the Argentina midfielder ahead of the 5pm cut-off, with the Blues insistent that the chances of a departure are all but over.

Fernandez has wanted to link back up with former manager Enzo Maresca at the Etihad Stadium, with Chelsea having told the player’s representatives in May that they would facilitate a transfer if a £120m figure was met.

Those terms have now been removed and while City are unlikely to believe a potential deal is dead, they probably would not commit to the sort of outlay Chelsea initially demanded.

City are waiting for Rodri’s future to be finalised, with Barcelona still confident of securing the Spain captain. City want in excess of £60m for the World Cup winner.

The two clubs remain in negotiations over a fee and Rodri – who underwent back surgery after the World Cup - returned to the club’s training ground for pre-season testing on Friday.

Enzo Fernandez is expected to stay at Chelsea for the full season after their self-imposed deadline for clubs to bid for him passed without incident

The 30-year-old travelled back to Manchester on a Ryanair flight to Liverpool on Thursday evening and met Maresca hours later.

Maresca admitted that City still have a significant amount of work to do in the transfer window, with Tijjani Reijnders on his way to Al Qadsiah in Saudi Arabia for £52m. Tottenham are looking to wrap up a deal for Savinho, with City facing Arsenal in the Community Shield on Sunday.

Maresca has suggested that there could be further outgoings in the coming weeks.

‘We’ll see what happens with some more, there is a change in this moment,’ the Italian said. ‘We are in a moment where players that were here many years have already left or [others who] probably can leave.

‘And that means there is a change. We're going to try to do our best. At the moment the transfer window closes, we need to be good enough to find as soon as possible solutions for the team.’

The 46-year-old refused to discuss players from other clubs, adding that ‘I don’t think it’s good when people from other clubs speak about our players’ after a summer of discussion around Rodri in Spain.

Reijnders had decided to pursue other opportunities after a lack of starts last season and Maresca believes there are others in the same boat.

‘They all work every day, they all do sessions every day and at the end of the week they all want to play a game,’ he said.

‘When they don’t play, they struggle to understand or they struggle to see the reason why and I can understand that after one season some of them would like to play a little bit more.

‘It’s a bit difficult to convince players when they are already convinced. You need to change their thoughts, that is not always easy.

‘Tijjani’s situation is like James Trafford’s situation and some more players but I think when the club, the player, the manager, they all think the same way, that probably the best decision for a player is to go, you have to go.’

Sports.title: Cristian Romero confirms his Tottenham exit as he admits he 'wasn't perfect' in heartfelt social media message to fans - with £34m Atletico Madrid move still yet to be announced by the club
Sports.content:
Cristian Romero confirms his Tottenham exit as he admits he 'wasn't perfect' in heartfelt social media message to fans - with £34m Atletico Madrid move still yet to be announced by the club

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Tottenham captain Cristian Romero has posted a farewell to fans ahead of confirming his move to Atletico Madrid.

Atletico have agreed a £34million deal in principle.

The Argentina international posted on Instagram: 'Today, I say goodbye to a place that, for five seasons, was much more than a club. It was my home, my challenge and the place where my family and I built such an important part of our lives.

'I leave with a heart full of memories and enormous pride for everything we lived and achieved together.

'When I arrived, I had a clear dream: to leave my name in this club's history. I knew the only way was through hard work, sacrifice and achieving something that had seemed so difficult for so long: lifting a trophy again.

'**And we did it.**

Cristian Romero confirmed his Tottenham departure ahead of a move to Atletico Madrid

View this post on Instagram

'The journey wasn't perfect, but I don't want that to define my goodbye. I choose to remember the happy moments, the lessons, the people who stood by me and, above all, the love I received during these five years.

'Thank you to everyone at the club who shared this journey with me. Coaches, teammates, staff and every person working behind the scenes you are all part of my story and have a place in my heart.

'And to the fans: Thank you for loving me, respecting me and making me feel like one of you from day one. Thank you for every hug, every song, every flag, every applause and for always being there.

'I know I wasn't perfect, but one thing gives me peace: I always gave everything. I defended this shirt with pride and with all my heart.

'THANK YOU FOR EVERYTHING. I'm leaving the club, but a part of my heart will always remain here.

'Once I was one of you. Today, I leave as one of you forever.

'With all my love and respect.'

Daily Mail Sport reported Premier League champions Arsenal had contacted the agents of the Spurs captain over what the deal would be, but Tottenham were unaware of the Gunners' interest and unwilling to sell 28-year-old Romero to their north London rivals.

The central defender was free to leave Spurs for the right price after the club bolstered their defensive ranks earlier in the transfer window.

The additions of Marcos Senesi on a free transfer and Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton for £52m mean Roberto de Zerbi is well stocked for the season ahead.

Sports.title: Arsenal's Highbury store cordoned off by police tape after alleged 4am break-in
Sports.content:
Arsenal's Highbury store cordoned off by police tape after alleged 4am break-in

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Arsenal's official store near the Emirates Stadium was cordoned off by police this morning following an alleged overnight raid.

One of the doors was left on the ground with another hanging off its hinges following the break-in.

The shop on Drayton Park, north London was targeted between 3.30am and 4.30am, according to the Metropolitan Police.

Police tape surrounding the pavement by the shop told people not to cross as the authorities carried out their investigation.

Police cars hung around for hours and a forensic team was deployed.

'The Met is investigating a theft at the Emirates Stadium shop, Drayton Park, which occurred in the early hours of Friday, 14 August,' a spokesperson said.

Arsenal's club shop was cordoned off on Friday morning after an alleged overnight raid

'We understand the concern such incidents cause to retail workers and local communities.

'Although no arrests have been made at this stage, officers are working at pace to conduct forensic examinations and gather CCTV to identify and locate those responsible.'

Arsenal's club shop sells some of the priciest gear in the Premier League.

The base price for a men's home shirt for the 2026-27 season is £85.

However, prices can soar with modifications - an authentic away shirt with Bruno Guimaraes' name and number on the back costs £146.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan

Semi-final: Italy vs Northern Ireland

Semi-final: Wales vs Bosnia and Herzegovina

Final: Wales/Bosnia and Herzegovina vs Italy/Northern Ireland - Tuesday, 7.45pm kick-off

Play-off Path B:
