World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: As big musicals struggle, Brisbane's indies are innovating to keep the spotlights on
World.content:
While Australia is seeing multi-million-dollar musical theatre productions collapse mid-tour under the weight of soaring costs, resilient, small-scale models are using every available means to find ways to thrive in the local market.

Brisbane's independent companies say while the community's appetite for musical theatre is enduring, they are not immune to mounting economic pressure and are calling for more support.

A self-sufficient cycle

Taylor Atley is the creator and artistic director of Millennial Productions, and started the company in 2021 to produce and advocate for high quality theatre in Brisbane.

But Atley said those aspirations come at a significant cost.

Taylor Atley used her house deposit to start Millennial Productions. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"[The cost of putting on a show] varies, so typically I like to have about $25,000, which is a very low and conservative budget, but that in the past has also gone up to about $80,000 as well," Atley said.

" We're not immune from it. We're in the same boat as everyone else. "

The company aims to keep prices down for attendees, with tickets selling for $35 for the past five year. This year, that increased to $45 to keep up with outgoing costs.

Millennial Productions is completely self-funded, and expenditure does not cover salaries. All cast, crew and creatives involved with the company are volunteers, with cast members also contributing to their own insurance.

Its funds come from ticket sales, fundraisers and food and beverages sold at shows.

"It started with me investing actually my house deposit into the business … to get it off the ground and now, luckily it was able to pay me back, and it's a self-sufficient cycle," Atley said.

Brisbane's independent theatre companies are proving the community's appetite for musical theatre is enduring. (ABC News: Erin Byrnes)

The independent theatre company's success comes as a string of major musicals including Beetlejuice, Waitress and Back to the Future have cancelled, scaled down, or cut short national tours.

Production companies have cited a rise in production and travel costs, as well as changes in consumers' ticket-buying habits.

Extreme financial creativity

Staging high-quality productions is an expensive undertaking for both large and small-scale theatre shows, with tech, lighting, venue hire and licensing fees among the elements populating budget spreadsheets.

Independent operators say their ability to deliver professional standard productions has emerged from extreme financial creativity and resourcefulness.

Millennial Productions has forgone physical programs to help reduce the costs of putting on a show. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"Community theatre is all about being creative. There's no other way … we really have to think things through line item by line item," Atley said.

For their recent production of The Addams Family, Millennial Productions completely recycled and repainted set pieces from previous shows, and swapped physical programs for digital ones to eliminate printing costs.

For their recent production of The Adams Family, Millennial Productions completely recycled and repainted set pieces from previous shows. (ABC News: Erin Byrnes)

The production team also resorted to loading up "as many cars as possible" with multiple loads to bump in and out of the theatre, which Atley said was more economical than a truck hire and diesel costs.

"The viability piece is hard, because we're having to make cuts left, right and centre to make this work," she said.

Brisbane's independent theatre companies are proving the community's appetite for musical theatre is enduring. (ABC News: Erin Byrnes)

Similarly for independent company A Night at the Musicals (ANATM), keeping ticket prices affordable while maintaining high standards requires a strenuous balancing act.

ANATM presents two staged musical theatre concerts a year, as well as monthly industry nights called Broadway Mixers where local emerging performers take to the stage alongside industry professionals in a stripped back showcase.

A Night at the Musicals presents two staged musical theatre concerts a year. (Supplied: A Night at the Musicals)

The Broadway Mixers, which are hosted out of a bar in Woolloongabba, consistently sell out, sometimes within the day of tickets going live online.

Company director Alex Watson said ANATM's larger scale productions are typically able to pay for themselves in one cycle, with tickets ranging from $54.95 to $74.95. But the model is constantly being pushed to its limit.

"You can do anything with time, energy and passion, and if we don't raise the ticket prices but the artists are getting paid more … something has to be sacrificed," he said.

Alex Watson says more support is needed for musical theatre at all levels. (ABC News: Hannah Moon)

"We've tried our absolute best to make [ticket prices] manageable ... but there is a point where we reach a ceiling where we don't feel comfortable going higher on ticket prices in fear of losing audience."

He said all levels of the musical theatre industry need more support.

"At this independent level, the risk is you don't see it at all. It'll be gone forever," he said.

"[Full scale] musicals are one day, something we want to do … but there are elements that we've never had to play with in our variety concerts that constitute a cost that we haven't fronted yet, which is really scary to think of," he said.

With both large and small companies struggling to cover costs, Watson said more government support could help ease operating pressures.

Broadway Mixers hosted by A Night of the Musicals typically sell out. (Supplied: A Night at the Musicals)

A spokesperson for Queensland Arts Minister John Paul Laengrook said the government hopes to grow the state's experience economy, and highlighted recent theatre upgrades delivered in line with election promises.

"The Crisafulli Government is committed to investing significantly in the state's arts, cultural and creative sectors, including the independent theatre companies and performers that create jobs and contribute to our economy."

A Night of the Musicals presents two staged musical theatre concerts a year, (Supplied: A Night at the Musicals)

Taking risks in smaller environment

Performers and organisers in the theatre community have also speculated the cancellations could lead to companies opting for 'safe' revivals of shows that have already performed well in the Australian market, like the recently announced expansion of The Lion King, rather than run the risk of introducing new, unfamiliar material to audiences.

Atley said many companies were having conversations about what shows would be economically viable.

"What can we put on a stage? But also, what are people going to buy tickets to?" she said.

Australian theatre calls for lifeline The local theatre industry hopes a live performance incentive modelled on a successful UK scheme will provide salvation.

"It's really unfortunate because I know everyone else is having the same conversations and then we see the same shows over and over, which then floods the market and causes even bigger issues."

ANATM is using their platform to bring fresh art to Australian shores, performing new songs sweeping Broadway, and The West End at their variety concert later this year.

"As far as we know, we're going to be some of the first people putting on those songs and exposing them to an Australian audience, which will be really great," he said.

"It's really special that we can take those risks in a smaller environment without worrying about doing a national tour to get audiences to see that work."

World.title: The weirdest by-election in recent UK history marked a return to the status quo
World.content:
It was a bizarre by-election from the start.

Despite a major-party boycott, voters faced the longest ballot paper in British electoral history, with a record number of candidates — including a comedian dressed as a bin and an Australian running to "reclaim woke".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage easily won back the seat of Clacton after resigning and immediately recontesting it in July in protest over a parliamentary probe into undeclared donations.

The result was never really in doubt, but the finale was anything but predictable.

Mr Farage declared victory hours before the official result, then skipped the count.

The ballot paper for the by-election for the parliamentary seat of Clacton. (AFP: Henry Nicholls)

Reform said police had warned him of a "credible threat", though it's understood police did not advise him to stay away.

That left his most high-profile rival, Count Binface, to claim victory "out of the candidates who bothered to turn up".

Mixed response from locals after result

Count Binface emerged as Nigel Farage's main rival in the by-election. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

Count Binface became the most successful comedy candidate in British Parliamentary history, winning 9,455 votes — more than a quarter of the electorate.

Mr Farage won 22,239 votes with a turnout of 44.37 per cent.

At the general election of 2024, he got 21,225 votes, with a turnout of 58.7 per cent.

In a post online, UK director of polling group More in Common, Luke Tryl, said Mr Farage would be pleased with his vote tally but Count Binface's share showed that opposition to Reform is also motivating voters.

In the seaside town at the centre of the political circus, locals had mixed views.

"It's a joke, an absolute joke. I just think the whole thing is a farce," said Emma, who has lived in Clacton with her partner and five children for 16 years.

"We laugh at it every time we see it come up on the news."

Elliot wants to see better representation for his area. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

But for first time voter Elliot, voting for Count Binface was an act of political agency.

The twenty-year-old said he was disappointed, not only with the result, but with the fact Mr Farage failed to attend the count.

"We feel under-represented," Elliot said.

" I'd love to have some actual representation here. It's disappointing again, but hopefully the local area will realise that. "

Clacton resident and long time Farage supporter Marie did not think it necessary for Mr Farage to attend the vote count. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

A few hundred metres along the boardwalk a longtime supporter of Mr Farage, Marie, defended his absence.

"He was already thanking him last night at his party, wasn't he? He was," she said, referring to a private gathering Mr Farage attended where he declared victory hours before the official result.

The 60-year-old Clacton resident did not believe it was necessary for Mr Farage to attend the public count, despite it being a longtime UK tradition.

"I just think it was out of order that he had to choose to do the by-election in the first place, because everyone's against him," Marie said.

Farage wins Clacton as Count Binface takes more than a quarter of votes The Reform UK leader secured 62.8 per cent of the vote, but Count Binface’s extraordinary second-place finish was the surprise of the night.

Not everyone believed the claim the by-election was Mr Farage versus the establishment.

"They're all the same, they're all out to play with their own nests," 63-year-old Mick said.

Like many others we spoke to along the foreshore, Mick hasn't voted for years.

"It's just a bunch of clowns, isn't it?" he said.

"The biggest clown won."

Despite the constant circus comparisons, the by-election's returning officer, chief executive of Tendring Council Ian Davidson, told the ABC the election was extremely serious.

"In this area here you have some of the most deprived areas in England. You also have more people with mental health issues that are ahead of population than anywhere else in England," he said.

The area has faced decades of economic and social decline thanks to a decline in tourism and high economic inactivity.

"So for us it really isn't a joke," Mr Davidson said.

"We want our MP being in parliament, fighting for us. Whoever that MP may be."

Clacton lively for election day

Clacton-on-Sea is the closest sandy beach to London, around 130 kilometres from the capital. (ABC News: Andrew Greaves)

The day of the by-election also happened to be the hottest day of the year in England. The foreshore was packed with families and rainbow beach umbrellas.

As the closest sandy beach to London, around 130 kilometres north-east of the capital, it was a popular spot.

Long lines of locals and tourists queued up for ice cream or fish and chips in front of the town's iconic amusement park on the pier.

The seat of Clacton is much broader than Clacton-On-Sea — it includes rural villages, farmland and several seaside towns.

No matter where you go there, no-one's apathetic about their re-elected local member.

His constituents either love or loathe him.

One of the local taxi drivers told us he didn't want to talk about politics before volunteering that he planned to vote for Mr Farage.

The grandfather had lived in Clacton for 16 years and agreed with the MP's approach to immigration.

"I'm not racist but you've got to look after your own," he told me.

Some locals told us Mr Farage was a frequent visitor. Others claimed he was never there.

Nigel Farage visits The Ship on the day of voting in the Clacton by-election. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

One place Mr Farage has frequented over the years is his favourite local pub, The Three Jays.

When we dropped in on polling day it was covered with Reform signs.

The landlord jokingly told us it's "Nigel's pub". Many of the regulars consider Mr Farage a friend.

Inside, patrons drunk beer on Reform coasters, seated under Union Jack bunting while listening to a soundtrack of 80s classics.

David and Margi treated themselves to a pub lunch after voting for Mr Farage.

"I think he's brilliant," Margi said.

Neither one was concerned about the expenses scandal that triggered his resignation.

"Like he said, he's going to need protection for the rest of his life," the 78-year-old said, referring to Mr Farage's claim he needed the five million pound "gift" for security.

David and Margi treated themselves to a pub lunch after voting for Nigel Farage. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

But not everyone is so keen on Mr Farage.

Back in the pub car park, a man driving past in a blue hatchback slowed down when he saw our microphone.

"Nigel Farage is rubbish," he yelled, before taking off again.

Given the unusual nature of the vote, analysts disagree over its broader significance.

Loading...

Before he called the by-election, Mr Farage was riding high in the polls. Since then, the political landscape has shifted significantly, with the ruling Labour party enjoying a bump after a change in prime minister.

"Certainly since this by-election was called and Mr Burnham became prime minister, Reform's vote has been dropping. Not a lot, one or two points, but it is behind Labour in many polls now," UK election guru Sir John Curtice told the ABC.

Apart from the polls the result has meant a return to the status quo.

Mr Farage is still the MP, and the parliamentary investigation into Mr Farage's finances that was paused during the campaign has already restarted.

World.title: Excluded from early learning, kids like Tommy 'falling through the gaps'
World.content:
June 30 seemed like an ordinary day for four-year-old Tommy Schumacher.

That morning, his parents packed his bag and sent him off to his early learning centre in Milton, on the NSW south coast.

However, a few hours later, the family received a phone call and an email from the centre's management in Canberra.

"I am writing to inform you that unfortunately we are no longer able to support Thomas' place at Budawang, effective immediately," the email said.

Tommy lives with Perthes disease and uses a wheelchair. (Supplied)

The decision had "not been made lightly" and it followed legal advice received that very day, the email stated.

His belongings would be handed over when Tommy was collected that afternoon.

His mother Jessica said the sudden nature of the decision was hard for Tommy to comprehend.

"They just basically pushed him out the door. There was no transition for him," she said.

"It's not OK."

Tommy's mother Jessica feels let down by the centre. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

When he was two years old, Tommy was diagnosed with Perthes disease, meaning the blood supply to the ball of his hip was lost.

"[The] femoral head in his hip died. It lost blood supply," Ms Schumacher said.

"The bone went from a ball to a little pancake and was slowly growing back."

Tommy's condition means he should not put weight on his legs, so he uses a wheelchair and needs to have his nappy changed.

The nappy-changing process is what ultimately led to his exclusion from Budawang.

"The early learning centre [said] that their change area now isn't big enough to facilitate him," Ms Schumacher said.

Tommy pictured with his brother Jackson and their family dog Bear. (Supplied)

Centre says Tommy was 'loved'

A spokesperson for Budawang said the centre was "truly saddened" by the experience of Tommy and his family.

"Thomas has been a very loved member of our community and we tried our best to care for him safely as long as we possibly could," the spokesperson said.

The centre said it implemented measures to meet his needs, including changes to the playground and furniture to improve accessibility and inclusion.

A Budawang spokesperson says the centre is "truly saddened". (Supplied)

According to Budawang, an occupational therapist's review determined there was not enough physical space to safely change Tommy.

It followed a nappy-changing incident earlier this year in which Tommy was mistakenly removed from his wheelchair and showered.

Budawang said it needed to create a "private and hygienic area large enough to fit a portable hoist, a suitable changing area, bath, Thomas' wheelchair, Thomas and two educators".

"We had been working with our landlord to explore how the changes required could be accommodated, but we are a very small community centre and creating such a space would require significant building modifications, planning permissions and capital works," they said.

The site is owned by the NSW Department of Education.

Tommy visited parliament

Tommy and his family visited state parliament and watched question time. (ABC News)

The Schumachers believe Tommy was treated unfairly and cannot see a world in which they would send their son back, even if necessary works were carried out.

They have not been able to find an early learning centre that can accommodate his needs.

And the NDIS has denied the family's request to fund support workers during the day.

"Tommy is just falling through the gaps of the system with no supports in place for him," Ms Schumacher said.

Both Tommy's parents work full time, so the four-year-old's grandparents are caring for him five days a week.

Last week, Tommy and his family visited state parliament and watched question time, during which Shadow Early Education Minister Felicity Wilson raised his case.

The four-year-old's case was raised by the shadow early education minister. (Supplied)

Ms Wilson said it was "disappointing" the four-year-old's disability was preventing him from accessing early childhood education.

" Tommy, like any other child … really needs access to quality early learning. It's the foundation of the future of the rest of their lives. "

She said Education and Early Learning Minister, Prue Car, should intervene.

"We'd call on her to make sure that she finds a place for Tommy so he can get the education and care that he needs, just like any other child, regardless of their ability," Ms Wilson said.

Ms Car said Tommy's case was "very concerning".

"The Department of Education owns the land that the early learning centre is on and manages the licence agreement," she said.

"But, obviously, this was a decision made by the provider."

Prue Car commented on Tommy's situation. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Nonetheless, she vowed to explore potential solutions.

"I will go away and ensure that we are doing everything possible we can do within our remit," she said.

However, funding for disability support in long day care centres was the responsibility of the federal government, she said.

Nowhere to turn

Tommy's case highlights the barriers many children with disabilities face when trying to access early childhood education.

In 2022, Children and Young People with Disabilities Australia (CYDA) surveyed 181 parents and caregivers about their experiences.

One in five reported their child being refused enrolment, while nearly a quarter said they were offered reduced hours.

There are barriers many children with disabilities face when trying to access early childhood education. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Access to child care more generally is worse in regional areas of NSW.

A 2024 analysis by the Mitchell Institute found there were 0.85 places per child in the Sydney suburb of Chippendale.

However, in Ulladulla, where the Schumachers live, there were 0.47 places per child.

In the region directly surrounding the town, that figure drops to 0.15.

The Minns government is in the process of building 100 public preschools, but the closest will be at Sanctuary Point, a 45-minute drive away.

Ms Schumacher said she hoped Tommy's case would draw attention to the exclusion some children with disabilities face.

World.title: Trial project sees everyday locals settle refugees in their backyard
World.content:
Alain Mukungu thought moving to a town with the same name as a piece of fruit meant he had to become a farmer.

"Orange means it's a farm where they are growing so many oranges," he said with a laugh.

"They want us maybe to go and do farming or something like that."

After spending more than two decades in a refugee camp fleeing the war in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mr Mukungu said he was willing to move anywhere.

"Wherever they'll take me, wherever I'll go, I'll accept," he said.

" At least I'll be free. "

Kate Baxter (left) and Peter Warren (right) welcomed Alain Mukungu and his family to Orange through the CRISP program. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

Mr Mukungu, his wife and seven children were met at Sydney Airport by a group of residents from Orange called Hearts and Hands.

They were a collection of everyday Australians who put their hands up to be a part of the Community Refugee Integration and Settlement Pilot (CRISP) program.

They drove the family back to the regional city, where Mr Mukungu's first reaction was concern.

"I see the place is too small, is there any way I can work here?" he said.

"I wanted maybe like in the big cities where there are companies [and] industries."

But now, a year and a half on, Mr Mukungu works in social support services, has a driver's licence and owns a car.

He is watching his family thrive in the regional community, as his children get their own licences and save for vehicles.

Alain Mukungu, his wife, and seven children moved to Orange on the NSW Central Tablelands. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

"We feel like being home, [Hearts and Hands] is part of our family," he said.

" If it was [only] ourselves, maybe by this time we're still far from where we are today. "

Trial program made permanent

The federal government has now made the CRISP pilot program permanent after it welcomed more than 950 refugees across the country during a four-year trial.

It involves groups of locals banding together to welcome a household into their community over a 12-month period.

Hearts and Hands coordinator Kate Baxter, from the Orange Presbyterian Church, said she learnt about the program four years ago and relished the chance to support refugees.

"I didn't think that living in the country that was necessarily something that would even be an opportunity," she said.

Kate Baxter says it is not only about helping households with appointments, but establishing a friendship. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

The volunteer community members receive training and support from the supervising body Community Refugee Sponsorship Australia (CRSA) to connect with the family, help them with housing, set up services like Centrelink and Medicare, and fundraise for their needs.

Enriching yet challenging experience

Mr Mukungu's family is one of three households the Hearts and Hands group has helped settle.

Ms Baxter's husband, Peter Warren, said it had been a joyful and challenging experience.

"I remember when we first took this on, we felt a little bit like, 'This is like fostering somebody,'" he said.

"You can't say to them, look, this is not working … you have to be able to deal with the situations that arise.

" People don't leave their country for no reason. "

Alain Mukungu and his family have lived in Orange for a year and a half with the help of the CRISP group Hearts and Hands. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

Ms Baxter said her life had been deeply enriched by the connections she had made with refugee families.

"It's building a friendship because when these families arrive, they know nobody," she said.

Ms Baxter recalled visiting her first household from Afghanistan for dinner, and the children were being secretive in one of the rooms.

After the meal, they led her down the hallway and opened the door to a cake, decorations and music.

"They said, 'We want to celebrate Mother's Day for you,'" Ms Baxter recalled.

CRISP groups help refugee households navigate community services like Centrelink, Medicare, housing arrangements and school enrolments. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

"It was just an absolutely lovely moment that showed how you can connect with people who are nothing like you in terms of your culture, background and life experience."

Mr Warren said it had been profound to share in the households' cultures too.

"It's not just the welcome we provide but the welcome they provide as well," he said.

Review finds high levels of belonging

A University of Queensland review found that refugees who settled through the CRISP program had comparable, and in many cases better, outcomes to the government-supported equivalent.

For refugees in regional areas, it found they experienced a similar high level of belonging to their city counterparts, but achieved "notably higher" employment rates.

More than 950 refugees were settled through the CRISP program across the country in places like Orange. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

It did note regional refugees had difficulty accessing specialist services, and felt isolated at times due to fewer opportunities for cultural connections.

In Orange, Mr Mukungu has never met another Congolese person but has met people from Zimbabwe, Nigeria and Kenya.

"These African people, they are busy," he said.

Alain Mukungu says his family would not be where it is today without the support and guidance of the Hearts and Hands locals. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

"Now imagine if I had not these people [Hearts and Hands] who I was supposed to meet?

" They are with us most, and we feel like we are in a safe place and we know some people. "

Program 'doable' for any Australian

CRSA chief executive Lisa Button said she felt heartened by the strong outcomes from the CRISP regional refugees.

"It's not that surprising when I think about the sorts of people who are stepping up to be part of this program and how well connected they tend to be in their local communities," she said.

Ms Button said it was not something to enter into lightly, but said it was "doable" for any Australian.

"This is a real opportunity to walk the talk of your values," she said.

Lisa Button (right) welcoming CRISP families at Sydney Airport. (Supplied: Lisa Button)

"We've all had opportunities to build our lives here and succeed, and if it's not us, it's our ancestors unless you're an Indigenous Australian.

"Think about the Australia you've benefited from … and the Australia that you wish to see in the future."

World.title: Showery days ahead after week of sunny Queensland skies
World.content:
Scattered showers will fall on much of Queensland's east coast this weekend, with the state's south-west also in for overcast and potentially stormy weather heading into next week.

The Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) has forecast scattered showers in Queensland's south-east, Central and Cassowary coasts today, North Tropical Coast tomorrow, and isolated showers in the eastern Darling Downs through the weekend.

An 'unusually' warm winter Climate experts point to climate change and El Niño as the reasons behind a warmer winter.

BOM senior meteorologist Felim Hanniffy said the Sunshine Coast region would see the most frequent rain, with localised falls of up to 20 millimetres expected on Saturday and 10mm on Sunday.

"But certainly, for other parts of the south-east, including the Gold Coast, there will be a lot more cloud around, a lot more showers, particularly from Saturday afternoon onwards and then persisting into Sunday and for the early days of next week as well," he said.

"We may even see a tick up in the showers and rainfall totals as we head into the early days of next week in South-East Queensland."

Mr Hanniffy said a different weather pattern was at play compared to last week's dry westerly bursts, which had brought colder mornings and clear days.

"This weekend and into next week, the winds will be coming from the south-east off the sea," he said.

" It does mean milder or warmer overnight minimums and then plenty of showers around and a lot more cloud around during the days as well. "

Later in the weekend it could also become blustery at times along the coast, Mr Hanniffy said.

"We are looking at a pretty showery picture for this weekend in the east."

Mild temperatures expected

Minimum temperatures are expected to be near average in the state's south-east and Cape York today, and below average elsewhere, with fog forecast around the Central Coast and patches of morning frost in the southern and central interior.

Tomorrow will bring cooler-than-average conditions in the far north and north-west, as well as a chance of morning fog between Ingham and St Lawrence.

Mr Hanniffy said an average maximum of 22 degrees was expected in the state, a "little bit on the cooler side for August", but with no major cold snaps to come.

"The overnight minimums are holding up into double digits as well, just due to the fact that the winds are onshore," he said.

"So, we're not expecting any kind of significant cold mornings really for most of next week."

A separate weather system concentrated in the state's far west is also forecast to bring increased showers and some thunderstorms late tomorrow and early next week.

World.title: The fight to protect an 85-year-old fire station and its 'haunted' history
World.content:
Sitting atop a high ridge, a heavy red-brick Art Deco building has loomed over the gold-rush town of Gympie for the best part of a century.

The bells and sirens of the Gympie Fire Station have rung out since 1940, a mainstay in the town even as trucks, equipment and training evolved.

The fire station in 1955, about 15 years after it first began operating for the town. (Supplied: John Oxley Library)

The building is unlike any other in the town, with its distinctive rounded spotter's tower and even the occasional ghost story to hold the town's imagination.

Gympie firefighters moved to newer premises earlier this year, far better suited to their modern trucks and equipment.

The Queensland Fire Department (QFD) has confirmed it is "exploring options" to offload the old site.

But residents and historians say while the building's future is unclear, it is too important to be lost to progress or development.

A big cost for a country at war

The Gympie Fire Station was a controversial project, built in the first years of World War II for 6,800 pounds ($710,000 in 2025 terms), a seemingly great deal, paid for by the council, government and insurance companies.

A newspaper report after its opening hinted at the frustration over the cost.

The fire station has Art Deco flourishes unique in the former gold-mining town. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

The then minister for health and home affairs, Ned Hanlon, who would become Queensland's premier in the years following, said the government's policy was to "build well and build truly".

By the time it was vacated earlier this year, it had become the state's oldest, still-operational station.

Despite its impressive presence, a tragedy in its first years of operation would become an inescapable part of its history.

In March 1943, 20-year-old Kevin James Bennetts fell from the spotter's tower and died the following day in hospital.

Despite some changes, eventually the size of vehicles became too big for the aging building. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

The young man was a relieving fire spotter, called up for a 4pm-to-midnight shift, and was watching two fires to the station's south when he fell.

The tragedy involving its distinctive tower has become an important part of the building's history and lore.

The push for a heritage listing

Gympie historian Jack Carr said he had always been struck by the fire house's "inter-war functionalist style", fully faced brickwork and Art Deco flourishes.

Jack Carr says he fears the building could be demolished one day if not protected. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

His love of the station inspired him to fight for its heritage listing.

"Like with lots of heritage, once it's going and once [a future] development is approved, it's too late," he said.

"[Heritage listing] doesn't prevent reuse of the site, and really reuse is encouraged because if the site is not being used, it's going to deteriorate."

The building is no longer needed by the fire department, which has moved to new premises in Monkland. (Supplied: Jack Carr)

The QFD did not grant access into the building, but in his application, Mr Carr said the first floor of the building retained "all of the original 1940 rooms", along with lead-light French doors, fittings and cornices.

The spotter's tower now has a roof and is glassed-in, and there is an extension on one side, but the original building remains intact.

"I personally would like to see either a business or a community-inspired centre go into this so the public can appreciate it," Mr Carr said.

A view from the inside

Gympie station officer Cameron Nicol spent close to 20 years in the building, having arrived from Mount Isa in 2008.

He said there was no doubt it was a "grand old building", but it was no longer the right place for modern firefighters.

"Certainly, time has passed it by in terms of its suitability for current-day firefighters, mainly the size of the trucks," Mr Nicol said.

"The trucks have gotten bigger, and unfortunately it got to the point where we could barely fit our fire trucks in there.

"It's a pretty unique building … Try furnishing a round room."

The tower of the fire station was eventually covered and glassed-in, and provides some of the best views of the town. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

He said the building's position, at Gympie's highest point, gave it the best views of the town.

" What will become of it I don't know, but I would surely hope that it's put to good use. "

The building's age and style have occasionally given rise to tales of unusual sounds or sightings in local newspapers over its lifetime.

Over its 86 years, the "grand old building" in Gympie has been the subject of tales of haunting noises and interactions. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

Mr Nicol said, over the years, there had been experiences he could not explain

"Look, I'm one of the biggest sceptics when it comes to that sort of paranormal stuff," he said.

"But there's certainly been things that have happened that I can't explain.

"We kind of had to be there to understand or feel it, whether it's haunted or not.

"I'm not discounting it."

'A lot quieter now'

Julie Bindley lives across the street from the fire station, which is now quiet after years of sirens and alarms.

Julie Bindley says she wants to see the building preserved. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

But she said the crews were always thoughtful, even when heading to an emergency.

"Half the time they wouldn't put [the sirens] on until they went past and down a bit," she said.

And while she had heard the building may have a haunted history, she said that was part of its charm.

"It just adds a bit of character," she said.

World.title: Nationals 'fighting' to win Bendigo as Jacinta Allan exits politics
World.content:
The Nationals' campaign to take the regional city of Bendigo has one less hurdle, as longtime member for Bendigo East Jacinta Allan resigns from politics.

Former Victorian premier Ms Allan has been largely absent from her electorate since losing the Labor Party leadership to Ben Carroll last month.

On Friday morning, she broke her three-week silence to announce she would not be recontesting the seat at the November state election.

Andrew Lethlean is a publican and is the Nationals' candidate for Bendigo East. (ABC Central Victoria: Shannon Schubert)

For six months, Nationals candidate for Bendigo East, Andrew Lethlean, has been running his campaign to oust Ms Allan after 27 years.

He said Ms Allan's resignation did not change anything for him.

"We have missed out; we had a city-centric government and Jacinta Allan was leading that city-centric government," Mr Lethlean said.

"The fact the regions have missed out so much is the reason I'm running.

" Our policy now is to get 25 per cent of the investment into the regions. Whether Jacinta Allan was there or not did not change my focus. "

Andrew Lethlean's office in the centre of Bendigo. (ABC News: Shannon Schubert)

Nationals leader Danny O'Brien said Ms Allan's time as premier and a minister "hadn't been a good experience".

"It's not a surprise that she's gone, absolutely. We wish her all the best, but unfortunately Victoria is left with the worst, and that's a concern for all Victorians," Mr O'Brien said.

"We need a fresh start. Andrew Lethlean will be fighting very hard for Bendigo East irrespective of who his opponent is."

Nationals leader Danny O'Brien and Bendigo West candidate David Hutchings in Bendigo on Friday. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

Associate professor of politics at Monash University Zareh Ghazarian said that while Mr Lethlean was expected to be very competitive in the upcoming election, Ms Allan's resignation "changes the political dynamic of the seat considerably".

"The expectation was that the National Party was on an upward trajectory in that part of Victorian politics," Dr Ghazarian said.

But he said a new Labor candidate could be more competitive than the former premier, and a One Nation candidate could shake things up even further.

"I suspect that Bendigo East as an electorate is going to definitely be one of the seats to watch on election night," he said.

" I expect it to be a very close result. "

Labor Party to begin candidate search

Rank-and-file members of the Bendigo East branch of the Labor Party will now begin the process of finding a candidate to run against Mr Lethlean despite backing Ms Allan to stay in the seat.

In a letter seen by the ABC, the branch's 80 members wrote to Ms Allan three days after her resignation as premier in late July, saying they were "right behind you".

On Friday, Bendigo Trades Hall Council secretary Luke Martin said the branch had no-one in mind as a candidate and that its 80 members would work to find a candidate to nominate for preselection.

In the letter, the branch's members praised Ms Allan for her investment in public schools, hospitals, and transport and her "tireless advocacy for regional communities like ours".

Luke Martin says the branch is working to find a new candidate to nominate for preselection. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Ms Allan's noticeable absence since her resignation as premier more than three weeks ago is also fuelling the Nationals' campaign to take Bendigo.

On Friday, they announced accountant, volunteer firefighter and emergency responder David Hutchings, as the candidate for Bendigo West to take on incumbent MP and Speaker of the House, Labor's Maree Edwards.

And the litmus test from her constituents was that, although Ms Allan had done a lot for Bendigo over her 27 years, many believed it was time for her to resign.

Residents say resignation was the right decision

Charlotte Spencer says Jacinta Allan made the right decision to exit politics. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Bendigo resident Charlotte Spencer said she thought it was the right decision for Ms Allan to resign and wanted more focus on climate action and more open areas.

"I'm looking forward to seeing who steps up to take her place," she said.

"She's facing a lot of backlash in the media, and maybe some of it is justified, but I don't know that she would have been able to do her job as well as she would with all of the pressure that she is under right now."

Betty Shalevski hopes Andrew Lethlean will be a fresh face for Bendigo. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Resident Betty Shalevski also said it was the right decision for Ms Allan to resign.

"I think it's really good because I think if she didn't resign she would have been voted out. So I think she has done herself a favour," Ms Shalevski said.

"I think Labor will be a different face but the same policies, so I think we need a new leader like Andrew [Lethlean].

"Crime is number one, mental health is just out and everywhere and not really contained."

The Greens have announced Michael Tolhurst as their Bendigo East candidate, and Liz Wright is running as an independent.

World.title: Telstra records profit and CEO pay rise as remote areas struggle for service
World.content:
A massive Telstra outage across Australia caused havoc earlier this year, interrupting day-to-day life, from trains and eftpos machines to the State of Origin NRL bunker.

But for large tracts of regional and remote Australia, these kinds of Telstra interruptions are not one-off inconveniences, they are a daily possibility — and there's growing evidence it's doing detriment across the bush, causing havoc to businesses and even putting lives at risk.

Telstra outages are the norm in many parts of rural and regional Australia. (Reuters: Jeremy Piper)

A new report from the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman has examined complaints from nearly 27,000 regional Australians about the shortfalls of telcos outside of the cities.

Its findings show what many living in these areas are already well aware of — unreliable connectivity and services, unplanned outages and an inability for quick fixes to problems.

Ombudsman Cynthia Gebert said "people were paying more, they were waiting longer to get things resolved, and they were facing much greater risks when telco services fail".

Cynthia Gebert says a lack of connection can put lives at risk. (Supplied: Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman)

"We've seen examples of consumers who have been unable to make phone calls in the event of natural disasters," she said.

" When you can't even get a connection, that's when lives do start to end up at risk. "

The report's release coincided with some interesting figures that also dropped this week: Telstra had recorded a $2.4 billion full-year profit, with a hefty pay bonus for its chief executive.

So with Telstra's evidently healthy bottom line, is enough being done by the company to fix the dicey state of connectivity on Australia's backroads?

Natural disasters blamed for outages

Last weekend, Telstra was down for 40 hours after a bushfire in Far North Queensland, impacting hundreds of people, and triggering calls for better connectivity in the bush.

Wadeye hit by months of rolling phone, internet outages Wadeye has been without a stable mobile phone service for nine weeks, leaving locals unable to make calls or access the internet.

Earlier in the year, in the remote Northern Territory community of Wadeye, Telstra was offline for more than nine weeks, leaving many feeling unsafe, and unable to use the internet or make calls.

The Wadeye outage happened during a period of severe flooding in the NT's Top End, which Telstra cited as the reason for the long-running technological failure in the area.

Ms Gebert said for a company the size of Telstra, there should be better back-ups in place for when such disasters occurred.

"I've spoken with people who work in those communities myself, and [they've said] 'we know this happens every year'," she said.

Telstra has been criticised for not preparing for natural disasters in regional areas, like the Top End's wet season. (ABC News: Glen Armstrong)

"'We know that the wet season will impact the infrastructure; why is Telstra not preparing in advance to have what it needs there to be able to repair what they know will be a problem, year in, year out?

"There's more that can be done to prepare and pre-empt these issues so people aren't left isolated for months on end.

"There is a real need for the telco industry to step up and deliver for remote Australians."

No apologies over rolling outages

In the NT's remote east, the small town of Nhulunbuy has long struggled with unreliable Telstra service and unannounced outages that can last for days at a time.

Nhulunbuy business owner Donna-Marie Grieve said Telstra recently dropped out for about 48 hours, during which her printing business lost valuable time and earnings.

"We couldn't contact anybody, so we lost outside customers; I had meetings that I couldn't link into," she said.

Donna-Marie Grieve says the sudden disconnections have cost her business. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"And there was nothing given back to the customer — our bill was still the same; there was no 'I'm sorry, we appreciate your time'.

" They just want your money and as soon as they get it, it's 'thank you very much', and if the phone's down, the phone's down. "

At the Garma Festival, held early each August about 40 kilometres from Nhulunbuy, major sponsor Telstra erects a tower that gives festival-goers five bars of reception.

That poses the question: if Telstra can provide this temporary measure to a festival where tickets can cost more than $5,000, why can't it do the same for the town down the road?

"I can understand why consumers would look at that and throw their hands up in the air around, 'well, why not us?'," Ms Gebert said.

"Why not support us in the way that you've evidenced you can support other communities or events when required?

"And that really goes to the core of 'have we got the system set up to ensure consumers are able to access the services that they should be able to access?'"

Yingiya Guyula wants Telstra to improve coverage in Nhulunbuy. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Local member for the north-east Arnhem Land region, Yingiya Guyula, has this week written to Telstra to ask for "the temporary Garma tower to be moved to Nhulunbuy, as a measure to support the Nhulunbuy community who have had very poor connectivity for many years".

"Mr Guyula is urging Telstra to provide an interim solution for the town," his office said in a statement.

Telstra defends operations in remote Australia

In its defence, Telstra is the only telco that has managed to bring mobile coverage to some of Australia's most remote corners, with no sign of Optus, Vodafone or others in those areas.

Telstra's NT regional general manager, Nic Danks, said the company was working to help better connect some of the nation's most remote communities, but that it took significant time and resources to be able to do that properly.

"Delivering permanent coverage in remote communities is a complex undertaking, requiring land access, approvals, power, transmission, construction and ongoing maintenance," he said.

Nic Danks says Telstra is working to connect more remote communities to mobile services. (Supplied: Telstra)

In relation to the Garma tower, he said Telstra's technology there had been honed over 12 years of working with the festival, and that it wasn't so simple to translate it to other areas.

"We use a temporary mobile solution, Cell-on-Wheels (COW), that requires extensive planning and logistics for a short-term event," Mr Danks said.

"This is connected via existing fibre in the ground which was connected a number of years ago.

"The temporary connectivity solution at Garma cannot be replicated across remote communities.

"We have a very limited fleet of COWs and they are deployed for short-term events and in times of emergencies."

Mr Danks also said Telstra does do months of preparation prior to natural disaster seasons.

"No network can be completely immune to the impacts of severe weather, particularly in some of Australia's most remote regions," he said.

There are calls for greater regulations for telcos operating in remote areas. (Adobe stock)

"But we prepare for disaster seasons and network resilience through back-up batteries, generators, portable recovery equipment, network hardening programs and new technologies designed for remote locations."

Ms Gebert said there needed to be greater clarity around the regulatory obligations of Telstra and other telcos operating in the bush.

She's calling on the federal government to toughen up the frameworks that currently exist, "so that there's clear obligations on telcos, whether it's Telstra or anybody else, about who's providing what, when, how and to what quality standards, so people can rely on it".

"People expect to be able to use their mobile wherever they are — at the Garma Festival or in remote communities," she said.

"There's no obligation on the telcos at the moment to provide that, and that's not what people expect."

Anika Wells says the federal government is working to improve telecommunications services across Australia, including in more remote areas. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

A spokesperson for federal Communications Minister Anika Wells said the government "will always look at how we can improve the telecommunication system for Australians".

"We are progressing the Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation, a transformative reform that will significantly improve mobile connectivity across Australia," the spokesperson said.

"This will require Telstra, Optus and TPG to provide reasonable and equitable access to outdoor SMS and voice calling across Australia — providing connectivity to some of the country's hardest to reach places."

The call has now gone through to Telstra executives about whether they'll make changes to deliver better services in the regions — but it's yet to be seen if they'll actually pick up.

World.title: From playboy to bankrupt. The $1.8b rise and fall of Jon Adgemis
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesPubs From playboy to bankrupt. The $1.8b rise and fall of Jon Adgemis Kishor Napier-Raman August 15, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Aspiring pub baron Jon Adgemis once lived a gilt-plated life. The former KPMG rainmaker (he made partner aged 28) cruised Sydney’s eastern suburbs in a black Maserati, entertained associates on a luxury Italian vintage yacht, arrived at the Melbourne Cup by helicopter, and paraded a series of glamorous Birkin-toting girlfriends at society events. Jon Adgemis has been in the sights of the ATO, which raided his offices in 2024, for at least two years. Dominic Lorrimer Then the good times came crashing down. The Australian Taxation Office began circling his debt-fuelled businesses, before eventually forcing them into bankruptcy last October owing $1.8 billion. This week, liquidators from BRI Ferrier spent days picking through the wreckage at a Federal Court examination, and the details weren’t pretty. The yacht, Hiilani, has been sold to pay Adgemis’ debts. So have most of the cars. Model Cheyenne Tozzi, who split from Adgemis in 2017, has been asked to give evidence at the examination, which this week has finally shed some light on the billion-dollar mystery of how Adgemis’ Public Hospitality Group collapsed.



After leaving KPMG, Adgemis set his sights on building an entertainment empire to rival that of another perma-tanned eastern suburbs playboy, Merivale’s Justin Hemmes. He made a bet on Australia’s post-pandemic appetite for pleasure, buying up 22 entertainment venues in Sydney and Melbourne. Crucially, he made the bet using others’ money, fuelling his purchases with cheap debt from investors wooed by unrealistic valuations. Jon Adgemis had owned the private yacht Hiilani, which once belonged to Hollywood star Shirley Temple. The finer details of how Public Hospitality collapsed are particularly damning. In documents supplied to the court, the ATO said it was examining about $1 billion in spending incurred by one of Adgemis’ companies, alleging that it had received $77 million in GST refunds as part of a sham tax arrangement. Alexander Andruska, a Woollahra councillor and a long-term Adgemis lieutenant said that those refunds were essential to running the business. He alleged that his former boss had used that money to fund his exorbitant lifestyle.



“It was very stressful. I wanted to bloody blow my brains out,” Andruska said of trying to manage Adgemis’ finances. Related Article Pubs ‘One disaster after another’: Failed pub baron’s former accountant turns on him Accountant Sam Stringer, who was engaged by Adgemis after an audit by the ATO, told the court that the companies were not in a good financial position, and that trying to lodge their tax returns was a “mammoth” task. “We were given very little information. They were extremely disorganised and impossible to get information from,” he said. On Monday, Damien Hodgkinson, a co-founder of teal independent bank-roller Climate200 and an associate of Adgemis’ since their time as KPMG partners, was in court. The court heard that the pair had conspired to install Adgemis’ friend Marco Bettelli as sole director of Linchpin, a supposedly separate company that began operating some Public Hospitality Group venues amid financial troubles last year.



While several of Adgemis’ associates were grilled by the liquidator’s barrister Michael Rose, the man at the centre was conspicuously absent. Adgemis spent just seconds in the witness box, before his lawyers moved a motion to have the matter set aside as an abuse of process and to have the liquidators’ solicitors, ERA Legal, barred from acting. If Adgemis’ examination proceeds, his lawyers want it conducted in secret, away from the prying eyes of the media, a move that is being challenged by news organisations including this masthead. His sister, Despina Adgemis, took a similar approach, failing to appear on Thursday when scheduled. Her lawyers, Hamilton Locke, said she had never received a summons. Rose, counsel for the liquidators’, said that she had, whereupon her lawyers produced a medical certificate saying she was unable to attend. Despina is married to Rodd Boland, another KPMG man whom Andruska alleged was made a “straw director” by Adgemis of several companies last year. Boland and Adgemis previously lived at a Rose Bay property owned by Jon and their mother Rose, which was seized by lenders last year. While Adgemis’ family appears to be sticking by him, former friends are jumping ship. Andruska, who has worked with Adgemis since 2012, tried to downplay their friendship. “I do have a soft spot in my heart for Jon, but at the same time, he has caused me over a decade of stress, heartbreak and financial ruin,” Andruska told this masthead. “It’s a very toxic relationship.”





Madsen is currently being sued in a bankruptcy judgment by HG Capital, which invests on behalf of wealthy Vietnamese Sydneysiders, over the millions lent to a collapsed company that he and Adgemis were directors of. Preliminary hearings in that matter, to which Adgemis is also a party, were also underway this week in the NSW Supreme Court, just downstairs from where the Adgemis examinations took place. All that’s left now of Adgemis’ businesses is a mountain of debt, a conga-line of cranky creditors, and hefty legal bills. Adgemis is understood to be footing his own legal bills, and is currently working as a consultant for a number of clients. He is represented by solicitor Jamie DiMeo and barrister Miles Condon, SC, who reportedly command fees of $15,000 a day. On Wednesday, high-profile criminal lawyer Bryan Wrench, who is busy acting for Alan Jones in his indecent assault trial and lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood, who is facing the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s probe into a Liberal Party sub-faction, made a cameo in court. Wrench and Adgemis have had a relationship for some time: the solicitor most recently represented the businessman during ASIC’s prosecution of Cameron in 2021, and more recently when he pleaded guilty to a low-range drink-driving charge in 2024. And what of the pubs at the heart of his empire? Most are being sold off or restructured. Some never opened, and those that did hardly set the dining scene alight. Controversial celebrity chef George Calombaris was made Public Hospitality Group’s culinary director, later joining Hodgkinson’s Linchpin, where he started serving up “Aussie, old-school, Chinese food” out of the Empire Hotel in Annandale. Good Food delivered Calombaris’ efforts at Double Happy a scathing 11.5 out of 20. “One night, there’s a cluster of dead flies floating in the soy sauce on our table,” national restaurant editor Callan Boys wrote.
