World.title: Why getting simple super advice has become an expensive nightmare
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementFinancial planning Opinion Why getting simple super advice has become an expensive nightmare Bec Wilson Money contributor August 15, 2026 — 5:01am

August 15, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you walk into a financial adviser’s office at the age of 58, approaching retirement with about $700,000 in superannuation, a mortgage, a few hundred thousand dollars invested outside, what should happen next? And if you walked into a super fund advice appointment, with the same amount of money, and the same mixed picture, what can they do to help you? What can they advise you on, and more importantly, what can’t they? Simple super advice should be easy. So why does it feel like such a maze? Simon Letch Most Australians would expect broadly the same thing from both: help understanding whether they have enough, what sort of retirement they can afford, what to do about the remaining mortgage and whether their super and investments are in the right place, and taking the right amount of risk, and, ultimately, a clear plan for what steps they should take next. But what happens next can really surprise people because, despite starting with the same problem, the two advice models can’t offer the same help.



A comprehensive financial adviser is legally allowed to look across your broader financial life, including your super, investments, mortgage, tax position and retirement goals. But increasingly, many advice businesses are also built around providing ongoing investment management. Part of the reason is that the regulatory burden and the cost of providing comprehensive advice has made smaller, one-off pieces of advice difficult to provide profitably. So what begins as a request for retirement advice can become the start of a much longer commercial relationship, with the client’s super and investments moved onto a platform and managed on an ongoing basis by the advice business or an investment manager connected to it. [Everyday consumers] just want to understand their choices and get trustworthy advice about their retirement. A super fund comes at the same retirement problem from the opposite direction. It already has your money and increasingly, it wants to keep looking after it throughout your retirement. Funds are building retirement products, guidance and advice services to help members make that transition to retirement with them. This could make retirement advice vastly more accessible and affordable for millions of Australians.



But the advice a fund can offer its members has some significant boundaries. It is largely limited to advising on the money invested within the fund rather than the bigger picture of your financial life or the alternatives available to you. That can significantly limit how far they can go in considering things like the age pension, or even your broader retirement picture, to make the journey easier for you. Some funds hold separate financial advice licences that allow them to provide comprehensive advice, charging you personally for that at a higher rate. But that’s not what every member should expect when they contact their funds. These two faces of advice are increasingly colliding with each other. Financial advisers build their businesses by targeting new clients, often from people whose money is currently sitting in a super fund. Super funds are meanwhile trying to build more sophisticated retirement and advice offerings, to serve their members well enough that they think twice about leaving.



There’s nothing particularly surprising about either strategy. They are rational commercial business goals. But somewhere in the middle is the everyday consumer, who doesn’t want to be fought over, and isn’t particularly interested in who wins this battle. They just want to understand their choices and get trustworthy advice about their retirement. Editor's pick Opinion

Retirement living The simple $174,000 question many retirees still get wrong Bec Wilson Money contributor They should be able to get help working out whether they have enough, what their choices are and what they should do next, without having to 



Not in the same way as before Hayne, and not necessarily with the same conflicts, but the principle is worth watching right across the industry. When the person giving the advice benefits from where your money ends up, the incentives matter. And there’s one incentive Financial Services Minister Daniel Mulino should look very closely at: how much of our super can be used to pay for financial advice and how much should be used. Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Alex Ellinghausen The differences are striking. Australian Super allows for an advice fee deduction of up to $7700 or 2.5 per cent of a member’s balance, whichever is lower. Australian Retirement Trust allows up to 2.5 per cent capped at $8800 with an additional $1500 for a new advice relationship. Unisuper allows for $8800 or 2.5 per cent, too. Hostplus caps advice fees at 2.5 per cent of balance or $8000 and HESTA caps them at $5500, or 3 per cent.



Compare that with the platform end of the market, where permitted advice fees can be much higher. And in some cases, there is no fixed dollar cap on ongoing advice fees. HUB24, for example, allows ongoing adviser service fees of up to 4.4 per cent of a member’s total account balance. Higher amounts are possible subject to approval. On a $700,000 super balance, 4.4 per cent is $30,800 per year. ASIC itself is worried about where these limits are heading. Its platform review released in June found one trustee had a dollar-based cap of $25,000 while another was planning to introduce a $30,000 cap. And three of the six platforms it examined had no upper limit on what could be deducted. These aren’t necessarily the fees people are actually paying, but they are the amounts the different systems permit to be deducted from someone’s retirement savings. An adviser may be able to deduct, with the client’s consent, substantially more in advice fees after moving a client from a traditional super fund onto a platform. And because those fees come directly out of retirement savings, rather than the household bank account, consumers may not feel them hitting their hip pocket nearly as hard. The Super Members Council says regulators should take the incentive seriously. It found that platforms that had higher advice fee caps were attracting stronger flows of money from people switching funds, even after accounting for costs, performance and size.



The Financial Services Council offers a different explanation for the strong advice-led outflows from super funds to platforms, saying platforms can provide greater investment choice, tailored portfolios and the ability for advisers to manage super and investments outside super in one place. Editor's pick Opinion

Budgeting Five emergency money moves that could save you thousands Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor Both arguments can be true. A platform can be entirely appropriate for someone who wants or needs that level of investment management. But the SMC data has to raise some legitimate questions about the way advice is paid for influencing where advisers recommend their money goes. And then, alongside this, we have to mention the consumer who’s simply stuck in a pretty ordinary super fund, who’s looking across the market and saying, ‘there must be another fund with better retirement products and services for what I need’ but who can’t find an adviser to help them review their super and move to another fund. That kind of advice should be easy to provide and find on a one-off basis. Instead, the regulatory burden and the cost of providing advice can make it unattractive for advisers unless it leads to a broader ongoing relationship.



There are so few advisers offering this kind of help these days that when I asked the Financial Advice Association Australia to help me find some, even it struggled. That’s an advice gap of a different kind – another one that needs addressing. And that’s the mess that Mulino needs to confront this week, head on. On Tuesday, he is expected to outline the next phase of the government’s financial advice reforms, known as Delivering Better Financial Outcomes. Most people won’t watch. Most don’t even know or care what DBFO is. But they should care about the outcome because these new rules could shape how everyday Australians get financial advice for decades to come. It’s time to finish the job. Australia needs more affordable and accessible financial advice. Super funds need greater scope to help members navigate retirement. Advisers need to be able to provide useful advice without unnecessary cost and complexity. And we must make room for simpler forms of digital advice. But getting more advice to people is only half the job. I’d like to see the government put the purpose of advice properly at the heart of these reforms: helping consumers understand their choices and make informed decisions that help them achieve their real goals. Mulino is going to upset somebody whatever he does. Advisers are worried about super funds moving further into advice; super funds want greater freedom to help members and retain them.



Platforms have billions of dollars flowing in that they don’t want to see slow. The lobbying in the back rooms has been fierce. But that’s precisely why the government needs to stop refereeing the industry’s turf war and tell us what it thinks a trustworthy consumer advice system should look like, because this isn’t it. Please, for the whole industry’s sake and the sake of the consumers, finish DBFO. Give Australians more places to get affordable help. Make the choices, limitations and commercial incentives behind advice transparent. And give advice a clear purpose – for both financial advice businesses and super funds – that puts the consumer at the heart. Bec Wilson is author of the bestseller How to Have an Epic Retirement and the newly released Prime Time: 27 Lessons for the New Midlife. She writes a weekly newsletter at epicretirement.net and hosts the Prime Time podcast. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: Fast-track process begins for Wellington's second Mt Victoria Tunnel project
World.content:
The fast-track process has begun for a multibillion-dollar project that would radically change inner-city Wellington - but critics say it's on the "fast-track to nowhere".

On Friday, the fast-track application for the SH1 Wellington Improvements project - which envisions the construction of the second Mt Victoria and Terrace Tunnels - was officially lodged.

NZTA said it was a "significant milestone" for the project and would allow officials to protect the route.

But while $185 million has been approved for design, consents and early works, funding for major construction of the plans had not been provided, and there was no start date for building to begin.

In a Wellington City Council meeting earlier this month, councillors opposed to the plan labelled it a "ghost road" and a "ghost project", but the minister in charge insisted the government was committed to delivering it.

Wellington's Terrace Tunnel at the northbound entrance. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

What's ultimately on the cards?

An additional Mount Victoria tunnel was a National Party campaign promise, with improvements in the area discussed for years.

NZTA has previously said the total costs to design, purchase land and construct the project would cost between $2.9b and $3.8b.

It would significantly change central city roads, including adding a second Mt Victoria and Terrace Tunnel, and the roads around the Basin Reserve would be re-designed so traffic would move in both directions.

Changes would also be made in Te Aro, with three lanes on Vivian Street and Karo Drive, as well as a widening of Ruahine Street and Wellington Road in Kilbirnie en route to the airport.

Approximately 3.2 hectares of Town Belt would be taken for the project, Wellington City Council officials said in a recent agenda, while hundreds of privately-owned and commercial properties will either be purchased by NZTA or will be right next to it.

NZTA has previously said it had identified 176 properties it might need to buy, and another 146 properties where it might need to buy below-ground land, for the construction of the two tunnels.

So far, $33m has been spent on contractors and consultants.

An image showing NZTA's proposed Mt Victoria tunnel. NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi

'Ghost road' or 'gift horse'?

Debate reignited over the controversial project in a council meeting earlier this month, as councillors discussed a list of priorities officials would take to the fast-track panel.

Council officials will highlight key concerns with the project, advocating that less Town Belt land is taken, that people still have the ability to walk safely around the Basin Reserve, that there's adequate walking and cycling space through the Mount Victoria Tunnel, and that disruption from building the tunnels and roads is considered.

The Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) said while timelines varied, on average it took 117 working days for a decision to be made on a fast-track application.

The panel will decide whether to approve the project, approve it with conditions, or decline it within a timeframe.

Motukairangi/Eastern Ward councillor Jonny Osborne questioned why the project was going through the fast-track process at all.

"I would note the project has no funding attached or start date. So you really have to ask yourself why are they fast-tracking it? It's fast-tracked to nowhere.

"But anyway, that's for them to decide, we at council must continue this charade."

Osborne is among a number of Green Party-backed councillors who are [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/580659/green-mps-councillors-launch-campaign-against-second-mt-victoria-tunnel-in-wellington opposed to the project, saying it "utterly ignores" the reality of climate change by increasing the number of cars on the road, including around Hataitai and Kilbirnie.

"I just want to make it clear that we as a council expect that any of the risks that arise from changes to travel patterns that may happen if this ghost project does happen are mitigated ... especially around schools and other community facilities that are frequently used by schools or other at-risk communities," Osborne said.

An artist's impression of the Mt Victoria tunnel seen from Hataitai. Supplied / NZTA Waka Kotahi

Pukehīnau/Lambton Ward and fellow Green party councillor Geordie Rogers, who described the project as a "ghost road", backed an amendment Osborne put forward which sought to use the fast-track process as a route towards pedestrianisation of Cuba Street.

He said the project would increase traffic on roads such as Taranaki Street, Ghuznee Street and Abel Smith Street.

The measure ultimately failed, with Wellington Mayor Andrew Little saying it was a "waste of time" to use the fast-track process for a separate debate on pedestrianising Cuba Street.

"Our role as council is to mitigate the worst aspects of that project."

Not all councillors agree on the issue. Independent Pukehīnau Lambton ward councillor Nicola Young has said she wants the project to go ahead, but doubted whether it would happen for years - or even decades.

The late Tony Randle, who had represented the Takapū/Northern Ward, voiced his support for it, saying it would ease long-standing bottlenecks in the city.

This was crucial if the city wanted to grow, he had said.

"I hope this project is not a charade...this is a project the Government has come and offered us, and don't look a gift-horse in the mouth.

"This will make Wellington better because we are struggling with congestion."

Inside Mount Victoria Tunnel. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Minister insists project will go ahead

In a statement, Transport Minister Chris Bishop said it wasn't true the Mt Victoria Tunnel project was on a "fast-track to nowhere", or was a "ghost road".

"The project is in the major project pipeline and we are committed to delivering it.

"The SH1 Wellington Improvements project will unlock economic growth, improve productivity, and give Wellingtonians a safer, faster and more reliable connection between the region, the CBD, the hospital and the airport."

A spokesperson for the EPA said the panel can approve a project without government funding attached, so long as it meets statutory criteria of having significant regional and national benefits.

The panel will meet with several invited parties, she said, which change depending on the project.

NZTA's project sponsor, Robyn Elston, said the application is now being reviewed by the team at the EPA.

When it has been accepted as complete it would be made public on NZTA's website, Elston said.

World.title: Probe into fatal dog attack continues
World.content:
A police investigation is continuing after a young child was killed in a dog attack on Friday afternoon.

Emergency services were called to Basingstoke Street in Aranui, Christchurch around 4:45pm after reports of a child sustaining serious dog bite injuries.

"Upon arrival, emergency services located a young child in a critical condition," Senior Sergeant Dan Overend said.

"Despite the immediate efforts of first responders, and a member of the household, the child sadly died at the scene."

Overend said the dog involved was known to the occupants of the address and lived at the property.

"Police remain at the address carrying out a scene examination, and enquiries into the circumstances that led to this tragic incident are ongoing.

"Occupants of the address are assisting police with enquiries."

World.title: Aucklanders get first look inside new Karanga-a-Hape Station
World.content:
Thousands of Aucklanders are expected to get their first look inside the City Rail Link's (CRL) Karanga-a-Hape Station Saturday, as the city counts down to the opening of the $5.5 billion project.

The station is the second of three new or redeveloped stations to be opened to the public as part of a series of free "First Look" events ahead of the CRL opening to passengers on 13 September.

Karanga-a-Hape Station, in the heart of the city, features New Zealand's longest escalator, taking passengers 33 metres underground beneath Pitt Street.

Its design also includes a ceiling shaped like three Kauri snail shells, reflecting the Kauri forests that once covered the Karangahape ridgeline.

The Karanga-a-Hape Station design includes a ceiling shaped like three Kauri snail shells. Supplied: CRL

The station's opening comes after a decade of construction on the country's largest transport infrastructure project.

The CRL includes twin 3.45km rail tunnels beneath Auckland's city centre, two new underground stations at Karanga-a-Hape and Te Waihorotiu, and the redevelopment of Maungawhau Station.

When it opens on 13 September, trains will run directly through the city centre for the first time, rather than stopping at Waitematā Station.

Three 'Atua panels' designed by artist Reuben Kirkwood form the threshold element at the Karanga-a-Hape Station entrance. Supplied: CRL

Auckland Transport says the new link is expected to double the number of Aucklanders who live within a 30-minute train journey of the city centre.

At peak times, trains will run through the city centre every five minutes, while services elsewhere on the network are expected to run at an average of about 10min intervals.

Off-peak services will run every 15min throughout the day, including weekends, compared with every 20min currently.

The Karanga-a-Hape underground station will house the longest escalator in New Zealand, at 40 metres long Supplied: CRL

The station's opening date was formally announced last week by Transport Minister Chris Bishop and Auckland mayor Wayne Brown.

Bishop said the opening would mark a turning point for Auckland after a project that had been discussed for about a century and had caused years of disruption for businesses and communities during construction.

The CRL has cost $5.5b and taken about 10 years to build.

The public will have another chance to explore the new network next Saturday, when Te Waihorotiu Station will be opened for a final First Look event on 22 August.

World.title: Pacific Music Awards thriving on stage, struggling behind the scenes
World.content:
The Pacific Music Awards marked it 22nd year this week celebrating Pasifika excellence in music, however organisers say the event is struggling financially.

A fixture on the New Zealand Pasifika calendar for over two decades, the awards is usually held at Manukau's Due Drop Events centre attracting a large audience with the event simultaneously livestreamed.

On the night, RnB crooner Sam V who took home the best Pacific Soul/RnB award for the fifth year running, criticised the government's level of arts funding in his award's speech.

"Mr Paul (Goldsmith) from National, you mentioned that our government is investing in the arts, I mean it's good lip service but if that's the case then the PMAs struggling don't exist," he said.

"A quick search on Google, I think you'll find that our government spends billions on our defence force - a defence force that protects us from tall poppy syndrome maybe... I'm pretty sure if we can put billions in our defence force then we can keep celebrating Pacific excellence."

The Pacific Music Awards 2026 Held at the Due Drops event Centre in Manukau ,Auckland 12 August 2026. Images Copyright Stijl 2026 Mandatory Credit Stijl / Emma Beavis Emma Beavis

However, Goldsmith, who attended the awards, said he "disagrees with those characterisations".

In a statement sent to RNZ Pacific, the minister said that the government is serious about the getting the country's finances back in order.

"The Ministry and Crown entities have delivered a two per cent baseline saving, along with everyone else in this year's budget, because as a country we are still running substantial deficits."

Goldsmith reaffirmed the government's commitment to the arts in a speech at the awards, and further clarified in his statement that $1.7 billion is invested in the sector for over four years.

Yet for the Pacific Music Awards Trust, the reality of running the event is becoming precarious, pushing them to what the awards trustee Petrina Togi-Sa'ena describes "as trying to survive and keep the event alive".

In a Facebook post from mid-July, Togi-Sa'ena wrote the Trust was seeking public donations starting from $10.

"It's always humbling having to ask our community for support, when we know it's already challenging times for our people."

Paul Goldsmith at last nights PMAs Tagata Pasifika

Funding at a glance

The Pacific Music Awards receives funding through multiple government-supported agencies including Creative New Zealand, NZ on Air, New Zealand Music Commission and Pacific Media Network.

While most of the agencies have not publicly disclosed how much they have given to the awards, NZ on Air contributed up to $33,000 in the last financial year compared with up to $24,000 in 2024.

Other media reports state that Auckland Council also allocated $35,000.

Togi-Sa'ena told RNZ Pacific that existing funds have mostly gone towards the event's production and stage, trimming back spending on travel for awards finalists and winners and catering for guests.

Signature Choir. Stijl / Charl Louw

She said the trust secured several new sponsors last year, but added that there's been a reduction in government funding and other sources including gaming trusts are unable to provide more financial support.

Despite funding from various agencies, Togi-Sa'ena said the awards run on a year-to-year basis making it difficult to plan long-term. Creative New Zealand is the only major sponsor providing a three-year agreement.

"We're always in an annual cycle, so subject to each year it's working out what is the state of play each year, and then we're set in these specific timelines with funders and agencies as well," she said.

"We don't have the ability to grow, we don't have the ability for all those costs that we would love to have."

Public appeal generates support

The financial squeeze from the past three years led to a public fundraising appeal in July - Togi-Sa'ena said it was a hard call but the response has been encouraging.

"Donations have been coming in, it's created a bit more awareness, a couple of potential sponsors have reached out. Others have provided some additional support."

Togi-Sa'ena said they will be reviewing the awards format and are looking at alternative methods to raise revenue including ticket sales, community support and corporate funds.

She said that despite the uncertainty with funding, there is still a strong push from the Pasifika community to keep the event going.

World.title: Rugby: Caleb Clarke out of South Africa tour with shoulder injury
World.content:
Winger Caleb Clarke will return home prematurely from the All Blacks tour of South Africa after suffering a serious shoulder injury.

Scans revealed Clarke damaged a shoulder tendon during the 54-0 win over the Sharks in Durban on Wednesday morning (NZT) and will need surgery.

A timeframe for his return is unclear until after surgery is complete.

All Blacks coach Dave Rennie said an injury replacement won't be called for the 27-year-old.

"We are comfortable with the outside backs cover we have at the moment, so will not be bringing another squad member in to replace Caleb unless further injuries necessitate it.

"We are all feeling for Caleb and really sorry to see his Rugby's Greatest Rivalry tour come to an early end. He's an important member of our group, both on and off-field, so we look forward to him making a full recovery."

Clarke has been largely a first-choice selection on New Zealand's left wing for the last four years and has scored 16 tries from 35 tests.

He was a strong chance to win selection for next week's first test against the Springboks in Johannesburg, with his powerful ball-carrying and aerial ability valued.

Caleb Clarke and Quinn Tupaea. www.photosport.nz

Clarke couldn't hide his disappointment.

"I am gutted to be going home because I've loved my time here so much," he said.

"But I am staying positive and excited about what's ahead, so will make the most of my recovery to make sure I'm at my best when I'm ready to return to rugby."

Clarke is the third All Blacks player ruled out of the tour through injury after hooker George Bell sustained a calf injury in training and centre Billy Proctor injured his shoulder in the tour-opening win over the Stormers.

Those players were replaced by hooker Bradley Slater and first-five Richie Mo'unga respectively.

Clarke wasn't in New Zealand's team for their next tour match, against the Bulls in Pretoria on Sunday morning, their last game before the first test.

Captain against the Bulls, Codie Taylor, said he was unsure of the fitness status of fullback Damian McKenzie, who hobbled off early in the match against the Sharks with an ankle problem.

"I'm not sure where Damo's at at the moment in terms of his injury," Taylor told journalists.

World.title: Pacific news in brief for 15 August
World.content:
Fiji

Fiji now has 11 political parties registered to contest the upcoming general elections.

The Fiji Sun says Fiji's Registrar of Political Parties, Ana Mataiciwa, approved the registration of the Liberation of Fiji Party (LFP) this week.

Mataiciwa says the LFP, registered under the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) Act 2013, had met all legal requirements.

Fiji Liberation Party join a list of new parties launched over the last 24 months, including One Nation, NeXTGEN Alliance Party, People First, Kingdom Unite All Peoples Party and We Unite Fiji Party.

Fiji's elections are expected to be held by February next year.

Tuvalu

Tuvalu's Prime Minister Feleti Teo has invited Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to attend the Pre-COP31 Leaders' Event in Tuvalu in October.

The invitation came during Teo's courtesy meeting in Funafuti with Japan's Ambassador to Fiji, with accreditation to Tuvalu, Hiroshi Tajima, in Funafuti.

The meeting focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation and discussions on climate change, regional cooperation, peace and security, and other areas of mutual interest.

Teo said he'd welcome direct participation between Japan and Pacific leaders on climate change, resilience and climate finance

West Papua

A new satellite fire-monitoring platform, FireWatch, had detected more than 96,000 hotspots across Indonesia as of late last month, including Papua region..

All up, an estimated approximately 103,000 hectares of land burned nationwide during the first half of 2026,

It includes a high numbers of hotspots in South Papua, where large-scale agricultural development has transformed vast areas of lowland forest and wetlands.

Environmental groups say it highlights the need to assess ecological and hydrological risks before converting peatlands for development.

And as El Nino tightens its grip, forecasters warn the fire risk could increase more.

Guam

US Pacific territories are under the microscope as Washington is launching a taskforce to fight birth tourism, where foreigners come to the country to have children.

Key hotspots for birth tourism include Guam and the Northern Marianas.

The US State Department says the taskforce will review the birth tourism space - and either kick out those come in for it, or shut the gate on them when they try.

So far it says it has revoked more than 600 US visas from foreign nationals across the globe, calling birth tourism a pervasive practice.

Republicans have targetted special visa waivers allowing Chinese nationals to travel to these territories.

Northern Marianas

The Northern Mariana Islands' delegate to the US Congress wants the territory to receive half of any federal revenue generated from potential seabed mining around the islands.

The US has recently invited bidders for seabed mining licenses in American Samoa, and will soon do the same for the CNMI.

A keen Republican supporter of President Trump, but a critic of his critical minerals agenda, Kimberlyn King-Hinds said a 50/50 split of the licensing revenue from mining companies is only fair.

She said it would be too difficult to lobby against seabed mining in the area altogether, but with a lack of science, there are dangers that ought to be addressed.

World.title: Sydney-based boxing trainer calls for head to roll in Fiji
World.content:
Former Fiji Professional Boxing president Lepani Wilson has called on current Fiji Boxing Commission Chairperson Adi Narayan to resign.

Wilson, who is currently based in Sydney as a boxing trainer, said Narayan has lost touch with reality, and does not have any control of boxing in Fiji.

He pointed to the recent fiasco involving Fiji heavyweight boxer James Singh, who was knocked out in the first round of a bout in Melbourne last weekend.

Singh hit the canvas after Tongan heritage boxer Tevita Pomale pounded him into submission in just the first round of their fight.

Narayan told The Fiji Sun in Suva on Thursday he did not know about Singh's trip and only knew about it after he saw coverage on social media.

He said the boxer and others who also fought at the same program and others in Australia last weekend, did not obtain proper release to fight overseas, which breached Part 14(3) of the Boxing Act.

"Honestly, I was quite surprised to see the video circulating on social media, and there was no release obtained from BCF for Singh's overseas fight," Narayan told The Fiji Sun.

"No boxer shall participate in a professional contest in another country except with the approval of the Commission given under Section 10(e)."

Adi Narayan, Boxing Commission of Fiji chairman. FBC

Narayan said the Act states the penalty is a fine of $100,000 or imprisonment for five years.

In his response to Narayan's claims and statement, Wilson said the chairman has "sadly lost the plot".

"What he is telling Fiji is that he does not know what is happening and has lost control,

"There's too much issues happening under his watch and it is time to go. He should do the honourable thing and resign."

Wilson said Singh and his camp should also be taken to task, "because that show they put up was pathetic".

"The guy looked like he never trained, he was unfit, he got smacked and punched around, and he did not show any effort at all."

He added the poor showing is not a good result for Fiji Boxing in general and the Boxing Commission should be serious about their existence and why they were set up in the first place.

"I call on the Ministry of Sports, the boxing fraternity to get the chairman out. Nothing personal but he is not performing as he should be," Wilson claimed.

"If he does not know that someone is leaving to come and fight overseas then that is a shame."

Meanwhile, Wilson slammed the hefty fine of $100,000 included in the commission's Act.

Wilson said fining a boxer that amount of money is "ridiculous".

"I believe they need to review that and have suspensions in place instead.

World.title: Hockeyroos and Kookaburras tackle World Cup with fresh perspectives
World.content:
Kookaburras midfielder Liam Henderson has the attitude of a winner.

It is a confidence that comes with being part of a team used to sustained excellence, backed by a growing reputation as one of hockey's global rising stars.

And in his second year on the national team, the 22-year-old is ready to deliver at the World Cup which begins this weekend.

"We think we can win it. And if other teams don't think we can, we'll just prove them wrong," he told ABC Sport from the team's base in Belgium.

Liam Henderson (right) is heading to his first World Cup. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

The Kookaburras are ranked fourth in the world, and won the last of their three World Cup titles in 2014.

Recent FIH Pro League victories over the top two ranked teams, Belgium and Netherlands, mean Henderson's confidence is justified.

"Everyone brings their natural game. We're a force to be reckoned with," he said.

"The last two games we played against the two world's best, we had two wins and two losses. We can beat them. And if it's our day, anything can happen."

The Kookaburras have won the World Cup three times. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

The team's last major tournament was the Paris 2024 Olympics, which ended in an uncharacteristic quarter-final exit.

There has been significant change since then with a new coach, Mark Hager, and the retirements of some of their longest serving players including Eddie Ockenden, Aran Zalewski, and Andrew Charter.

But a hallmark of the Kookaburras throughout their history has been a constant ability to regenerate and maintain their position amongst the world's top teams.

"As a hockey community, we're always watching our national teams. And when you watch them, something you aspire to do is just be in that team," Henderson said.

The Kookaburras are ranked fourth in the world. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"And once you're there, I think every chance you get, you just want to work as hard as possible.

"I think another piece of that is the group that we have at the moment are all so close.

"We're such good mates, all of us, and such a welcoming team that you just want to play for each other. It's something you really want to be a part of."

Hockeyroos to rise up

The men's tournament will be played in Wavre, just outside of Brussels, played concurrently with the women's event in Amstelveen, Netherlands.

That is where the Hockeyroos are based, led by the most experienced player in the team, co-captain Kaitlin Nobbs, heading to her third World Cup.

She is part of one of the sport's most illustrious dynasties, with both parents having represented Australia, alongside her grandmother, aunty, and uncle — the Kookaburras coach.

Kaitlin Nobbs is playing at her third World Cup. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

"Coming into this one it marks the 40th anniversary from when my mum went to a World Cup as well representing the Hockeyroos," Nobbs told ABC Sport.

"So looking at the past and reflecting and seeing where we've come from, where the Hockeyroos have come from until now, it means the world to be able to go out and represent the team and captain them."

Her dad, Michael Nobbs, died earlier this year, and has provided her with extra motivation to excel.

"I think he would be so chuffed that I'm playing and enjoying the game and trying to take the most out of it that I can," she said.

"He loved hockey more than anyone and loved watching me play. So I'm sure he'll be watching and following along from wherever he is."

The Hockeyroos are ranked eighth in the world, and after winning the last of their three Olympic golds in 2000, have not managed to reach those heights again, although bronze at the 2022 World Cup was a highlight.

Katrina Powell took over as coach just before the Tokyo Olympics in the wake of systemic cultural issues in the women's program, and after stepping down last year, she was replaced by former South Africa men's international Rhett Halkett.

The Hockeyroos have had a period of change over the past two years. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"I think we are more than capable of playing in the finals for a medal," Nobbs said.

"Rhett comes from a bit of a European background, so we've changed up how we've played in the past year.

"This year in itself has been enough stress for the next four years or the last four years because we've had to play Pro League, qualify for this World Cup, change our structure, change our way of play.

The Hockeyroos celebrate a penalty shootout win over the Netherlands, to secure a spot in next year's FIH Pro League. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"So it has been a crazy journey, but I think all of those things give you experience and evidence leading into big tournaments like this that you can lean on."

Growing the game

The interest in hockey is at a different level in Europe, particularly in Belgium and the Netherlands, and it is something Henderson is embracing.

"Just walking around the streets, you're seeing billboards, you're seeing [players] on bus stops," Henderson said.

"I think the general population know more about the game."

Henderson has also started to make a name for himself in India, another hockey hotbed, after fetching the highest price at the Hockey India League auction last year — around $71,500.

While not in the same ballpark as the IPL, it is a lucrative league for Australians, who usually juggle studying or work alongside playing.

"I was actually in the gym with a few of my teammates when [the auction] was going down," Henderson said.

"It was more just shock. I'd only played 11 international games at that stage. And I think just showed potentially what people think I can do.

"The team obviously were very successful, we won a tournament. It was such a valuable experience for me. You can't put a price tag on that."

Henderson and Nobbs also play in Australia's domestic league, Hockey One, and hope to see its continued growth.

"It's finally a competition that gets talked about, I think, internationally and really good players from abroad wanting to come over and be part of that competition," Nobbs said.

"We obviously compete with a lot of sports in Australia, cricket, soccer, netball, everything.

"So to have a product like that growing and something exciting that young kids can come and watch is definitely a good thing."

World.title: What went wrong for the Suns this year and how 2027 can be much better
World.content:
Sometimes an essay is needed to describe what has happened on the footy field. Sometimes a book will only start to scratch the surface.

But sometimes a single word will do it best. As the Gold Coast Suns filtered off a frigid Manuka Oval after beating GWS, one word seemed to sum up the mood in a nutshell: Finally.

For the first time since May 15, the Suns had entered the winner's circle. At the time of their last win, the Suns sat fourth on the ladder, with many believing they were poised for a real shot at a deep finals run.

But as the weeks drew shorter and the nights colder, their hopes faded.

By the start of July, the hopes of a top-four finish had effectively vanished. Two weeks later, their finals hopes were on life support. By the end of the month, even the wildcard spots were taken off the table.

Damien Hardwick summed up the year via the slightly misheard words of one of the big four of American thrash metal.

"There's a great line by Metallica that I'm going to butcher, where 'sometimes you can see the light at the end of the tunnel, but it's a freight train coming the other way'. That's how it's felt this year. That's the reality of it," he said.

Despite the season being lost, both Hardwick and his playing staff were overjoyed with the win.

"It's been … it's been a while. The boys were really hungry for a win today and I thought we brought the spirit and it was great to sing that song again," Suns star Matt Rowell told ABC Sport after the win over GWS.

For one week, everything worked as it should for the side many thought to be a premiership contender. The win wasn't just one in isolation, it also practically ended the season for their Expansion Cup rivals the Giants.

For both sides, the hope is that a small slice of pain in 2026 will set them up for success in 2027. But to do so, there has to be an understanding of what exactly went wrong.

Hardwick's hard year with Gold Coast

Of all the jobs in elite football, that of the senior club coach may be the most coveted and the most stressful. The coach operates as not only a leader to the players but also a figurehead for the club.

It's a job that many, if not most, of the league's assistant coaches and football staffers aspire to. But for roughly every 10 aspirants to the ranks, there's only ever one opening. Those lucky enough to sit in the big chair often do so after mentoring by a few others.

Of all the jobs in elite football, that of the senior club coach may be the most coveted, and the most stressful. The coach operates as not only a leader to the players but also a figurehead for the club.

It's a job that many, if not most, of the league's assistant coaches and football staffers aspire to. But for roughly every 10 aspirants to the ranks there's only ever one opening. Those lucky enough to sit in the big chair often do so after a few others have mentored them.

Few coaches have been more highly credentialed in recent years than Hardwick. Beyond the three flags the Tigers won under his guidance, his impact across the league is clear.

While Hardwick served an apprenticeship under a more kick-mark style operator in Alistair Clarkson, his own method differed to that of former co-worker Chris Fagan. Instead, the influence of Hardwick is best seen through the defensive-first-yet-free-flowing styles exhibited by Collingwood and GWS under former Hardwick assistants Craig McRae and Adam Kingsley.

Hardwick's teams have an idiosyncratic stylistic footprint. Under his reign at Richmond, the Tigers overhauled teams with chaos, not control. The side often lost the marking battle but played surge football, running on adrenaline and enthusiasm. Instead of a side built on winning and scoring from clearances, their drive came from scoring on the intercept.

McRae and Kingsley, alongside West Coast's Andrew McQualter, have regularly influenced proceedings in September. The Hardwick school sits as a counterbalance to the way that sides such as Brisbane pick through defences by controlling the ball.

Despite being so influential to how football is played in 2026, Hardwick is quick to note that this may not have been his finest year.

"I feel I haven't had my best year as a coach with regard to bending a little bit of my system of how we want to play," he said. "So those realisations are very, very important. And these are the things that actually your greatest growth comes from."

In the wake of teams inspired by the control-heavy game styles influenced by Alistair Clarkson's Hawthorn sides, Tigerball was risky, dangerous and exciting.

All good coaches evolve over time. And all good "brands" are strategised against and countered. Football is not a solved game with a perfect way to play.

The developing Suns Hardwick inherited were quite different from the Tigers he left. Instead of building from a rock-solid counterattacking defensive unit, they led with the contested, stoppage game the premiership Tigers largely eschewed.

In 2025, Hardwick bent to accommodate both strands, leaning on rising stars Anderson, Rowell, Miller and Humphries to dominate in the middle and using Noble, Rioli and Jeffrey to provide drive on the counterattack.

There were clear parts of the game plan that held strong across both seasons. Gold Coast continued to lean on handball more than most and played into chaotic situations.

But the other part of the balance, that of the stoppage game, fell away.

Last year, the Suns finished +3.3 in clearance differential and third in the league for scoring differential from stoppages.

This year — with a group in flux with early season injuries to Matt Rowell and the incorporation of Christian Petracca — the Suns sit last for clearance differential and fourth-worst for stoppage scoring differential.

Notably, the win in Canberra came in one of the hardest, most contested games of the season. The game was cold, wet and physical and played largely at ground level. The sides combined for just 96 marks all day — about half of the average game this year.

"We love the wet weather footy, as you can tell, and I think it really suited us today," midfielder Bodhi Uwland told ABC Sport post-game.

ABC AFL Daily podcast Corbin Middlemas and Ben Cameron are joined by a rotating cast of AFL legends, including some of the sharpest minds in the game, to pull apart the biggest stories in Aussie Rules.

"We like being a contested team, that surge mentality, like getting the ball forward. And I think we really showed that today and we're able to really adapt to the conditions."

The Suns played for territory first and results later in Canberra. Despite dominating hitouts and clearances, the Giants still scored more from stoppage. But the high defensive wall that the Suns were able to establish helped the Suns re-enter the winner's circle.

Reigning Brownlow Medallist Rowell led the way for the Suns with one of the finest games imaginable in tough conditions. Despite the number of accolades he has already accumulated in his short career, the game may have been one of his best yet.

"That's one of the best performances I've seen from Rowell, to be honest, like, especially from behind the ball. Seeing him u-turning out of stoppage, shrugging tackles and just getting it forward … and he did it so consistently throughout the game. It was an amazing performance." Uwland said.

It wasn't just his teammates who were effusive about his effort.

"Yeah, he's a difference maker. It's a pleasure to have a guy like that in our footy club who, you see, the way the game plays today." Hardwick added.

"You know, it's 40-odd possessions, 22 contested, I think 18 tackles and 12 clearances as well. It's just one of those games you go, 'Wow'.

"You know, they're video game numbers, but he revels in those conditions. You know, that's the way he plays the game and it's such a pleasure to watch those players that give absolutely everything."

Rowell's preseason Origin injury threw the Suns' midfield balance off at the start of the season and left the side looking for what was their best look through the middle as the season developed. The Suns are blessed with highly capable players at the contest, with more bodies than opportunities most weeks.

The game in Canberra was a hint of what it could look like when it worked for the Suns.

Despite reports in the media of a loss of connection in recent weeks, at least in wake of the win the connection between coach and group seemed to be growing and evolving through the adversity.

"We haven't had the year we've wanted, but I think he's been really impressed by the way we've kept our spirit as a group," Rowell said.

"Even though we can't make finals, we've still got a lot of pride as a group. I think that really showed today. Yeah, Dimma's (Hardwick's) connection with the group is growing each game."

Suns keen to rise in 2027

In the wake of the Canberra game, attention for both sides turned, at least a little, to next season. The balance between running out a season where a premiership is an impossible task and preparing for the next one is a tough balance to strike for all teams.

"Yeah (2027 starts now). We have spoken about that. You look at Sydney — a great example from last year. You know, they had a disappointing year, much like we have this year, and they sort of went to work on some things. Look where they are now." Hardwick said after the game.

"That was our challenge. We spoke to the players about it. Noah and his leaders have just been absolutely leading the charge in that space."

Given how few competitive games there are each year, not a single one needs to be wasted. A flag is always the goal for each of the league's 18 clubs, even if it's not this year's.

Having shown the quality to win a final last year, Gold Coast's prospects of recovery look reasonably bright. Roughly half of the teams in the 18-team era to win a final then dip to double-digit ladder placings returned to finals the following year.

Most of the rest took two years to get back, with Melbourne and Collingwood grabbing the 2021 and 2023 flags. Most encouragingly, only three times since 2012 has a finals-winning team immediately crashed down the ladder and failed to recover at all.

These gap years have almost become routine as footy becomes ever more even and competitive. Almost every year since 2020, at least one side has found itself dipping and another recovering from such a dip.

The one slight pause for both the Suns and Giants is the relatively low placement of all four of the Hardwick-styled teams in 2026. Of the four, only McRae's Pies will play finals, entering via the wildcard round. As always, the question will be whether that style of play is conducive to winning football in 2026 and beyond, or whether the next evolution is upon us already.

Still, the Gold Coast list might be the most talented in the league. If they can get the strategic balance right, and a little luck to fall their way, the sky is the limit for this Suns group.

World.title: Freo locks up minor premiership after downing Crows in thriller
World.content:
Jye Amiss has kicked five goals and Caleb Serong played a starring role as Fremantle snared just the second minor premiership in the club's history with a 24-point win over Adelaide in Perth.

Scores were level early in the final quarter of Friday night's blockbuster following Crows forward Riley Thilthorpe's second goal of the night.

But buoyed by a thundering 55,010-strong crowd, Fremantle did what it has done all season — blowing its rival off the park with a devastating burst.

Michael Frederick started the run when he nailed a tough set shot after being tackled high.

Jye Amiss (centre) kicked 5.1 in the win while Josh Treacy (right) took six contested marks. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Although Josh Treacy, Luke Jackson and Andrew Brayshaw missed their shots after that, Amiss bobbed up for his fifth goal of the night by snapping from the goalsquare.

And when Isaiah Dudley dodged and weaved his way through three Crows players before unleashing a successful snap, the margin was 22 points and it was game over.

Dockers ruckman Mason Cox rubbed it in by roughing up an opponent and then pointing to the scoreboard after kicking a goal in the dying minutes of the 16.16 (112) to 13.10 (88) win.

The triumph boosted Fremantle's record to 19-3, securing the club a second minor premiership to go with their 2013 efforts.

It also meant Fremantle will end the home-and-away season with a perfect 12-0 record at Perth Stadium.

Adelaide (14-8) now faces a huge battle to snare a top-four berth, with the loss even leaving them vulnerable to slipping into the dreaded wildcard spots from seventh to 10th.

Amiss finished with 5.1 in a powerful display, Josh Treacy was huge with six contested marks but a wayward 1.4, Dudley kicked three goals, while Serong was influential with 29 disposals, 12 clearances, 536m gained and two goals.

Crows playmaker Izak Rankine racked up a monster 14 disposals in the opening term on the way to 39 possessions, 10 clearances, 717m gained and one goal.

Adelaide star Izak Rankine finished the match with a game-high 39 disposals. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Adelaide had an interesting lead-in to the match, with players forced to evacuate their hotel just hours before bounce down due to a fire alarm going off in their hotel.

Amiss missed an early set shot sitter from 15m out as Adelaide skipped out to a two-goal lead.

But Amiss soon made amends, nailing three other set shots for the term — from 50m, 40m and 35m — to give Fremantle a 13-point edge by quarter time.

Fremantle led by just five points at half-time, and the third quarter was a rollercoaster ride featuring four lead changes and five occasions when the scores were even.

Fremantle skipper Alex Pearce suffered a huge scare when his heavily-strapped left knee hyper-extend during a collision, leaving him hobbled for the next couple of minutes.

The action was fierce and fast, but it was Fremantle who produced more of the memorable moments.

Treacy hurt himself while completing a team-lifting tackle on Max Michalanney.

The Fremantle powerhouse dusted himself off after a few deep breaths and kicked a goal moments later.

Serong nailed a goal from just inside the centre square following a dazzling series of handballs from the Dockers.

And when Brayshaw dribbled one through with the outside of his right boot, Fremantle turned for home with a seven-point edge.

The Dockers kicked five goals to three in a powerful final term to wrap up top spot on the ladder with one round to spare.

AAP

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all of Friday night's action as it happened.

World.title: Quick hits: Tempers flare as Aussies wilt, Starc's heart-in-mouth moment
World.content:
Mitchell Starc vents his frustration at a Bangladeshi batter, while a star is born on treacherous Darwin turf.

Here are the quick hits from another torrid day for Australia against Bangladesh.

1. Smith grounds one

Smith downed a chance in the morning session. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

There is toiling, and then there is whatever the Australian bowlers were doing during the first session of day two.

The much-vaunted Aussie quartet, with Cam Green and Beau Webster in support, combined for just a single wicket during the opening two hours of play.

The ball found its way past Bangladeshi willow on a few occasions, but for the most part, chances were at a premium.

So, it was far from an ideal time for the usually so-reliable hands of slipper-supreme Steve Smith to let him down.

But with rookie opener Tanzid Hasan already past 50 and Australia having just taken their first wicket of the day, Smith floored one.

Tanzid edged a Nathan Lyon delivery into the elbow of Alex Carey, the ball ricocheted towards slip, and a diving Smith was unable to gather cleanly.

It was far from a sitter, but one Smith will be disappointed to have missed.

Tanzid given a life on 62.

2. Tanzid Hasan's maiden Test ton

Coming into this series, there were serious questions surrounding Bangladesh's opening pair, with the Tigers having struggled to nail down a reliable top two in recent years.

Up steps Tanzid Hasan, the 25-year-old opener playing just his second Test match.

Tanzid was considered and composed against the much-vaunted Australian attack, providing the foundation for a brilliant Bangladeshi team effort.

Tanzid completed a sparkling maiden century on day two. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

He already had an ODI century to his name, having scored 107 against Pakistan in Mirpur in March, and he also has scored five first class tons for an average of 39.60.

Talk about nervous 90s, though.

First, Pat Cummins whacked the 25-year-old on the arm with a vicious, 140km/h bouncer.

Then, Tanzid almost holed out to the substitute fielder at long off when on 96, skying a Lyon slower ball with a lofted drive that plugged in the outfield after falling just short of the fielder.

He moved to 99 with a neat clip, and then celebrated his century with a push down the ground off Lyon, a superb hundred celebrated accordingly.

3. The Darwin turf bites at the Australians

Starc got tangled in the turf while taking a catch. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

However, Tanzid was unable to turn his maiden Test ton into a truly big one, holing out to Lyon only a matter of balls later.

But Australian hearts were in Australian mouths as Mitchell Starc slid to make the catch and then flipped over ungainfully.

Starc, wincing as he got up, looked to be in some discomfort, and the replays showed that the Darwin turf may have been to blame.

The fast-bowler's knee had been caught in the grass, with a cloud of dust and thatch of grass disengaging from the ground.

Starc was tangled up awkwardly by the Darwin turf. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Thankfully, Starc appeared to recover well, but it wasn't the first time the Marrara Stadium outfield had appeared a little loose, with the ever-energetic Marnus Labuscagne ripping out his fair share of greenery.

With the surface only likely to disintegrate more dramatically over the coming three days, both teams should be wary of not getting twisted up in the outfield.

4. Steve Smith's hat-trick of slip catches

Australia desperately needed something to happen to interrupt the Bangladesh momentum — and it arrived with the new ball.

Josh Hazlewood, Mitch Starc and then Pat Cummins all extracted edges with the new pill, claiming the wickets of Hossain Shanto (84), Litton Das (0) and Mushfiqur Rahim (36) as Bangladesh crumbled from 3-297 to 6-308.

And all three of them were caught by Steve Smith at second slip, making dramatic amends for his earlier fumble.

That trio of catches put Smith level with Joe Root with 218 catches, the most ever by a non-wicketkeeper in Test cricket.

Australia's pacemen are worth their weight in gold, but Smith certainly pays his way in the field to help them out.

5. 'Get off the wicket!'

Tempers flared late on it Darwin. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

With that new-ball blitz an increasingly distant memory, and with the Australian bowlers beginning to wilt in the late Darwin sun, the hosts' frustration was on full display late in the evening session.

Into the 103rd over of the innings, Starc was bowling to all-rounder Mehidy, who was well set and intent on seeing the day through.

Mehidy set off for a single and came very close to colliding with the Australian spearhead.

Starc wasn't impressed.

"It's my follow through, not your follow through. Get off the wicket," Starc could be heard saying through the stump mic.

"I didn't see!" Mehidy could be heard saying during the next over, still perhaps apologetic about the near-collision.

But of course, the all-rounder shouldn't be taking the altercation personally.

The Australians' frustration was all of their own making.

6. You call that a knife?

Nathan Lyon used a knife to clean his spikes. (Supplied: Fox Sports)

There's nothing worse as an athlete than getting mud or grass caught between your cleats or spikes.

Nathan Lyon clearly had this issue during the second session, when going through his usual array of warm ups and stretches on the boundary at Marrara Oval.

But what can you do about it when in the middle of a Test match as you're about to prepare for a bowling spell?

Turns out, you ask someone in the kitchen if they have a spare a butter knife they don't mind soiling with some outfield dirt.

Much like the Northern Territory's best known international export, Crocodile Dundee, one can almost imagine one of the locals querying Lyon's choice of implement with quips like "you call that a knife …"

World.title: NRL top eight all but locked in after Souths win
World.content:
Canterbury have been left needing a minor miracle to make the NRL's top eight after succumbing to a 22-6 defeat at the hands of South Sydney.

Led by a rampaging David Fifita, the Rabbitohs took a major step towards returning to the finals for the first time since 2022 with a workmanlike victory at Stadium Australia on Friday night.

But the Bulldogs' hopes of featuring in September are all but over.

Should North Queensland see off Parramatta on Saturday, Cameron Ciraldo's men will be four points adrift of the finals places with just three full rounds of the regular season left to play.

Canterbury take on St George Illawarra, Penrith and Brisbane to round out their campaign and will no doubt look back on this loss to Souths as a game that got away.

Stephen Crichton, Jethro Rinakama, Lachlan Galvin and Jacob Preston were all either held up or stopped short of the line in the first half.

And as South Sydney, who moved up to sixth, pulled away in the second half, the Bulldogs didn't have the firepower to go with them.

The Rabbitohs withstood plenty of early pressure but struck in the 23rd minute when Fifita, who finished with 144m and six tackle busts, pounced on a Cody Walker grubberkick.

Walker was the conductor for their second as the Bunnies shifted from right to left, the veteran playmaker sending Tallis Duncan through a hole to set up Alex Johnston.

The Rabbitohs were far too clinical for the wasteful Bulldogs. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

Souths led 10-0 at halftime after Preston was penalised for a double movement and they moved out of touching distance from the restart.

Dogs hooker Bailey Hayward dropped the kick-off and Duncan crashed over on the left edge on the ensuing set.

Rinakama trudged off with a knee issue soon afterwards and the Bunnies pushed ahead further through winger Campbell Graham.

Missing a recognised goalkicker — Souths converted just one of their five tries — kept Canterbury alive though.

Enari Tuala finally scored on the hour mark but Canterbury's attack didn't have the spark to trouble Wayne Bennett's side, who completed the win with a well-deserved Matt Dufty try two minutes from fulltime.

Earlier, Manly's 'Fozball' fever dream is officially over after the Dolphins became the first team to hold the Sea Eagles scoreless at Brookvale Oval in 33 years.

In a match that failed to reach any real heights, the Dolphins had enough strike to pull away late and win 22-0, leapfrogging them above Cronulla into fourth spot.

The Dolphins' win did come at some cost, with in-form second-rower Connelly Lemuelu limping from the field in the second half with a hamstring injury.

But the story of the night was the Sea Eagles, whose finals hopes are now virtually over after six straight losses.

AAP
